payload.description:
## Context

Tier 1 of basicly-ze8z: deterministic, so the engine should assert it rather than an operator remember it.

Three concrete items, each currently memory-only or memory-assisted:

- **FORCE_COLOR** - when set, it breaks the piped-output test and fails pre-push on an otherwise clean tree. **Zero mentions anywhere in the repo**: this is pure operator memory. `basicly loop preflight` or `basicly status` should report it, and the test that cares should be hermetic against it.
- **Node resolution in non-interactive shells** - on WSL, `npx` resolves to a Windows node in a non-interactive shell, so the markdownlint hook picks the wrong binary. The `node` skill documents the workaround; the hook should resolve its own interpreter instead, the way basicly-dukb made the Claude hook resolve its own script path.
- **The out-of-loop export scrub** - every `br` write re-adds `source_repo_path` to every record on re-export. Loop landings scrub automatically; a direct `br` write does not, so an operator must remember to call `basicly.br.scrub_export` before staging `.beads/`. Make the write path scrub, or make the pre-commit gate do it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an environment carrying any of these hazards when a run or a commit is attempted then the engine reports or corrects it, and no step requires an operator to have learned it first
payload.title: Make the out-of-loop tracker export scrub automatic

payload.text:
[harness-info] CORRECTION, 2026-08-01, owner-prompted. Two of the three items on this bead were
filed from unverified operator memory and one of them is not a real hazard. Measured on this machine
immediately after filing:

- `FORCE_COLOR` is **UNSET**, and was never set or unset by any command in the session that filed
  this bead. It appeared only in an operator's notes. **Drop it** unless someone can produce the
  failing run: the note claims it fails the piped-output test and pre-push, but nothing here
  reproduces that, and building an assertion for an unreproduced hazard is cost without evidence.
  If it is worth anything it is a hermetic-test question (the test should not care what the
  environment sets), not a preflight check.
- **Node resolution needs no workaround here either.** `which node npx` resolves to
  `<redacted:posix-home-path>,npx}` (v24.18.0) with **no PATH manipulation**, and
  `npx --yes markdownlint-cli2` runs clean without it. The operator had been prepending an nvm path
  to every commit for nothing - doubly so, because shell env does not persist between tool calls, so
  the export never reached the next command anyway. The original WSL observation may still hold on a
  machine with no local node install, so this needs a *reproduction on such a machine* before any
  code is written, not a note repeated.

What survives, and it is the only item with evidence behind it: **the out-of-loop export scrub.**
Every `br` write re-adds `source_repo_path` to every record on re-export; loop landings scrub
automatically, a direct write does not, and the operator remembers. That one is reproducible on
demand and is worth making automatic.

The general lesson, which is the point of the parent epic: an operator note is a *hypothesis about
the environment*. Externalizing it unmeasured just moves an unverified claim from memory into code,
where it costs a gate and a test to maintain. Measure first, then externalize what survives - see
[[closed-blocker-is-not-a-working-gate]] for the same error made against a closed bead.

payload.description: Discovered 2026-07-20 landing basicly-5wpn through the harness loop. At the build->verify landing advance, the engine committed accumulated base .beads dirt directly to base main (a chore(beads) sync commit), then rebased the harness branch onto the new base. The harness branch carries its own tracked .beads/issues.jsonl snapshot (from the provisioning claim commit) of the SAME bead the base commit just rewrote, so the rebase hits a one-line conflict on that issue in issues.jsonl. It recurs every rework attempt (each landing re-flushes the mutated DB, producing a new divergent line) and escalated at the rework cap, leaving TWO redundant chore(beads) commits on main plus a dirty base tree and the code stranded uncommitted in the worktree. Matches the beads-tracker-vs-loop-worktrees hazard (never commit issues.jsonl on a harness branch). Repro: claim+classify a leaf task, let provisioning leave base .beads dirty, run loop advance to land. Fix direction: before rebasing the harness branch, reset/checkout the branch's .beads/issues.jsonl to base (or exclude it from the branch entirely so only the redirect-shared DB carries tracker state), and ensure base .beads is committed cleanly before the rebase rather than mid-landing. Recovered 5wpn via the sanctioned base-checkout path.
payload.title: Loop landing conflicts on tracker state when base .beads is dirty at land time

payload.text: Root-cause correction (my original description was wrong). Reproduced with real git: the failure was NOT an issues.jsonl merge conflict. The agent's work was never committed on the harness branch, so merge_worktree's git rebase aborted with 'cannot rebase: you have unstaged changes' — a non-zero exit that line 185 misclassified as 'rebase-conflicts'. With the work committed, rebasing onto a tracker-advanced base succeeds cleanly (the code commit does not touch .beads, and base already carries the advanced tracker line). Confirmed CASE A (dirty->abort) vs CASE B (committed->clean rebase). Two real defects fixed: (1) no worktree-readiness precondition before rebasing; (2) an operator-fixable state burned rework and escalated with a misleading message. Fix: _worktree_land_readiness bails before touching base with a clear 'commit the work on <branch>' message when the tree is dirty or the branch has no commits ahead; _verify_and_land and merge_queue treat 'not-ready' as a plain block, not a rework attempt. Verified against real git for dirty/committed/empty/untracked-only cases; new regression tests in test_merge.py; harness-loop skill now tells the operator to commit on the branch before advancing.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the skill eval harness when it runs then it reports per-skill trigger accuracy and behavioral lift as an actionable pass-fail report a deliberately removed skill is caught and the case format plus how to add one per skill is documented with the full gate suite green
payload.description:
We distribute a catalog of skills (core + technology-scoped) but have NO evidence any of them actually do their job: whether a skill reliably TRIGGERS on the situations its description claims, and whether loading it measurably IMPROVES the agent's output vs not having it. Without evals we cannot tell a working skill from dead weight, catch a regression when a skill is edited, or justify what ships in the always-on baseline.

Goal: add an eval harness plus per-skill eval cases that measure (a) trigger accuracy (does the skill fire when it should and stay quiet when it should not) and (b) behavioral lift (does the guidance change the outcome on representative tasks). Reference approach to adapt: https://github.com/addyosmani/agent-skills/tree/main/evals (eval cases per skill run against a model).

Scope to decide when picked up: eval file format and where cases live in the catalog; a basicly command to run them (and optionally a CI gate); which skills get cases first (start with the core universal skills and the highest-value tech skills); how to score trigger vs lift; cost/model controls so the suite is affordable to run.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An eval harness exists and is documented; at least the core universal skills have eval cases covering trigger accuracy and behavioral lift.
- Running the evals produces a pass/fail (or scored) report a human can act on; a deliberately broken/removed skill is caught.
- The format and how to add a case per skill are documented (catalog-authoring or a dedicated doc). Full gate suite passes.
payload.title: Skill evals: prove distributed skills actually change agent behavior

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a lane escalated at its rework cap when a human answers the escalation with a retry then exactly one further attempt is permitted for that gate on that node without changing the repo-wide cap and with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Found in the basicly-kjc5.22 dogfood run (feature basicly-hxnf, 2026-07-26).

Lane `basicly-hxnf.1` hit the merge rework cap, so the supervisor escalated it to the decision
queue asking "retry, re-dispatch, or park?". The operator answered `retry` with evidence that the
gate failure was not the lane's work. **The answer cannot be carried out.**

`policy.record_rework` only ever increments and `policy.rework_attempts` only reads; there is no
clear, reset, or decrement anywhere, and `basicly policy rework` exposes only `--record`. So the
counter stays at the cap, and the next landing attempt escalates again immediately. The queue item
is answered but the lane cannot move.

The operator's only levers are both wrong: raise `[policy] max_rework` in config, which loosens
the cap for *every* node in the repo, or land the lane by hand, which is exactly what
basicly-kjc5.22's acceptance criterion forbids. The escalation therefore offers three choices and
implements none of them.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Let a lane fail its landing gate until `rework: N/N attempts - ESCALATE (cap reached)`.
2. `basicly loop answer <decision-id> "retry"` — succeeds.
3. `basicly loop advance <lane>` — blocks and re-escalates at once; `basicly policy rework <lane> --gate merge` still reports the cap.
4. Expected: an answered `retry` lets exactly one further attempt through, without changing the repo-wide cap.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane escalated at its rework cap when a human answers the escalation with a retry then exactly one further attempt is permitted for that gate on that node without changing the repo-wide cap and with tests

## Scope

- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `src/basicly/decisions.py`
payload.title: An answered retry escalation cannot be acted on because nothing clears the rework counter

Found in the basicly-kjc5.22 dogfood run (feature basicly-hxnf, 2026-07-26).

Lane `basicly-hxnf.1`'s landing failed its `verify full` gate on
`tests/test_integration_loop.py::test_landing_blocks_instead_of_reworking_an_uncommitted_worktree`,
which failed with the known `br` clock defect (`updated_at: cannot be before created_at`). The
lane's own commit was three documentation files under `.basicly/core/skills/python/` and its two
projections — it cannot affect that test. Re-running the test in the lane's own worktree
immediately afterwards: 1 fail, 2 passes, no change in between.

The harness charged the lane a rework attempt for it, reached the cap, and escalated it to a human.
So a pre-existing upstream flake is scored exactly like a merit failure, and it cost the run its
acceptance criterion — two of three lanes landed unattended, the third was escalated for something
it did not do.

This is the harness-side half of the tracker defect that `basicly-vkh0` exists to remove; filing it
separately because the fix is different. `vkh0` stops the flake existing. This bead is about the
engine having no way to tell "the gate is unreliable" from "the work is wrong", so a flake silently
consumes a lane's bounded rework budget.

Design note: `basicly-kjc5.52` (fingerprint the environment behind a gate result) is adjacent — a
gate result that carries provenance is what would let a re-run be compared rather than merely
repeated.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Land a lane whose verify suite contains a test that fails intermittently for reasons unrelated to the lane's diff.
2. Observe `routed: <lane> -> decision - merge failed: verify full failed: pytest (rework 1/1)`.
3. Re-run the failing test unchanged — it passes.
4. Expected: a gate failure that does not reproduce is not charged against the lane's rework budget.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane whose verify gate fails on a check that passes when re-run unchanged when the landing is triaged then the failure is distinguished from a merit failure and does not consume the lane's rework budget with tests

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
payload.title: A flaky gate consumes a lane's rework budget as if the work were wrong

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the tracker stamps created_at at whole second resolution from a separate process when the wait meter is asserted under full suite load then the assertion tolerates a one second under-read as well as an over-read and does not fail the verify gate for clock granularity
payload.description:
## Problem

`_assert_interval` in `tests/test_integration_wait.py` guards only the upper side of the injected
wait offset. Its lower bound is bare:

```python
assert _WAITED_S <= waited_s <= _WAITED_S + elapsed_s + _SLACK_S
```

The meter computes `waited_s` as the harness clock (`policy._now`, monkeypatched to
`time.time() + 600`) minus the `created_at` that the **separate `br` process** stamped. The lower
bound therefore asserts that br's stamp never lands ahead of this process's `time.time()`. With
whole-second resolution across two processes under load, it can, and the interval reads one second
short.

The docstring already acknowledges the truncation ("the meter may read a second or two over") but
draws the conclusion in one direction only. basicly-o7z5 fixed the upper bound for the symmetric
reason - a loaded machine made two real br round-trips exceed a flat five-second slack. The lower
bound is the same defect class left in place.

This matters beyond a red suite: a flaky gate consumes a lane's rework budget as if the work were
wrong, which is exactly what basicly-55yh exists to prevent. A flake inside the `verify` gate is
therefore a factory-reliability defect, not merely a test annoyance.

## Steps to Reproduce

Observed on main at 7db0143 during `basicly verify --mode full`:

```
assert 600 <= 599
E       assert _WAITED_S <= waited_s <= _WAITED_S + elapsed_s + _SLACK_S
tests/test_integration_wait.py:59: AssertionError
FAILED tests/test_integration_wait.py::test_a_queued_decision_wait_round_trips_through_the_real_tracker
1 failed, 1997 passed in 40.39s
```

Load-dependent, so it does not reproduce in isolation:

- the same test alone, five consecutive runs: 5 passed, 0 failed
- `uv run pytest -q -n 4` immediately afterwards on the same tree: 1998 passed

So the tree is green and the failure is intermittent under the four-worker full-suite load that the
`pytest` verify check actually uses.

Expected - the assertion tolerates the tracker's whole-second stamp resolution in both directions,
the way its upper bound already tolerates real br round-trip cost, so a correct meter cannot fail
the gate on clock granularity.

## Scope

- tests/test_integration_wait.py

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the tracker stamps created_at at whole-second resolution from a separate process when the
  wait meter is asserted under full-suite load then the assertion tolerates a one-second
  under-read as well as an over-read and does not fail the verify gate for clock granularity
payload.title: The wait meter integration test can fail the verify gate on whole second clock granularity

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given an active grant that covers ship and is not spend halted when a lights out precondition is violated elsewhere in the session then the refusal names the violated precondition and the issue it belongs to rather than presenting a bare confirmation request, and given no grant at all then the output is unchanged, with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Found by the 2026-07-31 session retro. Shipping `basicly-kjc5.58` under an active L3 grant on
`basicly-kjc5` demanded a confirm code, while two earlier beads the same session shipped with
`delegated under L3 grant`. The behaviour is CORRECT - `policy._grant_approval` requires
`lights_out_violations` to be empty for a ship, the preconditions are session-wide, and the measured
cause was `rework escalation on basicly-kjc5.56 (gate verify: 2/2)`, a wrinkle in a sibling bead
elsewhere in the epic's 55-issue session. D3 deliberately drops ship back to a human on any wrinkle.

The defect is that the refusal is **silent about why**. `_grant_approval` returns `None` and the
caller mints a confirm challenge, so the operator sees only `CONFIRMATION REQUIRED` with no
indication that a grant existed, covered the checkpoint, was not spend-halted, and was declined for a
specific reason in a different issue. Diagnosing it took several tool calls reading `policy.py` and
then calling `lights_out_violations` by hand.

This will recur on every child ship under any epic carrying an unresolved wrinkle, which for
`basicly-kjc5` is every remaining bead in the model-tier chain.

Related precedent for the fix's shape: the deterministic grant refusals in `_grant_refusal` already
return an explanatory string rather than a bare failure, so the module already has the idiom.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Have an active L3 grant on an epic root and a rework escalation on any child in that session.
- Run `basicly loop run <other-child> --root <epic>` to the ship checkpoint.
- Observed: `checkpoint ship: CONFIRMATION REQUIRED` with no reason, and nothing indicating a grant
  was present and declined. Expected: the output names the violated lights-out precondition and the
  issue it belongs to, so the operator can either fix it or knowingly relay the code.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an active grant that covers ship and is not spend-halted when a lights-out precondition is
  violated elsewhere in the session then the refusal names the violated precondition and the issue it
  belongs to rather than presenting a bare confirmation request, and given no grant at all then the
  output is unchanged, with tests
payload.title: Name the violated precondition when a grant declines a ship

payload.description:
tests/test_rubrics.py::test_evaluate_deterministic_maps_exit_code fails on windows-latest CI. evaluate_deterministic splits the check command with shlex.split (posix), and the test embeds sys.executable, which on Windows is a backslash path (<redacted:windows-drive-path>). POSIX shlex treats backslash as an escape and mangles the path, so python is not found, the check exits non-zero, and the YES assertion fails. It is deterministic on Windows, not flaky.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Run pytest on Windows: tests/test_rubrics.py::test_evaluate_deterministic_maps_exit_code.
- The ok command {sys.executable} -c pass shlex-splits to a mangled path and exits non-zero.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The test builds the python path with forward slashes (Path(sys.executable).as_posix()) so posix shlex.split does not mangle it and Windows still accepts the executable path; both the YES and NO assertions hold on Windows and POSIX.
- No production change: realistic authored rubric commands use bare executables or forward-slash paths; a comment records why the test uses as_posix.
- pytest stays green on all platforms.
payload.title: Windows: deterministic rubric check test mangles the executable path via posix shlex

Fix:

2. Remove the redundant "Run pre-commit checks" CI step (full pre-push supersets it).

payload.description:
Retro finding from the 2026-07-18 foundry-followon session (basicly-58iu). While investigating br behavior (what `br lint` flags, a `br show --json` key name), throwaway beads were created and `br delete`d. `br delete` leaves a TOMBSTONE row in `.beads/issues.jsonl`, which the harness loop's tracker-state commit then captures — so junk probe beads reach the project tracker history unless pruned. `--ephemeral` is not a workaround: ephemeral beads do not export to JSONL but `br lint` also will not lint them (`total:0`), so a lint probe needs a real bead.

Put this guidance where the next agent authoring br probes will see it: add a short note to the `tool-br` skill (or a quirks fragment) covering the trap and the avoidance. There is no `br compact`/`purge`/`gc`; the only clean prune is `br delete <id> --hard --force` ("prunes tombstones from JSONL immediately").

## Acceptance Criteria

- The `tool-br` skill (or a quirks fragment) gains a concise note: investigating br by creating+deleting real beads leaves tombstones the loop commits; prune with `br delete --hard`, or avoid probing the live tracker; ephemeral beads are not linted.
- Authored as YAML catalog source and projected (`basicly skills-build`/`build`); `basicly catalog lint` and the relevant `*-check` gate pass.
- Fits within the always-on budget if placed in an applies_to:[all] fragment (prefer the on-demand tool-br skill to avoid baseline growth).

payload.description:
## Context

Session retro 2026-07-25, from the owner correcting `docs/agent-roster-design.md`. The design shipped a three-way cheap/mid/high tier split and the rule "route to the cheapest sufficient model", plus a persona justified as "cheap tokens replacing expensive ones". Two things were wrong and the owner corrected both:

1. Providers ship three-to-four capability classes with concrete names (claude: haiku, sonnet, opus, fable - opus the workhorse, fable the designer/architect; GPT: luna, terra, sol), so a three-way generic split does not map onto anything real.
2. A cheaper model is not cheaper work. Its mistakes come back as rework dispatches, extra review cycles, bounced merges and human attention, all charged to the same change - so the cheap dispatch routinely produces the expensive outcome. The unit of cost is total tokens plus wall-clock plus human interventions per landed correct change, never the price of one dispatch.

Root cause worth fixing in prose, not just in that document: nothing the harness distributes states the unit of cost or the tier ladder, so every agent that picks a model - and the roster design itself - reasons from per-dispatch sticker price. The correction is already argued in `docs/agent-roster-design.md` section R5 (basicly-eqp6); this bead is about distributing it as catalog guidance for the agents that act on it.

Constraint to respect: the always-on baseline is at its soft cap (see basicly-c5to), so this must be a scoped fragment or a skill section, not another `applies_to: [all]` fragment - or it has to pay for itself by trimming something.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a projected agent instruction surface when an agent chooses a model tier for dispatched work then the guidance states the four-tier ladder with its per-provider classes and the rule that cost is measured per landed correct change so a tier is chosen for reliability rather than sticker price with the projection gates green and the always-on budget not regressed

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/fragments/**`

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a lane branch whose diff adds a config schema entry and declares that key in the repos own config when the landing runs then it either lands or fails with a message naming the schema before declaration ordering rule and a regression test proves the bare unknown key refusal red first
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

Measured 2026-08-06 landing `basicly-o8p0`, whose single commit added a
`[worktree] append_only_paths` key to `config.CONFIG_SCHEMA` **and** declared it in
this repo's `basicly.toml`:

```
uv run basicly loop run basicly-o8p0 --root basicly-yc0x --autonomy L3
Error: basicly.toml: unknown key 'append_only_paths' in [worktree];
       [worktree] accepts base_branch, concurrency
basicly 0.6.0 refuses a config name it cannot honour rather than ignoring it ...
```

Observed — the landing died before verify ran. State at that moment:

| Where | `basicly.toml` has the key | `config.py` knows the key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| base checkout | no | no |
| lane worktree | **yes** | **yes** |

Expected — a lane that adds a config key and uses it can land.

## Cause: the landing runs the base engine against the worktree's config

`loop run` is invoked from the base checkout, so `uv run basicly` resolves the entry
point to **base's** `src/basicly/`, and that process then reads the **worktree's**
`basicly.toml` when it verifies the rebased tree. Base's schema has no
`append_only_paths`, and `basicly-1piy` — which landed hours earlier the same day —
made an unknown key a hard refusal rather than a silent ignore. So the pre-merge
engine validates the post-merge config and refuses it.

This is the same mechanism the `harness-loop` runbook already records — "`loop run`
imports `merge`/`verify`/`loop` from base at process start and never reloads them", so
a change to landing-scoring code is scored by the pre-merge version — but it is
**fatal rather than merely misleading**, and it reaches `config`, which every command
loads.

## Scope of the block

Any bead whose diff adds a `CONFIG_SCHEMA` entry and declares it in `basicly.toml`
cannot land in one commit. That is a standing tax on config-carrying work, and this
release ladder has several such beads ahead of it — `o486` (band calibration),
`3ifz` (learned parameters), and the roster's `[runner.roles]` section all add keys.

`basicly-1piy` is not wrong. Its commit message records that staged
warn-then-error was considered and rejected for consumers, with reasons that hold:
an engine that cannot honour a key and runs anyway is the defect it fixed. What the
note did not consider is **our own lanes**, where the reader and the file are one
commit apart by construction.

## Fix shape, cheapest first

- **Document the ordering rule and let it stand**: schema lands first, the
  declaration follows in a second landing. That is what unblocked `o8p0`, it costs one
  extra landing, and it needs no code. It belongs in the `harness-loop` skill beside
  the existing pre-merge-code warning, because nothing currently tells a lane author.
- **Or make the landing's config read tolerant of a key the merged tree introduces**:
  validate the worktree's config with the *worktree's* schema, since that is the code
  about to become base. This is the correct fix and the larger one — the landing would
  have to resolve the schema from the tree under test rather than from the running
  process.

Deliberately **not** proposed: relaxing `1piy`'s refusal to a warning. That reinstates
the defect it fixed, where the file states one behaviour and the engine performs
another.

## Regression test

Proven red first (`basicly-kjc5.49`): a lane branch whose diff adds a schema entry and
declares it must either land, or fail with a message that names the ordering rule —
not with a bare unknown-key refusal that reads as a config typo.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/verify.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`
- `.basicly/core/skills/harness-loop/skill.yaml`
payload.title: A lane that adds a config key and declares it cannot land in one commit

payload.text:
Reproduced a second time on 2026-08-06, landing basicly-lpsf:

routed: basicly-lpsf -> error - routing failed: basicly.toml: unknown key
'quiet_after' in [runner]; [runner] accepts agents, context_windows,
copilot_session_store, decider, default, default_tier, max_agent_processes,
runner_timeout, stall_after

Same shape as the basicly-o8p0 occurrence: the lane's single commit added quiet_after to
CONFIG_SCHEMA and declared it in basicly.toml, and the landing died before verify ran.
Two things this occurrence adds.

It cost more than one extra landing this time. The lane had already hit runner_timeout at
1800s having spent 25595734 tokens, so commit.salvage committed the worktree and the
refusal landed on top of a run that was already terminal. The failure was therefore
invisible until after the full spend, and the reported cause named a config key rather
than the ordering rule - which reads as a config typo, exactly as this bead predicts.

The workaround held and cost nothing, but by luck rather than design. The declaration was
deferred to a second landing and that was free because DEFAULT_QUIET_AFTER is already
1800.0, so the merged engine used the same value the declaration would have set. A key
whose declared value differed from its default would have landed with the wrong behaviour
for one landing, silently. Worth stating in the fix: the documented ordering rule is only
behaviour-neutral when the deferred declaration equals the schema default, and nothing
checks that.

Reproduced a THIRD time, 2026-08-07, on basicly-vkh0.19's landing. The lane added [tracker] mode = 'external' to basicly.toml in the same commit that taught CONFIG_SCHEMA the section, and loop advance refused it:

  Error: basicly.toml: unknown section 'tracker'; this file's sections are [catalog], [paths], [policy], [privacy], [runner], [verify], [worktree]

Mechanism confirmed: loop advance imports the engine from base at process start, so the version validating the config is the pre-merge one, and it refuses an unknown name by design. Same root as basicly-kjc5.57 (a change to the landing logic cannot take effect on the landing that merges it) - this is that shape applied to the config schema rather than to the landing code.

Workaround used, and its safety condition CHECKED rather than assumed this time: the declaration was deferred to a second commit on base (4e592a7) after the schema landed at 60ddf4d. The bead notes the workaround is only behaviour-neutral when the deferred value equals the schema default and that nothing checks it. Here it does - the declared value is 'external' and br.DEFAULT_TRACKER_MODE is MODE_EXTERNAL, confirmed by calling config.load_tracker_mode with the block present and absent and getting the same answer.

So the workaround held, but only because a human verified the equality the bead says is unchecked. A lane declaring a NON-default value cannot use it, and would need either a two-release deprecation or a schema that tolerates a forward-unknown section for one version. That is the choice this bead still has to make.

Reproduced a FOURTH time 2026-08-07, landing basicly-m4zv.2 on a three-lane supervised pass of basicly-m4zv. This is the first occurrence where the documented workaround does not apply, so the bead's 'cheapest first' fix shape is now insufficient on its own.

routed: basicly-m4zv.2 -> error - routing failed: basicly.toml: unknown key 'rank1_floor' in [catalog]; [catalog] accepts technologies

Same mechanism as basicly-o8p0 and basicly-lpsf: the single commit adds rank1_floor and rank1_floor_high_water to CONFIG_SCHEMA and declares both in basicly.toml, and the landing validates the worktree config with the pre-merge base engine.

WHAT IS NEW. The recorded workaround - schema lands first, declaration follows in a second landing - CANNOT be applied here, and this is the non-default-value case the previous note predicted had no route. Four repo-state tests require the declaration to be present, so a schema-only landing fails verify instead:

  tests/test_catalog_lint.py::test_the_shipped_catalog_clears_its_own_declared_floor
  tests/test_catalog_lint.py::test_the_declared_floor_leaves_headroom_below_the_measured_rate
  tests/test_cli.py::test_cli_catalog_verify_passes
  tests/test_cli.py::test_cli_build_verify_passes_on_clean_catalog

Both orderings therefore fail: declaration-in-lane dies before verify on the unknown key, schema-first dies at verify on those four tests. Measured directly - appending the two keys to base's basicly.toml and running 'uv run basicly check' from base reproduces the refusal in one command, and the lane worktree with schema and declaration together is green at 3103 passed.

COST. One re-dispatch of the lane (3 run records, 16,465,591 tokens total against a 14,036,709 first pass) plus a hand landing: rebase onto main, verify green in the worktree, git merge --no-ff from base, then 'basicly verify --mode full --issue' from base with the merged engine, which passed every gate and recorded verify=pass. Shipped normally after that.

CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX SHAPE. Documenting the ordering rule is no longer sufficient as the cheap option, because a bead whose tests assert the declared value has no ordering that works. The second option in this bead - validate the worktree's config with the worktree's schema, since that is the code about to become base - is now the only fix that covers this class.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a subprocess whose output is not decodable in the hosts preferred encoding when the engine captures it then the bytes are decoded as utf-8 explicitly and the text arrives intact or the failure raises rather than returning success with no output and given a test for it then the assertion is a real subprocess round trip with the encoding injected as test data rather than a parsed string on a utf-8 host
payload.description:
## Decision, 2026-08-06: adopted as a present defect, NOT as a section 12 requirement

The handover proposed this as a design rule for the replacement tracker. **Narrowed on
review**, and the narrowing is the point:

- **Adopted** for the call sites that exist today. They are real, verified, and one of them
  biases a decision we are about to take.
- **Declined** as a section 12 requirement. Section 4 puts the replacement in-process and pure
  Python, so its own ledger reads use no subprocess at all. Writing a process-boundary rule for
  a component whose design removes the boundary is a requirement with no subject - the kind of
  speculative rule this repo's core rules forbid.

So this is a bug against the current adapter, not a change to the tracker design. If the
replacement ever shells out, section 12 gains the rule then, with a subject.

## The mechanism - established, not inferred

Reproduced on Windows with Python 3.14 where the preferred encoding is `cp1252`, against a
child writing a word whose UTF-8 encoding contains byte `0x81`:

| Configuration | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `capture_output=True, text=True` | returncode 0, `stdout` is `None`, **nothing raised** |
| `stdout=PIPE, text=True` | raises `UnicodeDecodeError` - loud |
| `capture_output=True` then `.decode("utf-8")` | the text, intact |

With **both** pipes captured, `communicate()` decodes on reader *threads*, so the
`UnicodeDecodeError` kills a thread instead of propagating. The caller sees success and no
output. Piping only stdout raises properly - **the safe-looking, more convenient call is the
silent one**, which is why this survives review.

## Call sites, verified in this repo 2026-08-06

- `src/basicly/br.py:106-107` - the single seam the engine reaches the tracker through, in
  exactly the silent configuration: `subprocess.run([br_path, *args], cwd=repo_root,
  capture_output=True, text=True, check=False)`. **Every `run_br` call inherits it.**
- `src/basicly/tracker_surface.py:112` and `:127` - same configuration, on the telemetry path
  section 6 gates the schema decision on. **This is the sharpest consequence**: telemetry that
  silently under-reports would bias the decision, and the bias is invisible because the failure
  mode is an empty read that looks like an empty result.
- Seven files under `src/basicly/` pass `text=True` to a subprocess.
- `src/basicly/fleet.py` has **no** subprocess - it reads run records as files. So a future
  peer read would *introduce* this boundary where fleet does not have it, and `br.py:107` is
  the pattern a new reader would most likely be copied from.

## Why it is worth fixing now rather than waiting for cutover

The `br` adapter exists only until the replacement lands, which argues for leaving it. Against
that: `tracker_surface` is not the adapter, it is the instrument measuring the surface the
replacement will be designed against, and section 6 makes that measurement an input to the
schema decision. An instrument that fails silent is worse than no instrument, because a zero
reads as a measurement.

## The assertion this needs

**A test asserting on parsed strings cannot see this**, and neither can a suite that only runs
on a UTF-8 host. The assertion must be a **real subprocess round trip** with a non-UTF-8
preferred encoding injected as test data - per this repo's platform-hermetic rule, by injection
rather than by racing a host.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/br.py`
- `src/basicly/tracker_surface.py`
- `tests/test_br.py`
- `tests/test_tracker_surface.py`

payload.description:
Follow-up from the basicly-8z52 pilot (see docs/harness-eval.md). The pilot showed the skill-injection channel measurably changes behavior on a targeted discipline at trivial token cost, but was N=1, gates-off, and partly circular. Build the repeatable A/B eval so the whole-harness claim can be re-measured on demand.

Scope:
- A small fixed, versioned task set (5-8 tasks), each targeting one harness-enforced discipline, each shipping a HIDDEN objective check the arms never see (so a skill cannot trivially satisfy the scorer).
- A thin A/B driver: run each task under Arm H (harness: skills + gates + rework loop ON) vs Arm B (bare), reusing rubrics.evaluate() for C1-C4 and policy.rework_attempts for C5. No new telemetry.
- Pin a cheap model (Haiku) on both arms via RunnerSpec.model; reserve a strong model for judging; run across >=2 agent families (Claude, Copilot).
- Report per-criterion tables + arm totals; do not collapse to one number.

The key upgrade over the pilot: turn gates + rework ON for Arm H so the deterministic-gate and rework channels (the harness's largest claimed lift) are actually measured. Shares task-set and scorer plumbing with the per-skill eval basicly-4t9z; reuses the rubric primitive basicly-0122.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A versioned fixed task set (5-8 tasks) each with a hidden objective check; a thin A/B driver reusing rubrics.evaluate for C1-C4 and policy.rework_attempts for C5 with cheap-model runner arms and a strong-model judge across >=2 agent families and gates+rework ON for the harness arm; a report of per-criterion tables and arm totals; relates to basicly-4t9z and basicly-0122 and basicly-8z52

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a write dispatch driven through the single-track loop path when its recorded occupancy crosses the resolved runners ceiling then the lane finalizes early and spins exactly one follow-up bead exactly as a supervised lane does and a test proves it red first against a stubbed low ceiling
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
rg -n "ceiling_tokens|OVERRUN_MARKER|existing_followup" src/basicly/loop.py src/basicly/supervise.py src/basicly/cli.py
uv run python -c "
import json, pathlib
r = json.loads(pathlib.Path('.basicly/usage/run-records.json').read_text())['basicly-23ep'][0]
print(r['phase'], r['forecast_tokens'], r['context_tokens'])"
```

Observed - `ceiling_tokens`, `OVERRUN_MARKER` and `existing_followup` occur **only** in
`supervise.py`, and the finalize protocol has exactly one call site: `supervise.py:2284`. Nothing in
`loop.py` or `cli.py` meters the context ceiling. Expected - a guard the design calls a behavioural
protection (factory design D8, section 7.6) applies on every write dispatch, not only the supervised
one.

## Context

`record_dispatch` calls `runner.context_occupancy` on both paths, so the *measurement* is taken
everywhere - which is why the evidence below exists at all. Only the supervised path *acts* on it.

**Measured on this bead's own parent.** `basicly-23ep` was driven single-track with
`basicly loop run basicly-23ep --root basicly-yc0x` on 2026-08-04. It recorded a context occupancy of
**403051 tokens** against the then-declared window of 200000 and its derived trigger of 120000 - 3.4x
the trigger - and was **neither finalized early nor given a follow-up bead**. It ran to completion and
committed normally. The guard simply was not there.

Two things follow, and the second is the reason this is filed separately from basicly-23ep:

1. **The twelve `(context-ceiling overrun)` follow-up beads all came from supervised passes.** The
   single-track path has been dispatching unmetered the whole time, so the truncation history is a
   property of one of the two write paths, not of the engine.
2. **The two paths disagree about a bead's fate for reasons unrelated to the bead.** The same work,
   at the same size, is truncated-and-followed-up under `supervise` and completed under `loop run`.
   That is a nondeterminism in the engine's own output, in the family basicly-jr0l's determinism
   critique tracks.

This is Phase S's shape exactly - **an instrument built and never connected** - and the same shape as
`permissions-check` shipping wired to no gate and the import contract reporting `1 kept, 0 broken`
forever. It belongs with basicly-uexy's wired-or-deleted gate, which would have caught it: the
finalize protocol's symbols have no caller outside their own module.

**Do not treat this as an argument for removing the ceiling.** basicly-23ep corrected the window to
1000000, which puts the trigger at 600000, and 403051 is comfortably under it - so the guard is
now plausible rather than punitive, and wiring it is safe in a way it was not this morning. Wire it,
or delete it and say so.

## Fix shape

- One metering site both write paths reach, rather than a second copy in `loop.py` - a duplicated
  ceiling is how the two paths came to disagree in the first place.
- The follow-up-spinning half (`existing_followup` and the `[harness-overrun]` marker) is already
  idempotent, so the single-track path can reuse it unchanged.
- A test that drives the **single-track** path past a stubbed-low ceiling and asserts the lane
  finalizes and spins exactly one follow-up, proven red first (basicly-kjc5.49). A test that only
  exercises `supervise` is what let this ship.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`
payload.title: The context ceiling is inert on the single-track dispatch path

Git hooks gate only at commit time; Anthropic's model gates at tool time (PreToolUse, exit 2 blocks) and turn end (Stop). ## Design

- New stdlib-only script .basicly/core/hooks/protect-generated.py: reads the PreToolUse JSON payload from stdin, extracts tool_input.file_path, and exits 2 (block, stderr shown to the model with the edit-the-source alternative) when the target file carries a 'Generated by ... basicly' marker in its first lines or is the generated manifest json; fails open on malformed input or missing files.

- pre-commit config and git stage installation are unchanged by the new manager field (git hooks keep working; agent hooks never reach pre-commit).

- Dogfood: this repo's .claude/settings.json gains the wiring via hooks-build; piping a synthetic PreToolUse payload for CLAUDE.md into the script blocks it.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the finding-set ledger has entries from real rework rounds when the trade rate and the eventual outcome of those lanes are counted then a decision is recorded on whether a traded finding set is a stalled round or progress and either the threshold changes with tests or basicly-m4zv.5 Context sentence is corrected to match the landed behaviour
payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-08-06 by exercising `basicly-m4zv.5` from base after it merged, rather than by
reading its tests. The landed behaviour satisfies the acceptance criterion and contradicts
one sentence of the same bead's Context, so the AC passing hid a design question.

`basicly-m4zv.5`'s Context says:

> Compare the open-finding set between consecutive iterations, not the count - **a round that
> fixes one finding and introduces one is not progress.**

The landed implementation disagrees. Measured against base at 4cbc777:

```
history [{pytest, ruff}]  now {pytest, vulture}
  verdict=progressing  rounds=0  -> keep spending
```

`policy._compare_finding_sets` returns `STALLED` only on set identity and `DIVERGING` only on a
strict superset; everything else is `PROGRESSING`. A trade is neither, so it falls through and
the round keeps spending its cap. There is a test asserting exactly this -
`test_a_finding_set_that_traded_one_finding_for_another_is_progressing` - so it is a decision,
not an oversight.

## Which is right is genuinely open

The AC only ever defined three cases - unchanged once, unchanged twice, grows - and a trade is
none of them, so **the implementation is correct against the AC**. The question is whether the
AC was complete.

**For the landed behaviour (trade = progressing).** Fixing `ruff` while `vulture` newly fails is
real movement, and a lane that clears findings one per round is the normal shape of iterative
work. Escalating it would ask a human about a lane that is working, and at `[policy] max_rework
= 2` there is almost no room for a lane to be wrong once. The rework cap already bounds a lane
that thrashes forever, so nothing is unbounded either way.

**For the Context sentence (trade = stalled).** The count is unchanged and the *quality* is
unknown; a lane that trades a finding every round never converges and burns its whole cap
before the cap notices. That is the same failure this bead's parent exists to stop, one level
subtler.

**A third reading, which may be what the sentence meant.** The sentence's job may be to argue
against comparing *counts* - "a count cannot tell a trade from real progress, so compare sets" -
rather than to fix the verdict for a trade. Under that reading nothing is wrong and this bead
closes as already-satisfied with the sentence clarified.

## What would settle it

Telemetry, not argument. `policy.record_finding_set` now writes a `[harness-policy] finding-set`
marker on every rework round, so the data accrues from here on: count how often consecutive
rounds trade rather than shrink, and whether those lanes eventually landed or escalated. A trade
that usually precedes a landing is progress; one that usually precedes an escalation is a stall.
Decide from the ledger the way `basicly-m4zv.14` settled the `-n auto` question, and do not
change the threshold before the ledger has entries.

## Steps to Reproduce

```sh
uv run python -c "
from basicly import policy
A = policy.finding_signature(['pytest','ruff'])
B = policy.finding_signature(['pytest','vulture'])
print(policy._compare_finding_sets([A], B))"
```

Prints `('progressing', ('pytest','ruff'), 0)`. Expected, if the Context sentence governs, is a
stalled verdict.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `tests/test_policy.py`
payload.title: Decide whether a traded finding set is progress or a stalled round

payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
rg -n "return handler\(args\) if handler else 0" src/basicly/cli.py
rg -n "usage_command != " src/basicly/cli.py
```

Observed - six sibling dispatchers return 0 for a registered subcommand with no handler, and a seventh does the same in a different shape. Expected - the loud internal error `basicly-tcmy.4` added at the top level.

## Context

`basicly-tcmy.4` fixed exactly one site: the top-level dispatcher at `cli.py:4471-4483`, whose docstring at `:4468` says an unregistered subcommand is "indistinguishable from a command that ran". Every sibling group still has the defect.

| Site | Shape |
| --- | --- |
| `cli.py:2191` | `return handler(args) if handler else 0` |
| `cli.py:2240` | same |
| `cli.py:2273` | same |
| `cli.py:2791` | same |
| `cli.py:3461` | same |
| `cli.py:3564` | same |
| `cli.py:1758` (`cmd_usage`) | `if args.usage_command != "report": return 0` |

**Proven behaviourally, not by reading.** An `orphan` sub-parser was injected into each group at runtime - the technique `tests/test_cli.py:1640` already uses for the top level - and `cli.main([group, "orphan"])` called. All seven returned **exit 0, empty stdout, empty stderr**. The identical injection at the top level returns exit 2 with `internal error: subcommand 'orphan' is registered on the parser but has no handler`.

**Latent, not live.** Every sub-parser is `required=True`, so a user typing a bogus name already gets exit 2 (`uv run basicly worktree bogus` -> `invalid choice`). The defect fires only on a *registered* name with a forgotten handler entry, which is precisely the class tcmy.4 was filed for. All seven registries currently agree, so nothing is broken today. What is missing is the guard.

**The existing test cannot catch it, and that is the real finding.** `test_every_registered_subcommand_has_a_handler` (`tests/test_cli.py:1616`) does derive names from the parser, but its helper asserts `len(actions) == 1` against the root parser, so it never recurses. `test_a_registered_subcommand_with_no_handler_fails_loudly` (`:1627`) hard-codes the top-level site. `rg` for any of the seven `*_command` dests across `tests/` returns zero hits. So a group added tomorrow inherits the defect through a green suite - which is exactly what `cmd_usage` did, and why the original audit of this reported six sites when there are seven. **The fix must derive the site list from the parser; hand-listing seven is how the seventh was missed.**

Two adjacent sites, recorded as read-only evidence and NOT part of this defect: `cli.py:2259` (`listers[args.kind]` raises `KeyError` -> exit 1 with a bare-key message) and `cli.py:2245-2249` (an unmatched `kind` falls through to `cmd_agents_new` - mis-dispatch, not silent success).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given any command group that owns subcommands when a registered subcommand has no handler then the CLI exits non-zero and names the offending subcommand exactly as the top-level dispatcher does
- Given the guard when it is tested then the site list is derived from the parser so a group added later is covered without editing the test
- Given a group added with a missing handler when the suite runs then a test fails naming that group

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `tests/test_cli.py`

payload.description:
## Context

Filed 2026-07-31. `src/basicly/agents.py:24-46` records that the non-claude subagent roots were
"weighed and declined, so re-opening this needs new facts, not a fresh reading". This bead brings the
new facts, gathered from live authoritative docs at the owner's direction after basicly-kjc5.58 landed.

The declined reason for `.github/agents/*.md` was that it is "the same markdown format but a separate
root", and basicly-ajq "kept one root and bought portability in the content instead". The supporting
claim was that VS Code parses the Claude subagent format natively - which is still TRUE and is now
confirmed in VS Code's own docs: "VS Code also detects `.md` files in the `.claude/agents` folder,
following the Claude sub-agents format".

## The new facts

1. **VS Code is not the only copilot surface, and the others do not read `.claude/agents`.** The GitHub
   Copilot **cloud agent** reads `.github/agents/<name>.agent.md` (org/enterprise: root `agents/`), and
   Copilot CLI is documented on the same custom-agent surface. So our subagents do not exist at all for
   the cloud agent - the single-root decision covers VS Code only, which is narrower than the comment
   reads.
2. **Copilot custom agents DO support a `tools` allowlist**, so the objection that killed the codex root
   (basicly-crkl: no `tools` equivalent, therefore a silently lost read-only guarantee) does **not**
   apply here. The guarantee is expressible.
3. **Copilot supports a per-agent `model`**, which is the whole point of basicly-a3yi. Without this
   root, a declared tier can never reach copilot at all.
4. Copilot's frontmatter is a **superset** in places (`target`, `mcp-servers`, `metadata`,
   `disable-model-invocation`, `user-invocable`) and its body cap is 30000 chars, which
   `agents.MAX_BODY_CHARS` already enforces.

## The real costs, stated honestly

- **Tool names differ and the sources disagree.** VS Code's doc example is `["read","search","edit"]`;
  community material shows `codebase`/`terminal`/`edit`/`github`. Claude's are `Read`/`Grep`/`Glob`/`Bash`.
  So this needs a pinned, reviewed tool-name mapping plus a rule for a Claude tool with no copilot
  equivalent - and mapping wrongly would weaken the read-only posture check (`WRITE_TOOLS`), which is
  exactly the class of lost guarantee basicly-crkl refused. This is the bead's main risk, not the format.
- `agents-check` needs the `--all-default-roots` treatment `skills-check` already has, or a second root
  drifts unnoticed.
- A second root doubles the generated-file surface for `protect-generated` and the GENERATED_MARKER.
- No always-on cost: subagents are on-demand files.

## Decide, do not assume

The decision is whether the copilot cloud agent and CLI are real consumers for this distribution. If
they are, this root is required and blocks the copilot half of basicly-a3yi. If they are not, say so in
the comment so the next reader does not re-derive it - and then a declared tier is claude-only by
policy, which should be written down rather than left implicit.

Scope: `src/basicly/agents.py`, `src/basicly/cli.py`, `tests/test_agents.py`, `.basicly/core/targets/`.
payload.title: Reopen projecting subagents to the copilot agents surface with new facts

payload.text: TOOL-NAME VOCABULARIES CONFIRMED INCOMPATIBLE 2026-07-31, from the two authoritative references the owner supplied (code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference and code.visualstudio.com/docs/agents/reference/ai-features-cheat-sheet#_chat-tools). This upgrades the tool-name mapping from a cost to the bead's central risk. CLAUDE CODE: flat CapitalCase strings, and the doc states they are 'the exact strings you use in permission rules, subagent tool lists, and hook matchers' - Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Edit, Write, Agent, WebFetch, Skill, TodoWrite and ~40 more. COPILOT / VS CODE: hash-prefixed and NAMESPACED INTO SETS. Sets: #agent #browser #edit #execute #read #search #web. Individual tools are set-slash-name, e.g. #read/readFile, #search/textSearch, #search/fileSearch, #search/codebase, #execute/runInTerminal, #edit/editFiles, #edit/createFile, #web/fetch, #agent/runSubagent. The doc states these are the exact configuration strings, not display names. MAPPING FOR THE TOOLS WE ACTUALLY SHIP (all three agents: test-runner [Read Grep Glob Bash], code-reviewer [Read Grep Glob Bash], security-auditor [Read Grep Glob]): Read -> #read/readFile; Grep -> #search/textSearch; Glob -> #search/fileSearch; Bash -> #execute/runInTerminal. THE SET TRAP, which is the security finding: #read is NOT 'read a file' - it is a GROUP that also contains #read/problems, #read/terminalLastCommand, #read/terminalSelection and notebook readers; #execute also contains createAndRunTask, getTerminalOutput, runNotebookCell and testFailure; #edit also contains createDirectory and editNotebook. So the natural-looking mapping Read -> #read silently WIDENS the grant. Any mapping must target the set-slash-name leaf, never the bare set, and #edit must never appear for an agent our WRITE_TOOLS check certified read-only. A THIRD VOCABULARY EXISTS: copilot CLI's own preToolUse hook payload reported toolName 'bash' and 'task' - lowercase and unnamespaced - matching neither published list, while .github/agents/*.agent.md is shared between VS Code and the CLI via the target field. So the same tools: array is read by surfaces that may not agree on the vocabulary. SUSPECTED SILENT ACCEPTANCE - the decisive open question: a probe agent declaring tools: ['read'] (not a documented config string; #read is) loaded and RAN on copilot CLI with no complaint. Claude Code by contrast documents that if no entry resolves to a tool the subagent 'usually fails to launch with an error naming the entries'. If copilot ignores an unrecognised entry and falls back to its default toolset, then our mandatory-allowlist guarantee and the read-only posture validation are VACUOUS on copilot - a lost guarantee, the same class of objection that declined the codex root in basicly-crkl. This must be settled empirically before any copilot projection ships. An investigation is running to confirm loudly-vs-silently.

CORRECTION 2026-07-31 - my previous comment on this bead was WRONG on its central claim and on the security concern. Measured investigation, sources: docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/custom-agents-configuration and code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference. (1) GITHUB DOES NOT NAME ITS TOOLS DIFFERENTLY. It publishes an alias table that accepts Claude's PascalCase names as first-class compatible aliases: execute accepts shell/Bash/powershell; read accepts Read/NotebookRead; edit accepts Edit/MultiEdit/Write/NotebookEdit; search accepts Grep/Glob; agent accepts custom-agent/Task; web accepts WebSearch/WebFetch; todo accepts TodoWrite. All aliases are case-insensitive, both a comma-separated string and a YAML array are accepted, and unset defaults to all tools. This is deliberate claude-compatibility engineering, like the .claude/skills support. So the earlier claim that a mapping is required is wrong - our existing names already work. GitHub publishes no enumerated tool list, which is itself worth recording. The VS Code cheat sheet's hash-prefixed namespaced names and tool SETS are a THIRD vocabulary for VS Code chat, and the CLI's internal names are a fourth (measured: view, grep, glob, bash, create, edit, skill, sql). Do not merge them. The deepwiki/awesome-copilot list (codebase, terminal, edit, github) matches no vendor source and should be discarded. (2) COPILOT ENFORCES THE ALLOWLIST - measured deterministically, not judged: copilot --log-level debug writes the model request payload, so the actual granted tool schemas are observable. tools ['NotAToolAtAll'] granted only skill+sql; tools [Read Grep Glob Bash] granted view+grep+glob+bash+read_bash+stop_bash+list_bash+skill+sql. Behaviourally the nonsense agent refused both WRITE and SHELL and created no file. (3) THE FEARED LOST GUARANTEE DOES NOT MATERIALISE. An unrecognised entry is dropped with no error and no warning (unlike claude code, which refuses to launch and names the unresolved entries) - but it does NOT fall back to grant-all: an all-unrecognised list resolved to zero requested tools. Our four shipped names all resolve and none resolves to edit or create. The residual risk is functional, not security: a typo yields a near-useless agent rather than a loud failure. (4) REAL SMALLER FINDINGS, all measured: skill and sql are granted UNCONDITIONALLY and cannot be suppressed by our allowlist, so a read-only agent on copilot always holds two tools we never declared (sql writes to a per-session SQLite db, not the repo). Bash yields FOUR tools - bash plus read_bash/stop_bash/list_bash - same capability class, wider surface. NotebookEdit alone resolves to create AND edit, i.e. general filesystem write, so the narrowest notebook write tool on claude becomes full write on copilot - latent, since we do not ship it and WRITE_TOOLS would reject it in a read-only agent. Alias expansion is not uniform: Glob did NOT pull in grep, so a name with a 1:1 CLI counterpart maps narrowly while one without falls back to the broader primary set. (5) THE FINDING THAT MOST CHANGES THIS BEAD: the copilot CLI DOES discover .claude/agents/*.md - measured, a probe agent placed there appeared in the roster and its comma-string allowlist resolved correctly. So our shipped subagents are ALREADY live on copilot today. But GitHub documents only .github/agents/ and ~/.copilot/agents/ for agents; .claude/ is documented only for skills. So this bead's justification shifts: it is no longer 'make copilot work' but 'stop depending on undocumented discovery that no gate would catch if it regressed'. Cheap mitigation available at zero credit cost: copilot --agent <bogus-name> -p x errors and prints the discovered roster without an AI call, so a load assertion is testable for free. Investigation cost 25.29 AI credits over 4 dispatches.

OWNER DECISION 2026-07-31: take the FIRST branch of the AC - project subagents to the copilot agents root. Do not re-litigate. Reasoning that survived the correction: (1) the copilot CLOUD agent reads .github/agents/<name>.agent.md and our subagents do not exist for it at all, so the old single-root decision only ever covered VS Code; (2) the copilot CLI does discover .claude/agents but that is UNDOCUMENTED behaviour we are silently depending on - GitHub documents only .github/agents/ and ~/.copilot/agents/; (3) copilot custom agents support a tools allowlist so the read-only posture check IS expressible, which removes the objection that killed the codex root in basicly-crkl; (4) decisive one - copilot cannot intercept a spawn (repo-level hooks never fire, measured across three probes), so static per-surface emission is copilot's ONLY path and basicly-a3yi needs a root with a documented model slot to emit into. IMPORTANT correction to this bead's own premise: NO tool-name mapping is needed. GitHub publishes an alias table that accepts Claude PascalCase names as first-class and matches case-insensitively (read <- Read/NotebookRead, search <- Grep/Glob, execute <- shell/Bash/powershell, edit <- Edit/MultiEdit/Write/NotebookEdit, agent <- custom-agent/Task, web <- WebSearch/WebFetch, todo <- TodoWrite). An unknown name is dropped silently but fails SAFE - no grant-all fallback. So the AC's pinned reviewed tool name mapping is simpler than filed: pin the alias table as reviewed data and assert our declared names resolve, rather than authoring a translation layer. Accepted cost: a second projected root in the drift gate, and basicly install starts writing .github/agents/ which is consumer-visible and needs a changelog entry.

SURFACE VERIFIED BEFORE BUILDING 2026-07-31 (basicly-8sxf implementation). (1) FILENAME SHAPE AND ROOT confirmed against docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/use-copilot-agents/coding-agent/create-custom-agents: repository-level is .github/agents/NAME.agent.md verbatim ('This will open a template agent profile called my-agent.agent.md in the .github/agents directory'); org and enterprise level is a ROOT agents/NAME.agent.md in the .github or .github-private repo, which is not a repo-level projection target so we do not emit it. (2) SURFACES AGREE ON THE FILE: docs.github.com/en/copilot/reference/custom-agents-configuration states the configuration applies to 'GitHub.com, the Copilot CLI, and supported IDEs', and crucially that 'The configuration file name (minus .md or .agent.md) is used for deduplication'. That kills the basicly-ajq double-load objection outright: <slug>.md and <slug>.agent.md collapse to ONE agent. Confirmed empirically - with BOTH roots populated the free roster probe lists exactly three agents, not six. (3) FREE ROSTER PROBE, three runs, zero AI credits. BEFORE the change, from the worktree: 'No such agent: __bogus_probe__, available: code-reviewer, security-auditor, test-runner' (discovered via the undocumented .claude/agents path only). AFTER agents-build with both roots present: identical three-agent roster, so no duplication. DECISIVE run - .claude/agents temporarily moved aside so ONLY .github/agents existed: same three-agent roster. So the documented root alone now carries the whole roster and we no longer depend on undocumented discovery. Also probed a fresh consumer repo after a real basicly install: same three-agent roster there. (4) FRONTMATTER KEY SET re-read from the reference page: name is OPTIONAL and is a display name; description required; plus target, tools, model, disable-model-invocation, user-invocable, mcp-servers, metadata, and retired infer. Body cap 30000 chars, matching the MAX_BODY_CHARS we already enforce. We emit only name/description/tools - no model line for any family, preserving basicly-kjc5.58, and the claude: passthrough is now gated to the claude root so a Claude-only key cannot leak onto a surface we do not control. (5) ALIAS TABLE re-verified verbatim on the same page and PINNED as reviewed data in agents.COPILOT_TOOL_ALIASES rather than implemented as a translation layer: execute<-shell/Bash/powershell, read<-Read/NotebookRead, edit<-Edit/MultiEdit/Write/NotebookEdit, search<-Grep/Glob, agent<-custom-agent/Task, web<-WebSearch/WebFetch, todo<-TodoWrite; aliases case insensitive; comma string and YAML array both accepted; unset means all tools. GitHub publishes no enumerated tool list, so this table is the entire checkable vocabulary.

IMPLEMENTATION AND MUTATION PROOF 2026-07-31 (basicly-8sxf). SHAPE: agents.AGENTS_OUTPUT_ROOTS is now a pair of frozen AgentOutputRoot records (family, path, suffix, claude_passthrough) - CLAUDE_AGENTS_ROOT .claude/agents/<slug>.md and COPILOT_AGENTS_ROOT .github/agents/<slug>.agent.md. sync_agents and check_synced_agents both iterate every root, so agents-build writes both and agents-check compares both with NO opt-in flag - deliberately unlike skills-build --all-default-roots, because a root only some commands write is precisely how a second root drifts unnoticed. render_agent_md now takes root as a REQUIRED positional so no caller can silently project one family. uninstall prunes both roots by generated marker. PINNED MAPPING NOT A TRANSLATION LAYER: COPILOT_TOOL_ALIASES holds GitHub's table as reviewed data and does two jobs. First, _WRITE_TOOLS_FOLDED is DERIVED from WRITE_TOOLS union every alias of the copilot edit primary, so if GitHub adds a write alias, updating the pinned table widens the read-only posture check automatically instead of leaving a hole. Second, lint_agent_sources now refuses a declared tool that resolves to nothing in the table, because copilot drops an unrecognised entry with no error where Claude Code refuses to launch and names it - our own gate restores the loud failure. Create stays in WRITE_TOOLS but deliberately out of the alias table (it is the CLI internal write primary, not a published config alias). MUTATION CHECK ONE - let a write tool through in the copilot projection only (appended Edit to the copilot tools line): reddened test_render_agent_md_shape[copilot] AND test_projected_read_only_agent_grants_no_write_tool[copilot], the latter added for exactly this because the first only compared a literal string. Restored, 52 pass. MUTATION CHECK TWO - made check_synced_agents compare only the claude root: reddened test_check_synced_agents_catches_a_hand_edit_in_each_root_alone[copilot], test_check_synced_agents_flags_missing_and_stale and test_sync_agents_filters_and_prunes_every_root_by_selection. Restored. LIVE GATE PROOF: appended a line to .github/agents/security-auditor.agent.md, basicly agents-check exited 1 with '.github/agents/security-auditor.agent.md: content mismatch'; after rebuild it exited 0 with 'Projected agents are up to date.' PROTECT-GENERATED: both guards key on the marker rather than a path, so the new files inherit the protection; test_render_marker_stays_in_protect_generated_window is now parametrized over both roots to prove the marker stays inside the 10-line scan window. BREADTH FACTS RECORDED beside the pinned table in agents.py (skill and sql granted unconditionally and unsuppressable, Bash expands to four tools, NotebookEdit resolves to both create and edit, Glob does not pull in grep, unrecognised entries fail safe) and summarised in docs/architecture/architecture.md section 5. STALE COMMENT at the old agents.py:24-46 is rewritten - it now records the reopening with the measured reasons, keeps the codex decline intact, and states the dedup fact that retires the double-load worry. CONSUMER-VISIBLE: basicly install now writes .github/agents/ (verified end to end in a fresh scratch repo: 6 files written across the two roots, agents-check green, copilot roster probe green, uninstall removed both roots). Needs a changelog entry from the landing owner. Gates all green after the final edit: pytest 1860 passed, ruff check, ruff format, pyright 0 errors, basicly check, agents-check, skills-check --all-default-roots, catalog lint, hooks-check, plus markdownlint on the touched docs.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given loop supervise running with stdout attached to a pipe rather than a terminal when the supervisor prints a session or dispatch or routed line then that line is observable before the process exits with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Found in the basicly-kjc5.22 dogfood run (feature basicly-hxnf, 2026-07-26).

The run was piped through `tee` to a log so it could be followed live. For roughly twelve minutes
the only output was the lanes' own subprocess noise — markdownlint summaries and pytest tracebacks
from their pre-commit hooks. Not one `session:`, `adopted:`, `dispatch:` or `routed:` line
appeared until the process exited, at which point the whole orchestration history arrived at once.

Cause: `_cmd_loop_supervise` reports with plain `print`, and Python block-buffers stdout when it is
not a TTY. The lanes' output is not buffered because it comes from child processes writing to an
inherited file descriptor, so the operator sees everything *except* the thing the supervisor is
supposed to tell them.

This is the same blind spot basicly-jr0l.10 records for spend, generalized to every line the
supervisor prints. It matters because a long headless run is exactly the case where an operator
pipes to a log or a pager, and because it defeats "watch the run and intervene early" as a
mitigation for cost: the lanes had already finished and cost 3.36M tokens before the first
orchestration line was visible.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. `basicly loop supervise <root> | tee run.log` with at least one lane that takes minutes.
2. Observe `run.log` and the terminal while it runs: hook and test output from the lanes appears immediately, supervisor lines do not.
3. Wait for exit — every supervisor line appears at once.
4. Expected: each supervisor line is visible as it happens, piped or not.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given loop supervise running with stdout attached to a pipe rather than a terminal when the supervisor prints a session or dispatch or routed line then that line is observable before the process exits with tests

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cli.py`
payload.title: loop supervise hides its own progress when stdout is a pipe

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a push when the pre-push hook runs then it streams progress rather than showing one buffered line for its whole duration so a slow gate is distinguishable from a hang and given any check relocated from pre-push to CI then that check blocks the merge in CI so the floor is relocated rather than removed
payload.description:
## Measured

A complete pre-push run took **852s (~14 minutes)**, of which pytest was **798s**. It re-runs
gates that already passed at commit time: ruff, ruff-format, pyright x3, bandit, vulture,
wired-or-deleted, lint-imports, pytest, four projection checks and docs-claims.

A second attempt was abandoned after 11 minutes because another repository's quality gates were
running concurrently on the same machine - its `pip_audit` is network-bound - and the two
workloads competed for cores. Nothing was wrong with either; the machine was oversubscribed.
Recorded so the 852s figure is not read as a clean single-tenant measurement.

## Two consequences, and the second is the one to fix first

**A fourteen-minute push is a bypass generator.** This repo forbids `--no-verify`, which is the
right rule, and a gate this slow puts pressure on it anyway. A rule that depends on patience is
a rule with a half-life. Decide deliberately what genuinely must run pre-push versus what CI is
the correct floor for - the four projection checks and docs-claims are deterministic and cheap,
pytest at 798s is the whole cost.

**`pre-commit` buffers hook output until the hook exits**, so a long pre-push shows a bare
`pre-push-script....` line for its entire duration and is indistinguishable from a hang. That is
a **diagnosability** defect independent of the duration, it is cheaper to fix than the runtime,
and it is what makes the runtime feel like a failure. An operator who cannot tell a slow gate
from a wedged one will eventually kill one that was working.

## Constraint on any fix

Do not weaken the gate to make it fast. The repo rule is explicit: never defeat a gate to force
success. Splitting work between pre-push and CI is a **relocation** of the floor and must leave
the floor intact - anything moved to CI must actually block the merge there, or this becomes a
quiet removal.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/hooks/pre-push.py`
- `basicly.toml`
- `.github/workflows/`
payload.title: Pre-push runs the whole suite and takes fourteen minutes which pressures the no-bypass rule

payload.text:
measured 2026-08-06 at d58e8e2 on the 32-core WSL2 box, load average 0.20 at start (the only other
work was a network-bound lane agent, so effectively single-tenant):

  checks passed: 16/16 in 51.77s
  uv run python .basicly/core/hooks/pre-push.py  74.08s user 14.48s system 179% cpu 49.337 total

**51.77s for the whole set, against this bead's 852s.** ~16x. Three supporting facts:

1. There is no separate pre-push pytest to blame. `.basicly/core/hooks/pre-push.py` is 24 lines
   and calls `run_checks(project_root(), "full")` - the same `[[verify.checks]]` set, same runner,
   same `command = ["pytest", "-q", "-n", "4"]` (basicly.toml:195) that `basicly verify --mode
   full` uses. The 798s and this 51.77s are two measurements of one command.
2. basicly.toml:191 already records `-n auto` at 17.5s for 2119 tests on this box (2026-08-01),
   and 19.3s while 1297 concurrent external `br init` operations were driven at the same machine.
3. A lane landing earlier today ran the same gate at `2504 passed in 28.56s`.

So the runtime half of this bead is contention, not the suite, and **relocating pytest to CI is
not justified**: this bead's own constraint says a relocation must leave the floor intact or it is
a quiet removal, and trading a real local floor for ~30s is that bad trade.

## The diagnosability half has a root cause in our own code, and it is one line

This bead attributes the buffering to `pre-commit`. `pre-commit` may also buffer, but it is not
the binding cause and fixing it alone would change nothing.

`check_runner.py:204` emits a per-check progress marker already - `print(f"==> {name}")` - with no
`flush=True`. On a pipe, Python block-buffers that, while each check's *subprocess* writes
straight to the inherited fd. So the markers are withheld until process exit and the ordering is
inverted.

Demonstrated, not reasoned: in the 106-line capture of the run above, `==> ruff` is at **line 89**
while ruff's own "All checks passed!" is at **line 1**. Every marker arrived last, as a block.

That is why a slow gate is indistinguishable from a hang - not because nothing is emitted, but
because what is emitted cannot arrive until it no longer matters. Fix: flush the markers. Then
progress streams regardless of what `pre-commit` does with it.

## The instrument that would have settled this does not exist

`.basicly/usage/verify-run.json` already stores a per-check record (`name`, `status`,
`returncode`, `detail`) and omits duration. `verify-checks.json` carries usage counts only
(`pytest: 24`). `run-records.json` has `duration_s`, but for agent dispatches. And
`check_runner.py:236` already computes `total_elapsed` - it is printed and then discarded.

So "798s, of which pytest was 798s" rests on one hand-timed observation nothing can corroborate,
and this bead already concedes the machine was oversubscribed for the run it characterized.
Persisting per-check `duration_s` into the record that already exists is the cheap companion to
the flush, and it is what turns "the gate felt slow" into a queryable number.

Not acted on in this session - recorded so the next reader inherits the measurement rather than
repeating it. Verification boundary: I did not run this under deliberate contention, so I have not
reproduced the 852s, only established that it is not the uncontended cost.

payload.description:
Objectively test whether driving work through the basicly harness (the loop, distributed skills, deterministic gates, worktree isolation) produces higher-quality completed work than a standalone Claude Code or GitHub Copilot session with no basicly harness. Today this is asserted, not measured.

Design a low-token-cost evaluation:
- A small fixed task set (a handful of representative, deterministic coding tasks with objective pass criteria).
- Run each task both ways: with the basicly harness vs a bare agent, ideally across more than one agent (Claude Code, Copilot) to avoid single-agent bias.
- Score on completion quality, correctness (tests/gates), and rework/iterations.

Minimize token usage as a hard design constraint: use faster/cheaper models (e.g. Haiku) for the runner passes and reserve a stronger model only for judging; keep the task set small and deterministic; reuse existing signals rather than re-instrumenting - the run-record health signal (basicly-y886) and the rubric eval (basicly-0122). Relate to basicly-4t9z (skill evals), which measures per-skill behavioral lift; this bead is the whole-harness question, not per-skill.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A documented A/B methodology (harness vs no-harness) over a small fixed task set, with an explicit token-minimization strategy (cheap models for the runner passes, strong model only for scoring, small deterministic tasks, reuse of run-records/health and rubric signals).
- A scoring rubric covering completion, correctness, and rework, with objective pass criteria per task.
- A pilot run with results and a recommendation on whether basicly measurably helps and whether to make this a repeatable eval (and if so, what to build). References basicly-4t9z and basicly-0122.
payload.title: Research spike: is basicly measurably better than a standalone agent harness

Equal correctness on a hidden objective check (C2 tie), at ~32k Haiku tokens. Caveats: N=1, one agent/model, gates+rework off, and the C4 win is partly circular (H was told to stub). Recommendation: YES make it repeatable but scoped - filed basicly-7bur to build a fixed task set with HIDDEN objective checks + a thin A/B driver reusing rubrics.evaluate and the rework counter, cheap-model arms + strong judge, and gates+rework ON for the harness arm (the channel this pilot deferred and where the largest lift lives).
