payload.description:
## Problem

`basicly-agzx.1` is closed and its result (claude recalls 98% of 53 baseline rules, copilot 93% of 54, against 17%/6% no-guidance controls) has not been folded back into `docs/plan/implementation-plan.md`. Principle 5 of the plan's own section 3 says each phase ends by folding its result into the reference; this one did not.

Six places still read as though 1a had not run:

- Section 2 line 85: the always-on baseline row still asserts **The cliff concern stands** on a word-count argument, which the measurement refuted.
- Section 4 Phase 1 item 1a: written in the imperative as work to do, with no result, no pointer to the committed harness (`.scripts/recall_eval.py` + `.scripts/recall_rules.toml`), and the sentence that no cap change in either direction is legitimate until it runs. The cap policy is now asymmetric: lowering is housekeeping, raising still has no evidence.
- Section 4 Phase 1 exit criteria: three numbers owed, one now delivered; the partial state is not recorded.
- Section 4 Phase 4 priority line: still **P1 if 1a shows a cliff, P2 if it shows a slope**, a conditional that resolved to P2 routine tidying.
- Section 4 Phase 4 exit criteria: **1a's recall test re-run shows improved recall** is close to unsatisfiable now that the baseline measures 98%/93%; the achievable criterion is recall not degraded.
- Section 5 dependency graph and section 6 cut-list still carry 1a as pending work.

Codex stays unmeasured because its CLI is absent, and it is the family that matters most since `AGENTS.md` is the largest baseline and the only one that grows when a fragment is scoped. Any rewrite must say so rather than implying three families were measured.

## Notes

The result must be recorded narrowly. It is mechanism confirmed, never outcome improved: recall under a direct cue is an upper bound and says nothing about whether a rule binds during work, and `catalog-efficacy-design` section 4.1 forbids citing it as evidence of quality. What it kills is only the claim that the baseline is past the cliff so the tokens are wasted.

Docs-only, so no loop track per the ceremony threshold decision (`src/**` or `.basicly/**` requires the loop). Sibling of `basicly-imnu.6`, which covers the section 7 owner decisions and is deliberately separate.
payload.title: Absorb the recall test result into the implementation plan

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a reader arriving at the README when they read the opening section then it presents the same four pillars as the site with the contract sentence that the loop reads what the projector emits, claims commit-time enforcement rather than gating in general, and no longer describes basicly as only instructions skills and gates
payload.description:
## Context

`site/index.html` already leads with the four-pillar framing - guidance, gates, the loop, the
work graph - and says "Most agent harnesses ship instructions and skills. basicly also ships
the workflow and the state". `README.md` still leads with the projector alone: "One command
installs a complete coding-agent harness - instructions, skills, and gates." It never mentions
the loop or the work graph.

So the README lags the site by a whole positioning generation. A visitor arriving from the
repo homepage sees a config compiler and no sign of the 60% of the code that is the
orchestration engine (`loop.py`, `supervise.py`, `merge.py`, `decisions.py`, `rubrics.py`).

Owner decision 2026-07-30: adopt the site's four-pillar framing in the README so both surfaces
match, rather than inventing a third framing.

Both surfaces are also missing the strongest available claim, which is structural rather than
a feature list: the loop and the headless agents it dispatches both read the artifacts the
projection layer emits, so the config layer's output *is* the orchestrator's contract. Nothing
that implements only one half can copy that.

Competitive grounding gathered 2026-07-30, to keep the copy honest: `oh-my-agent` already does
SSOT-to-multi-runtime projection with a CI drift check, so "we project and we gate the
projection" is no longer a unique claim. What remains genuinely ours on that half is
enforcement at *commit time* - it installs no git hooks - so the copy should say commit-time
rather than implying gating in general.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a reader arriving at the README when they read the opening section then it presents the same four pillars as the site with the contract sentence that the loop reads what the projector emits, claims commit-time enforcement rather than gating in general, and no longer describes basicly as only instructions skills and gates
payload.title: Realign the README with the four-pillar positioning the site already ships

payload.description:
## Context

`docs/research/2026-07-26-sota-review.md` section 5 lists six "real, structural leads". Two of
them are now overstated, verified against sources on 2026-07-30:

- Lead 1, "enforcement is code and git hooks, not prose", and lead 3, "agent-agnostic
  projection from one catalog - others ship per-host adapters maintained by hand ... we
  generate, and we gate the generation". `first-fluke/oh-my-agent` keeps `.agents/` as a single
  source of truth, projects it into each runtime's native layout via `oma emit`
  (Agent-Skills-conformant skill folders, `AGENTS.md`, `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`), and
  ships "a drift check in CI keeping the generated output honest" plus `oma verify <agent>`, a
  deterministic per-agent check battery.

So generate-and-gate is no longer differentiating on its own. What survives is narrower and
should be stated precisely: oh-my-agent installs **no git hooks** - its drift check is CI-only -
so our edge is enforcement at *commit time*, which is a different guarantee from a check that
fails the build afterwards. It also has no autonomous ticket-driven loop, no worktrees and no
merge queue.

The review was also written before six comparables the owner surfaced. The most important is
`gastownhall/gastown`, from the same org as the beads tracker section 2.10 already analyses. It
covers the orchestration half in full - worktree-isolated agents, a Bors-style merge queue that
bisects to isolate a failing MR, a supervisor patrol tier, human-gated convoys - in Go, and it
requires `bd` 0.57+ **plus Dolt plus tmux 3.0+**.

That does not make our orchestration redundant, and the review should say why: Gastown sits on
the DB-authoritative fork section 2.10 deliberately diverged from, so it is evidence the fork is
real and widening rather than evidence we are reinventing. Our dependency floor on that half is
materially lighter - no database, no daemon, no terminal multiplexer.

Also not yet covered: `oh-my-openagent`, `Archon` (YAML phases plus worktrees plus validation
gates), `openai/symphony` (ticket-driven isolated runs), `hankweave` (checkpoint-gated
resumability over existing harnesses), `CCPM` (PRD to parallel agents over GitHub Issues).

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the ceiling rationale when it is read then it states the separating boundary between observed successes and observed failures makes no zero-failures claim and the gate fails both when the ceiling would refuse a success and when it would admit a size that failed
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

```
rg -n "zero lanes have failed" src/basicly/config.py
uv run python -c "
from pathlib import Path
from basicly import run_record
h = run_record.dispatch_history(Path('.'))
print({o: sum(1 for b,hh in h.items() for e in hh if e.get('outcome')==o)
       for o in {e.get('outcome') for b,hh in h.items() for e in hh}})
print([(b, e.get('returncode'), e.get('scope_tokens'))
       for b,hh in h.items() for e in hh if e.get('outcome')=='failed'])
"
```

Observed - the comment asserts no lane has ever failed, and the history reports `{'failed': 4, 'handoff': 181, 'executed': 23}`. Expected - the recorded rationale matches the record.

## Context

`basicly-3w44` raised the ceiling to 112000 and the value is right, but the reasoning committed beside it is wrong in a way worth fixing loudly, because the error is instructive.

**The false claim.** `config.py` says "Zero lanes have failed at any size, so this is a LOWER bound on a safe ceiling". There are **four failed dispatches**, all `returncode 143` (SIGTERM), across `basicly-kjc5.42`, `kjc5.43` and `kjc5.44`.

**Why they were missed - survivorship bias in the analysis itself.** The query that produced "47 lanes, zero failed" filtered on `isinstance(entry.get('scope_tokens'), int)`. **Every failed lane records `scope_tokens=None`**, so the filter excluded the entire failure population by construction and the conclusion was an artifact of the measurement. This is the same defect class the bead was filed to fix - a number that does not measure what it is read as measuring - committed by the fix for it.

**The value survives on better evidence.** Sizing the failed beads from the tree:

| Lane | Estimate | vs 112000 |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| `tcmy.31` largest completed | 105318 | admitted |
| ceiling | 112000 | |
| `kjc5.42` failed | 136668 | refused |
| `kjc5.44` failed | 136668 | refused |
| `kjc5.43` failed | 5734 | admitted - a 3823-token scope, so a timeout, not a size failure |

So 112000 separates the observed successes from the two large observed failures. That is a genuinely separating boundary and a far stronger justification than "nothing has failed yet".

**The gate is half a gate.** `test_the_ceiling_does_not_refuse_a_size_that_has_already_succeeded` binds one direction only. Now that failures are known to exist and are sizeable, the ceiling must also not **admit** a size that failed for size reasons. A one-directional gate would have let this error through, and did.

Note the `scope_tokens=None` on failures is itself a finding for `basicly-3w44` (b): a lane that dies records nothing about what it was sizing, so the most informative samples are the ones the telemetry drops.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the ceiling rationale in config.py when it is read then it states the separating boundary between observed successes and observed failures and makes no claim that zero lanes have failed
- Given a completed lane and a failed lane when the ceiling gate runs then it fails if the ceiling would refuse a success and also fails if it would admit a size that failed for size reasons
- Given a lane that fails when its dispatch is recorded then the record carries the scope cost it was sized on so failures are not silently excluded from any later analysis

## Scope

- `src/basicly/config.py`
- `tests/test_decompose.py`
payload.title: The ceiling rationale claims zero lanes failed and the gate binds in one direction only

payload.description:
Phase S's exercised-or-unproven gate. Filed 2026-08-03; it was a row in the plan with no bead.

No release tag while a capability the repo advertises has zero executions in the ledger. This is the gate that would have caught permissions-check, the vacuous import contract, vulture and recall_eval - each of which passed every existing gate while doing nothing.

It is the deterministic form of the quality-gate rule that a capability claim on a consumer-facing surface must be exercised before it is published: a claim in code is caught by a gate, one in a README is caught by a consumer. This makes the code half mechanical.

Scope note: the ledger is the existing usage ledger under .basicly/ledger and the run records under .basicly/usage. The gate reads what is already recorded; it does not add telemetry.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/release.py`
- `src/basicly/tracker_usage.py`
- `tests/test_release.py`
- `tests/test_tracker_usage.py`
- `CHANGELOG.md`

**Kept out of scope deliberately** (basicly-23ep): `cli.py` is over four thousand lines and
reading it would dominate the working set. If the refusal needs a CLI wiring point, add it as a
one-line call into `release.py` and declare the addition on the bead rather than widening scope
mid-flight - widening is what basicly-tcmy.5 did, and it moved a global constant and failed a
gate for two sibling lanes.

**Scope addition declared** (basicly-irrm, 2026-08-04): `tests/test_tracker_usage.py` and
`CHANGELOG.md` were added to the list above. `tracker_usage.py` gains a public
`surface_executions`, and this repo keeps a module's unit tests in that module's own test
file, so its tests belong there rather than in `test_release.py`. The `CHANGELOG` entry is
the `[Unreleased]` line for a user-visible refusal, which `basicly release` reads from the
tagged commit and so can only be curated before the tag. `cli.py` stays out: the refusal
wires through `blocking_reasons`, which the CLI already calls, so no CLI edit was needed.

payload.text:
Design proposal (2026-07-16, needs approval before build):

COMMAND SPLIT (from cli.py inventory)
- Consumer (run in a consumer repo, usually via the pinned uvx or the scaffolded VS Code tasks): install, uninstall, build, check, hooks-build, hooks-check, skills-build, skills-check.
- Contributor (author the catalog in this repo): list, skills-list, skills-new, agents-list, agents-new, fragment-new, catalog-lint, catalog-verify, review.
- Harness/agent-facing (either repo, drives the loop): worktree, verify, policy, decompose, loop, runner.
Proposal: encode the split in --help via argparse epilog sections (three grouped lists with one-liners) — no renames, nothing breaking.

UPDATE COMMAND: not needed — re-running install is the documented upgrade path (update was removed pre-release, basicly-zrj.12.1); the readme now says so explicitly.

OUTPUT STYLE, two options:
(a) stdlib-only polish: consistent status glyphs (wrote/removed/unchanged/error), aligned summary line per command (e.g. 'skills: 2 written, 50 unchanged, 1 pruned'), a single install epilogue table of what converged, dim/bold via ANSI only when stdout is a TTY. No new dependency.
(b) rich-based TUI: real tables for list/skills-list, progress spinners for install steps, colored diff-style drift reports for check/skills-check. Requires adding the 'rich' dependency — needs explicit approval per repo policy.
Recommendation: (a) first (cheap, portable, no dependency decision), (b) only if the plain version still feels flat.

Open for the user: pick (a)/(b) and approve the help-grouping approach; then this decomposes into per-command tasks.

User decision (2026-07-16): recommendation approved AND the new-dependency onboarding approved — implement the rich-based TUI (option b, which subsumes the stdlib polish) with the help-text consumer/contributor/harness grouping. Dependency addition of 'rich' is explicitly authorized.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the decision recorded then either a tier resolves to an ordered same-tier preference list which the generator refuses when the list mixes tiers and which is emitted as an array only to a surface documented to accept one, or the single-model contract is written down with the reason and the behaviour on an unavailable model is stated explicitly rather than left to the host default
payload.description:
## Context

Owner requirement described 2026-07-31: a tier should be able to fall back, so that if the tier's
model is unavailable on a family the agent still runs on another model of the SAME capability class
rather than failing or silently inheriting. Split out of basicly-kjc5.61 by owner decision to keep that
lane single-model and land on schedule.

All facts below were verified against live vendor docs today, not recalled.

## What each surface can actually express

- **GitHub Copilot / VS Code: an ordered list, natively.** `model` accepts "a single model name
  (string) or a prioritized list of models (array)", documented example
  `model: ['Claude Opus 4.5', 'GPT-5.2']`, tried in order. So copilot can honour a preference chain
  with no work on our side beyond emitting the array.
- **Claude Code: a single value only.** Subagent frontmatter `model` takes `sonnet`/`opus`/`haiku`/
  `fable`, a full model id (`claude-opus-5`), or `inherit`; it defaults to `inherit`. There is no array
  form. Claude Code resolves a subagent's model in this order: (1) the `CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL`
  env var, (2) the per-invocation `model` parameter, (3) the definition's `model` frontmatter, (4) the
  main conversation's model. Neither (1) nor (2) is usable for per-agent tiers - the env var is
  session-wide across ALL subagents, and the per-invocation parameter is chosen by the orchestrating
  model, not by the harness. So (3) is our only per-agent slot and it holds one value.
- **Claude Code's own degradation is NOT tier-preserving**: a value excluded by the org
  `availableModels` allowlist is skipped and the subagent "runs on the inherited model instead" -
  which may be any tier, higher or lower.

## The trap this bead exists to prevent

The roster's tier table (docs/design/agent-roster-design.md R5) maps the GPT classes as luna=low,
terra=medium, sol=high AND maximum. So an intuitive-sounding chain like "Claude Opus 5, else
GPT-5.6 Terra" **silently demotes a high-tier judgment to medium**. Any fallback list must be
constrained to same-tier members, and the generator should refuse a chain that mixes tiers rather
than trusting the author to get it right.

## The decision to make

1. Does a tier carry an ordered list, or exactly one model? If a list, is it authored per tier in the
   anchor source, or derived from the map by capability class?
2. What does an unavailable tier model mean where the surface cannot express a chain (claude)? The
   repo's standing rule is fail closed on an indeterminate answer, and "cannot tell" must never read
   as "safe to proceed" - so silently inheriting an unknown tier is arguably the wrong default and a
   refusal or a recorded not-honoured marker may be right. basicly-kjc5.59 already establishes the
   record-the-fallback-rather-than-imply-it stance for a family with no slot; reuse it, do not invent
   a second convention.
3. Whether the fallback is worth having at all given it is honourable on exactly one of our two
   required families today.

## Adjacent observation, not this bead's scope

Both families also expose a REASONING EFFORT axis independent of model choice - Claude Code subagent
frontmatter has `effort` (`low`/`medium`/`high`/`xhigh`/`max`, overriding session effort) and copilot
custom agents have `reasoningEffort`. A tier arguably wants to carry an effort as well as a model.
Worth its own bead if it turns out to matter; noted here so the observation is not lost.

Scope: `.basicly/core/schemas/agent.schema.json`, `.basicly/core/models/`, `src/basicly/agents.py`.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the decision recorded then either a tier resolves to an ordered same-tier preference list
  which the generator refuses when the list mixes tiers and which is emitted as an array only to a
  surface documented to accept one, or the single-model contract is written down with the reason and
  the behaviour on an unavailable model is stated explicitly rather than left to the host default
payload.title: Decide whether a model tier resolves to an ordered preference list

payload.description:
Recurring DX friction (hit at least three times: v0.2.0 release tables, basicly-h0f0, and noted again in basicly-yw28 prep). markdownlint MD060 uses the "aligned" table style, so editing any cell in a wide docs table (e.g. the command table in docs/architecture.md, ~490 chars wide) requires re-padding every pipe to match the header column widths, and `markdownlint-cli2 --fix` does NOT auto-repad the aligned style. Widening the FIRST column cascades a re-pad to every row. The reliable fix each time is a hand-run Python script that reads the header pipe columns and rebuilds the edited row.

Pick a durable fix so this stops recurring. Candidate directions: (a) add a small committed `.scripts/` helper that re-pads a markdown table to MD060-aligned style (invoked manually or as a pre-commit auto-fix); (b) relax MD060 for docs (switch the config to a non-aligned table style, or disable MD060) accepting ragged pipes; (c) split the offending wide tables so cells stay short. Evaluate the trade-off (aligned tables read better in raw markdown but cost edit friction).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Editing a wide docs table no longer requires a hand-authored re-pad script: either a committed helper does it, or the lint rule no longer demands aligned pipes.
- The chosen approach is applied to docs/architecture.md's wide tables and markdownlint passes.
- Decision (helper vs relax-rule vs split-tables) recorded.
payload.title: DX: stop the recurring markdownlint MD060 aligned-table re-pad friction in docs

payload.text: Decision: disable MD060 (table-column-style) in .markdownlint-cli2.yaml. Root cause investigated — MD060 default style 'any' requires each table to stay internally consistent with one pipe style, so editing one cell of an aligned table without re-padding every pipe errors, and --fix does not re-pad aligned. Chose disable over style:compact+--fix (which would churn every table to ragged) or a re-pad helper: minimal one-line diff, keeps existing aligned tables readable, ragged edits now lint clean. Verified with an inconsistent table (0 MD060) and architecture.md still passes.

payload.description:
## Context

`basicly-u6jq.1` has failed five times. Four were the **shared-anchor collision class**, closed in
`v0.7.1`: `basicly-4746` made the collision impossible, `basicly-bdd4` gave a bounced lane a brief
so its re-dispatch has something to do, `basicly-m4zv.5` stopped a non-converging rework round
spending the cap. The fifth, on 2026-08-06, was a different class entirely and had no bead.

Measured from `.basicly/usage/run-records.json`: of 527,629,368 tokens spent on 81 metered lanes,
**53,274,078 bought nothing that landed - and 47,784,950 of that (90%) sits in three long runs**,
each killed by `[runner] runner_timeout` with complete work uncommitted in its worktree. One of
them, `m4zv.5`, was finished work: it passed 500 tests and 16/16 full checks unchanged and was
committed by hand with no edits.

So the proof run does not fail because it is too big, too broken, or short of budget. It fails
because a lane that takes too long loses everything, and nothing watching a lane can tell working
from wedged.

## Why this is an epic and not one bead

The four blockers are one causal chain, and their order is load-bearing:

1. **`basicly-yvx9`** - preserve a killed lane's work. Independent of everything else, needs no new
   measurement, and recovers the 47.8M on its own. **Do this first.**
2. **`basicly-1lpo`** - a release epic can only fan out over parentless beads, so a cut drawn from
   existing epics cannot be one pass. Until this lands there is no root a three-lane proof can be
   dispatched from at all. **Note this epic has the same defect** (see below).
3. **`basicly-rupz`** - consume the per-turn event stream the harness already requests and
   discards. This is the unlock: it makes progress detectable and lets spend bind mid-dispatch.
4. **`basicly-lpsf`** - retire the wall clock as the working bound, now that something better
   exists. Blocked on `rupz` by construction.

Then `basicly-u6jq.1` is worth attempting again. Running it before 1 and 3 buys an expensive
failure and no evidence: 10 of 68 successful lanes finished past 80% of the cap, so a three-lane
pass has a material chance one dies.

## This epic is a grant carrier, not a fan-out root

**Do not run `basicly loop supervise` on it.** Lane seeding delegates to
`loop.run_until_blocked`, which provisions *parent-child* children only, while grant coverage walks
both edges (`policy.session_issue_ids`). Its blockers are declared via `blocks` because they belong
to four different epics of origin and nothing is re-parented, so this root covers them for the
grant and can seed none of them. That asymmetry is `basicly-1lpo`, which is itself one of the
blockers - so the fix arrives from inside. Until it does, drive each blocker with
`basicly loop run <id> --root basicly-jk3l`.

## Budget

Size the grant from the ledger, not from optimism: **6,975,813 tokens is the mean per *executed*
lane**, and a lane that dies at the wall clock has cost 16-21M. The `v0.7.1` phase was granted 20M
for three beads and overshot to 22,164,783 - because `spend_status` is consulted before a pass and
recorded after, with nothing in between, which is precisely what `rupz` fixes.

## Success Criteria

- A lane killed by the wall clock has its work committed and judged by verify, not discarded.

- A release-shaped root can fan out over work it did not parent.
- `basicly-u6jq.1` completes with zero human interventions attributable to a harness defect, and
  reports the intervention count with a cause for each.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `basicly.toml`

payload.description:
beads-commit-msg.py validates issue-id references with a too-loose regex '\b[a-z][a-z0-9]*-[a-z0-9]+\b' that matches ANY hyphenated word, not just the configured beads prefix. The beads rust tool (br orphans) scans commits with a prefix-anchored pattern '\b(<prefix>)-[a-z0-9]+(?:\.[0-9]+)*\b', matching the id token by word boundary anywhere in the message (trailing parenthetical or footer alike). Because our hook is looser, when a commit lacks a matching known id it reports a confusing 'unknown beads issue id: fork-drove, the-loop' listing hyphenated description words as offenders, obscuring the real cause (no valid trailing id). Investigation (br 0.2.16 binary) confirms beads matches the id anywhere by prefix, so the current trailing-paren format is fine and no footer migration is needed. Fix: align our hook's id detection with beads' prefix-anchored scanner, deriving the prefix set from the known ids.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Write a commit whose description has a hyphenated multi-word phrase (e.g. fork-drove-the-loop) and omit or typo the trailing beads id
2. beads-commit-msg rejects with 'unknown beads issue id: fork-drove, the-loop', naming description words as ids
3. The real cause (no valid trailing id present) is obscured by the red-herring candidates

## Acceptance Criteria

* beads-commit-msg detects candidate ids with a prefix-anchored pattern mirroring beads' own scanner, so non-prefix hyphenated words are never treated as ids
* the prefix set is derived from the known ids with no new configuration
* a commit with a valid trailing id passes regardless of hyphenated description words; a missing id yields the no-id error; a typo'd prefix id (basicly-nope) yields an accurate unknown-id error naming only that token
* regression tests cover the valid-id-with-hyphens pass and the missing-id and typo cases
payload.title: beads-commit-msg id detection should be prefix-anchored like beads own scanner

What makes it recur: `verify --mode full` runs one OS, and the three pyright legs
(including pyright-windows) pass locally, which reads as cross-platform coverage.

behaviour that types cannot express.

platform difference an input to the test. `_is_windows_interop` now reads the

string, so the new test would have caught this before the push. The rule is now
catalogued as the `platform-hermetic-tests` fragment scoped to `tests/**` - the
first user of the path-scoped tier, which was built and unused. It projects to

that correction is what settled the jr0l.21 -> jr0l.22 chain.

Deliberately no code or fragment change. No gate can catch it, it happened once,
and the strongest available prevention already exists - the design's invariants are

payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-25 while shipping basicly-kjc5.16. The decider confinement for claude and copilot is a blocklist of tool names in runner._DECIDER_DENY_CLAUDE / _DECIDER_DENY_COPILOT. A name that matches no tool is not an error: claude prints "Permission deny rule X matches no known tool" on stderr and carries on, so the tool that name was meant to deny stays allowed. That is a silent confinement hole from a typo or a renamed tool.

The hole was found only by running a real dispatch and reading stderr - exactly the pattern basicly-kjc5.55 exists to correct. CI has no agent CLI so this cannot be a plain verify check, but it can be an opt-in local check that fails loudly: dispatch a trivial confined prompt per available family and treat a no-known-tool warning on stderr as a failure. basicly runner list or basicly health is the natural home since both already report per-family capability.

Also worth covering: a tool added to either CLI later is allowed until it is listed, so the check should report the delta between the CLI tool inventory and the deny list where the CLI can be asked for one.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an agent CLI on PATH when the confinement check runs then a deny-tool name that CLI does not recognise is reported as a failure naming the family and the name, and given no agent CLI on PATH then the check skips with a message rather than passing silently
payload.title: Validate the decider deny-tool names against the agent CLI

payload.description:
## Context

Found while setting up the basicly-kjc5.22 dogfood run.

A headless claude -p dispatch shows no usage in its own terminal - there is no /usage display, so the operator watching the supervisor sees nothing. When the subscription seat allowance is exhausted the dispatch fails, and the supervisor cannot tell that from a dispatch that failed on its merits: it routes the failure to bounded rework and re-dispatches, spending the allowance that just ran out. At the default max_rework of 2 that is up to three failing runs per lane.

The signal exists and is already on the wire. The stream-json reader the claude adapter uses receives a system event with subtype api_retry carrying an error category, and rate_limit and billing_error are two of the documented values. The adapter currently skips unrecognized events.

This is the provider-side twin of D3. policy.spend_status halts on the ceiling we configure; nothing halts on the ceiling the provider enforces.

Correction after checking: cumulative spend is NOT missing. basicly loop session already prints per-lane last-run tokens and a session total from the run records, so an attached client can see exactly what headless dispatches consumed. The gap is only that loop supervise itself prints none of it while it runs, so the operator driving the pass is the one person who cannot see it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a dispatch that fails because the provider usage limit is reached when the supervisor routes the outcome then it is distinguished from a merit failure and spends no rework attempt and the pass stops dispatching rather than retrying
- Given a supervisor pass that dispatched lanes when it prints its per-pass summary then the tokens each dispatch consumed are shown without needing a second client to attach
payload.title: Detect a provider usage-limit refusal instead of reworking it

payload.description:
## Context

Found by the basicly-kjc5.22 dogfood run - the first time loop supervise orchestrated real work.

supervise.finalize_followup builds the br create argv as a list and then splices the parent flag in at index 3. Index 3 holds the VALUE of -t, so the splice lands between the flag and its value and br rejects the command with a value is required for --type. The overrun follow-up is never created, the lane dispatch is reported as failed, and the agents committed work does not land.

The insert index should be 4.

Reachable only from a supervised child lane. The splice is guarded by root_issue != issue_id, and a single-track leaf is its own root, so every prior run skipped the branch entirely. It needs a child lane that also crosses the D8 context ceiling - an intersection of two features that had never run together until the dogfood.

Observed twice in one pass, on basicly-kjc5.42 at 145570 tokens and basicly-kjc5.43 at 145489 against the 120000 ceiling. Detection and the finalize decision were both correct; only the bead creation failed.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Call supervise.finalize_followup with a root_issue different from issue_id
- Observe the assembled argv places --parent between -t and the type value

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane whose root differs from the lane itself when the context ceiling triggers the finalize protocol then the follow-up bead is created successfully with both its type and its parent set
payload.title: Follow-up bead creation puts the parent flag between -t and its value

payload.description:
## Context

Found while exercising the basicly-jr0l.11 fix against a real br workspace rather than the test fake.

supervise.finalize_followup reads acceptance criteria from the structured acceptance_criteria field alone (supervise.py line 779). policy.definition_of_ready deliberately accepts either carrier - the structured field or a ## Acceptance Criteria section in the description body (basicly-58iu) - and says so in its own docstring.

So a bead that satisfies the Definition of Ready through the body carrier loses its acceptance criteria the moment it overruns the context ceiling. The follow-up is created with the placeholder Complete the remaining acceptance criteria of X instead of the real ones, and the next agent dispatched against it has nothing to build to. Scope carries over correctly because it is parsed from the body by decompose.parse_scope_section; only the criteria are dropped.

Silent. Nothing fails, the follow-up looks well formed, and the loss is only visible by reading the generated bead.

The two readers should agree. Extracting the body section the way the scope section is already extracted is the smaller change.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Create a bead whose acceptance criteria live only in a ## Acceptance Criteria body section
- Call supervise.finalize_followup for it with an occupancy over the ceiling
- Read the generated follow-up: the criteria are the placeholder, not the originals

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an overrun bead whose acceptance criteria live in the description body when the follow-up is created then it carries those criteria rather than the placeholder, and given a bead using the structured field then that keeps working
payload.title: Overrun follow-up drops acceptance criteria held in the body

payload.description:
## Context

Review finding on the basicly-kjc5.42 work produced by the basicly-kjc5.22 dogfood run.

src/basicly/commit.py carries its own copy of the type vocabulary, the description charset and the scope shape, and says so: Mirrors commit-msg.py. The hook remains the gate, so the two now encode the same contract in two places and can drift. A type added to the hook and not to the module makes the assembler unable to emit a message the gate would accept, and the reverse produces a message the gate then rejects, which is the exact round trip D10 exists to remove.

Not urgent - both copies agree today and the gate is authoritative either way - but the drift is silent until someone edits one side.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the commit type vocabulary and description rules when either the hook or the assembler is changed then both read the same definition so they cannot disagree
payload.title: Commit envelope rules are duplicated from the commit-msg hook

## Context

Observed twice while landing basicly-kjc5.22 work: the first git commit inside a newly provisioned worktree took over ten minutes and had to be backgrounded, then succeeded normally on the retry. Seen in basicly-kjc5-44 and basicly-u6tw. Later commits in the same worktree are fast, so this is one-time setup cost - pre-commit building hook environments that worktree provisioning does not pre-warm.

It matters to the factory rather than to a person. Every lane pays it once, inside the runner_timeout budget, and a dispatched agent that spends its first ten minutes waiting on hook setup looks identical to a wedged lane: the StallWatchdog samples HEAD plus the dirty tree, and neither moves while pre-commit installs.

Provisioning already runs uv sync and npm install, so warming the hook environments belongs in the same place.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a freshly provisioned worktree when the first commit runs then it is not materially slower than a later commit in the same worktree, because provisioning has already prepared the hook environments
payload.title: The markdownlint hook depends on an ambient node it cannot count on

{"agent": "manual", "outcome": "handoff", "phase": "build", "prompt_sha256": "eb4caf9238ec486b93f30a06999a7cf7eebe1a12aa0830df797b473f76344159", "timestamp": "2026-07-26T14:55:22.293339+00:00"}

[harness-info] Measured in a freshly provisioned worktree, 2026-07-26. The recorded cause is wrong and the recorded symptom does not reproduce on this machine; a different, reproducible defect sits in the same place, so the acceptance criteria are amended to it rather than to a no-op.

Cause disproved. Every hook in the projected .pre-commit-config.yaml is repo: local with language: system, so pre-commit builds no hook environments at all - there is nothing for provisioning to pre-warm. hooks.install_hooks already passes --install-hooks, which is therefore a no-op for this config. Implementing the fix as written would change nothing.

Symptom not reproduced. Full hook chain in the fresh worktree: 5591ms, then 5046ms, then 5143ms. A 9 percent first-run difference, not ten minutes.

The real defect, reproduced every time. With nvm off PATH - the condition a dispatched agent runs in - there is no linux node anywhere (/usr/bin/node and /usr/local/bin/node both absent) and npx resolves to the Windows nodejs under /mnt/c. The markdownlint hook then fails in 653ms with: CMD.EXE was started with the above path as the current directory / UNC paths are not supported / markdownlint-cli2 is not recognized. Bypassing npx does not help - node_modules/.bin/markdownlint-cli2 carries a #!/usr/bin/env node shebang and needs the same missing interpreter.

So the hook depends on ambient PATH for a node it cannot count on. The symptom of that dependency is machine-dependent - a hard failure here, plausibly the recorded ten-minute stall on the other contributor machine - but the cause is single and fixable. Every lane pays it, which is what made it Phase 0 work in the first place.

Owner decision 2026-07-26: repurpose this bead to the reproducible defect.

payload.description:
## Context

Found in the basicly-u6jq.1 proof-run pre-flight, immediately after basicly-jr0l.8 shipped.

jr0l.8 gave loop supervise --runner and --autonomy, which set a process-local override so one session can differ from committed config. But the grant a session needs is issued by a separate command in a separate process, and policy grant has no equivalent flag - it reads [policy] autonomy from committed config alone:

    $ basicly policy grant basicly-jr0l --level L1 --token-budget 1000000
    grant: REFUSED (basicly-jr0l) - level L1 exceeds the [policy] autonomy ceiling (L0)

So the round-trip jr0l.8 removed from the run is still there for the grant, which is the one place it hurts most: a token budget only exists on a grant (policy.spend_status returns halted=False when no grant is active), so without an issuable grant a session has no spend ceiling at all.

This is the same fix, on a second surface. cli._apply_session_overrides already exists and is reusable; the work is a parser flag on policy grant plus a call, with the override recorded exactly as jr0l.8 records it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given policy grant invoked with an explicit autonomy override when a grant at that level is issued then it succeeds without any committed config change and the override is recorded, so a session can be granted a token budget without raising the repo ceiling
payload.title: Let policy grant pin the autonomy ceiling for one issuance

## Context

Found in the basicly-u6jq.1 proof-run pre-flight, 2026-07-26.

The D8 sizing governor refuses a decompose plan whose child falls outside the working-set band, but nothing checks the band when a lane is dispatched. grep finds no check_working_set, estimate_plan or working_set reference anywhere in supervise.py or loop.py.

So the band binds only on work that arrives through decompose. A supervised run over pre-existing leaf beads - which is exactly what loop supervise does over a ready set - dispatches whatever the scheduler ranks first, at any size, silently.

Measured on the real ready set under basicly-jr0l with the band at 8000..64000:

    basicly-kjc5.29    77601 tokens   ABOVE max, rank 1
    basicly-kjc5.32    57965 tokens   ok
    basicly-kjc5.49     4596 tokens   BELOW min
    basicly-kjc5.50    47847 tokens   ok

payload.description:
## Context

Found by the basicly-u6jq.1 proof run, 2026-07-26. The run halted before dispatching anything:

    halted:   L1 grant token_budget spent (30705839/5000000 tokens); the session is human-only until re-granted

Nothing was spent by that run. The 30705839 is entirely historical: policy.session_spend_tokens sums run-record tokens across every bead in the session, and the jr0l session includes kjc5.42, kjc5.43 and kjc5.44 - the children of jr0l.9, dispatched during the badly-sized 25M run - which alone account for 11946878, 9410817 and 9348144 tokens.

So a grant budget is a lifetime cap on the session, not a cap on what the grant authorizes. On any long-lived epic with dispatch history, every sanely-sized budget halts on the first pass.

That makes the spend ceiling unusable exactly where it matters most. D3 frames the budget as what a grant authorizes - "once run-record spend for the session reaches the grant token_budget, no new dispatches occur" - and the natural reading of issuing a grant with a budget is that the budget applies to the work that grant covers. Setting it above lifetime spend is possible but wrong-shaped: the operator has to know the history to pick a number, the number stops meaning anything, and it silently grows every run.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Pick an epic with prior dispatch history in .basicly/usage/run-records.json.
2. Issue a grant with a token budget smaller than that history: basicly policy grant <epic> --level L1 --token-budget 5000000 --autonomy L1
3. Run basicly loop supervise <epic> with lanes ready to dispatch.
4. It halts on the first pass with historical spend counted against the budget, and dispatches nothing.

Expected: the budget bounds spend attributable to the grant, so a fresh grant starts from zero.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/policy.py`

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a session whose beads carry prior run-record spend when a grant with a token budget is issued and a lane is dispatched then only spend recorded after the grant was issued counts against that budget, and a fresh grant on a historically expensive session admits dispatches with tests
payload.title: A grant token budget is compared against lifetime session spend not spend since issuance

## Context

Session retro 2026-07-25. Two distinct ways a test can look like a check while proving nothing, both hit while shipping basicly-kjc5.30, both absent from the projected prose.

First: a gate that loads its own configuration cannot be pinned by a config object built in the test. govern_working_set calls load_sizing_config(repo_root) itself, so a SizingConfig handed to a helper never reached it, and the default calibration_min_samples of 10 meant three samples drifted nothing. The regression test therefore passed with the fix deleted. The rule is that a test pinning a config-dependent gate must write that configuration where the production path reads it, and must then show the drift or the failure actually occurring.

Second: a module-level alias for an external dependency is a test seam, not incidental duplication. Consolidating six modules' private br access into one shared helper broke 32 tests at once, because each patches its own module alias. Before consolidating duplicated access, check what the tests patch - the duplication may be the seam.

Both belong in test-discipline, which already covers the neighbouring ground: prove the regression test fails first, and do not assert on internals. Neither rule is Python-specific or basicly-specific.

Note: basicly-kjc5.49 targets the same file with a third test-discipline rule. Whichever lands second rebases; the content does not conflict.

## Acceptance Criteria

payload.description:
## Context

Measured by the basicly-u6jq.1 proof run, 2026-07-26. Three lanes were forecast in band by the D8 governor and cost 34 dollars.

The governor forecasts *working set* - instruction overhead plus scope read-cost times a per-class build factor. That is an estimate of the context a lane needs. It is not what costs money, and nothing in the engine forecasts what does.

Two compounding errors, both measured:

    lane        forecast ws   actual context   ratio   actual spend   cost
    kjc5.32          57965           162203    2.8x       9430203    $7.73
    kjc5.50          47847           201088    4.2x      16002352   $11.73
    kjc5.51          48897           235743    4.8x      20594047   $14.69

First, the working-set forecast under-shot actual context by 2.8 to 4.8 times. Second, and much larger, an agentic loop re-sends its context every turn, so total spend is context times turn count - and nothing models turn count at all. Total spend landed at 160 to 420 times the forecast number, which is not a forecast error so much as a missing quantity.

The cost rollup basicly-kjc5.50 just landed is the carrier, and its first three records show the hole directly: every forecast field is null.

    "actual":   {"tokens": 16002352, "cost": 11.73, "wall_clock_s": 1474.7, "dispatches": 2}
    "forecast": {"tokens": null, "cost": null, "wall_clock_s": null}

Per model, not in aggregate. The same work costs different amounts on different models, and models are replaced constantly, so a calibration averaged across them is noise. That makes basicly-kjc5.29 - refuse to dispatch a runner whose model is unresolved - a hard prerequisite rather than a sibling: without recorded model provenance there is nothing to key a calibration on.

Wall clock matters as much as tokens for a factory, and basicly-kjc5.48 already covers predicting it from duration telemetry; this is the spend half of the same instrument, and basicly-7bur is where both get exercised.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a history of cost rollups keyed by model and task class when a package is sized at decompose then its forecast carries predicted tokens and cost and wall clock alongside the working-set estimate and the prediction is calibrated from that history rather than seeded, with tests
payload.title: Forecast spend and wall clock per model calibrated from run records

payload.description:
## Context

From the basicly-u6jq.1 proof run, 2026-07-26. A 5 million token ceiling admitted a pass that spent 46026602 tokens, and the halt fired on the following pass - after the money.

    halted: L1 grant token_budget spent (46026602/5000000 tokens under this grant; 76732441 lifetime)

The arithmetic was right; basicly-jr0l.17 had just fixed the baseline and it correctly reported spend under this grant. What is missing is that admission compares spend *already recorded* against the budget, so a pass is admitted whenever the previous ones happened to fit. With three concurrent lanes a single pass can spend an unbounded multiple of the budget and only be noticed afterwards.

The fix is emphatically not to interrupt a working agent. Cost is bounded by sizing the work, never by killing an agent mid-run - that is a standing rule here and the D3 admission design is correct. What the gate lacks is foresight: at pass admission, sum the *forecast* spend of the lanes about to dispatch and refuse the pass when it will not fit the remaining budget. Retrospective becomes predictive, nothing is ever killed, and a 5 million budget would have refused this pass instead of reporting it.

Depends on basicly-jr0l.21: a forecast-based admission gate is only as good as the forecast, and today there is no spend forecast at all. Sequencing them the other way round would replace a gate that fires late with one that fires wrongly.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a grant with a remaining token budget when a supervisor pass is about to dispatch lanes whose combined forecast spend exceeds that remainder then the pass is refused with the forecast and the remainder in the message and no lane is dispatched and no running agent is ever interrupted, with tests
payload.title: Admit a supervisor pass on forecast spend against the remaining budget

payload.description:
## Problem

`quality-gates / Quality gates on windows-latest` is red on `main` (run 30210828859). Four tests fail on Windows only; every one was added earlier in this session and verified on Linux alone.

## Steps to Reproduce

Push to `main` and read the `windows-latest` leg, or run pytest on a Windows host:

- `tests/test_markdownlint_hook.py::test_a_windows_interop_path_is_rejected_on_linux`
- `tests/test_markdownlint_hook.py::test_find_node_skips_a_windows_node_on_path_for_an_nvm_one`
- `tests/test_markdownlint_hook.py::test_the_launcher_never_invokes_npx`
- `tests/test_cli.py::test_a_printed_line_is_observable_before_exit_when_stdout_is_a_pipe`

## Root Cause

Two independent POSIX-only assumptions:

1. `_is_windows_interop` compares `candidate.parts[:2] == ("/", "mnt")`, which is a property of the host's path *flavour*, not of the path. On Windows `Path("/mnt/c/...")` is a `WindowsPath` whose anchor is `\`, so the rule cannot be exercised there at all - and `find_node` builds the Path itself, so no test-side change can reach it. `is_absolute()` is False for a rootless Windows path too.
2. `selectors.DefaultSelector()` is `SelectSelector` on Windows and `select.select()` accepts only sockets, so registering a pipe raises `WinError 10038`.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/hooks/markdownlint.py`
- `tests/test_markdownlint_hook.py`
- `tests/test_cli.py`

## Expected Behaviour

All three OS legs of `quality-gates` pass, with the same assertions being made on each - no platform skips, because the behaviour under test is not platform-specific.
payload.title: Fix the Windows-only test failures the jr0l.14 and 8veb tests introduced

payload.acceptance_criteria: Approving a checkpoint via confirm code or a covering grant answers its decision-queue item with matching attribution; decisions.pending excludes items on closed beads; a regression test proves a shipped bead leaves no pending item and that its [harness-wait] interval is closed exactly once.
payload.description:
## Problem

Five decision-queue items sat pending on `main` after the proof run - four ship checkpoints on beads that had already shipped, closed and merged hours earlier, plus one spend escalation for a grant that no longer exists. A fresh session reading `basicly loop decisions basicly-jr0l` sees five live human decisions on finished work.

It is not only cosmetic. `supervise.delegate_decisions` walks `decisions.pending(root)` and hands each item to the decider agent, so a supervised run would spend tokens deciding closed beads. `decisions.has_pending` also holds a lane, so a stale item on an open bead can wedge a lane that has nothing to wait for.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take any bead to its ship checkpoint under `loop supervise`, so the supervisor queues a `checkpoint` decision for it.
2. Approve it the ordinary way - relay the minted confirm code to `basicly loop run <bead> --confirm <code>`.
3. Let the bead ship and close.
4. `basicly loop decisions <root>` still lists the item as pending.

## Root Cause

Two independent gaps:

1. `policy.approve_checkpoint_guarded` records the approval marker but never answers the decision-queue item behind it, so the only thing that clears one is `loop answer`. The supervisor queues the ask; every non-supervised approval path leaves it open.
2. `decisions.pending` in `decisions.py` filters on `item.pending` alone and never on the bead's status, so an item on a closed bead is reported as awaiting a human regardless.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/decisions.py`
- `src/basicly/policy.py`
- `tests/test_decisions.py`
- `tests/test_policy.py`

## Expected Behaviour

Approving a checkpoint through any path answers the queue item behind it, attributed the way the approval was (human, or the grant that covered it). `decisions.pending` drops items on closed beads, so a drained queue means no outstanding human work. The wait meter keeps working: an item answered this way closes its `[harness-wait]` interval exactly once, not twice.
payload.title: A checkpoint approved by confirm code leaves its decision-queue item pending forever

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given an overrun bead carrying a non-default priority and one or more labels when finalize_followup creates its context-ceiling follow-up then the follow-up carries the same priority and the same labels as the overrun bead and a regression test asserts both against a fake br that records the create argv and the four existing unlabelled beads jr0l-18 jr0l-19 jr0l-20 and jr0l-24 carry the phase-7 label
payload.description:
## Problem

`supervise.finalize_followup` builds its `br create` argv with title, type, an optional `--parent` and `-d` body, and nothing else (supervise.py:922-925). Two classification fields the overrun bead carries are therefore dropped on the floor, and the follow-up is created with br defaults instead.

**Priority is silently reset to P2.** Verified with an ephemeral probe: `br create -t task` with no `-p` returns priority 2. The scheduler ranks by priority, so the continuation of a P0 lane is dispatched behind every P2 in the ready set. This is the consequential half and it is currently invisible because all three follow-ups the engine has produced (jr0l.18, .19, .20) continue P2 parents (kjc5.32, .50, .51), so the default happened to match.

**Labels are dropped.** All three follow-ups carry `labels: None` while their parents carry `phase-7`. Phase membership in the implementation plan is a label rather than a re-parenting, so an unlabelled bead drops out of every phase-scoped query silently - it is not merely untidy, it is invisible to `br list --label phase-N` and to any planning pass that uses one.

Both are the same root cause: the follow-up inherits the work but not the classification of the work. `issue_type` is already carried across (supervise.py:898-900), so the fix is the same shape, at the same call site.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take an overrun bead whose priority is not 2 and which carries at least one label - for example a P1 bead labelled `phase-7`.
2. Let its lane cross the context ceiling so `finalize_followup` runs, or call `finalize_followup` directly.
3. Read the created follow-up with `br show <id> --json`.

Observed: `priority` is 2 and `labels` is null, whatever the overrun bead carried.
Expected: the follow-up carries the overrun bead priority and its labels.

## Remediation of existing instances

Three follow-ups already exist with the defect and must be relabelled as part of this fix, since they are in the ready set now and would be dispatched with no phase membership: jr0l.18, jr0l.19 and jr0l.20 all take `phase-7` from their parents. `basicly-jr0l.24` also carries no label but was not engine-created - it is bookkeeping in the same sweep, and takes `phase-7` as factory-hardening work.

## Notes

Do not widen this to other fields. Assignee, estimate and due date are deliberately not inherited: the remainder is a different size than the original and a stale estimate is worse than none.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`
payload.title: Carry priority and labels onto a context-ceiling follow-up bead

payload.description:
## Problem

Found by the call-site sweep that basicly-jr0l.25 owed. That bead fixed dropped classification on the overrun follow-up path; `decompose._create_child` has the same defect on the far more common path - every feature decomposition, not just a context-ceiling overrun.

`_create_child` (decompose.py:688-703) builds its `br create` argv from title, type, `--parent` and the body. No labels. So decomposing a feature labelled `phase-2` produces children with `labels: null`, and because phase membership in the implementation plan is a label rather than a re-parenting, every child drops out of `br list --label phase-2` the moment it is created. The parent feature stays in the phase while none of the work under it does.

This has not bitten yet only because the phase decomposition was done by hand rather than through `basicly decompose`. The next session that decomposes a phase feature - m4zv.2 and a3ab.1 are both live candidates - silently loses the whole slice from its phase.

`ChildSpec` has no labels field and should not get one: the label belongs to the parent, and a plan that could re-declare it would let an agent-authored plan move work between phases. Inherit from the feature record instead, read once per decomposition rather than once per child.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take a feature bead carrying at least one label - for example a bead labelled `phase-2`.
2. Decompose it: `basicly decompose <feature> --plan plan.toml`.
3. Read any created child with `br show <child> --json`.

Observed: `labels` is null on every child.
Expected: each child carries the labels the feature carried.

## Notes

Priority is deliberately out of scope here, and this differs from jr0l.25. On the overrun path there was a real source value being dropped - the overrun beads own priority. Here there is no source value at all: `ChildSpec` cannot declare a priority and the feature record priority is not obviously the right default for each child, since a decomposition often contains work of mixed urgency. Adding a plan-declared priority is a feature request rather than a defect fix and is not built here.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/decompose.py`
- `tests/test_decompose.py`
payload.title: Carry the parent labels onto every decomposed child

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the copilot decider confinement when a decider is dispatched then the read tool is denied alongside shell and write and a test asserts read appears in the copilot deny list and the module comment cites the live probe that established read is a valid deny name rather than claiming reads cannot be denied
payload.description:
## Problem

`runner._DECIDER_DENY_COPILOT` is `("shell", "write")` and the comment above it states copilot "has no deny spec for reads (permissions.yaml records the same gap), so its corpus bound stays contract-level while writing tracker state is genuinely blocked".

That is false, verified by live probe 2026-07-26 against the installed copilot CLI. `--deny-tool=read` is accepted and enforced: copilot reports `Permission to run this tool was denied due to the following rules: read` and the dispatch returns the CANNOT_READ sentinel.

So the decider on copilot can read any file on the machine today. The confinement exists precisely to stop that - the module comment says "a file-read tool lets it answer from outside the corpus it is bounded to" - and for the copilot family the guarantee is simply absent while the code reads as though the gap were unavoidable.

Probe sequence that established it, each one dispatch against a canary file:
- `--available-tools=` alone does not confine at all; copilot read the canary through the shell tool.
- `--deny-tool=shell` blocks the shell path, and copilot then falls back to a native read tool and still succeeds.
- `--deny-tool=shell --deny-tool=write --deny-tool=read` returns CANNOT_READ.

Note `--available-tools` is documented as a whitelist ("Only these tools will be available") but an empty value was ignored rather than denying everything, so the blocklist remains the mechanism.

Found while building the arm isolation for basicly-agzx.1, where the same confinement is needed to stop a recall measurement becoming a file-read measurement.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a directory containing a file with a known value.
2. Dispatch `copilot -p "read <file> and report the value" --deny-tool=shell --deny-tool=write`.
3. Observe the value is returned via the native read tool.
4. Add `--deny-tool=read` and observe the read is refused.

Observed: the shipped decider confinement omits `read`, so a copilot decider is unbounded on reads.
Expected: `_DECIDER_DENY_COPILOT` includes `read`, and the comment states the verified position rather than the assumed one.

## Notes

Also correct the stale claim in the module comment and in `.basicly/core/permissions/*.yaml` if it repeats it. Per the repo rule on evidence, the new comment should cite the probe rather than assert.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/runner.py`
- `tests/test_runner.py

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a retro proposal that is not promoted to the shared catalog when it is recorded then it lands in a git-ignored machine-local inbox and a test asserts that path contributes to no projected output and no always-on file so no agent can read it without a human promoting it first
payload.description:
## Context

Plan §7.4, resolved by owner decision 2026-07-26. The decision is made; this bead implements it.

DECIDED: record but never inject. A machine-local file collects retro proposals and is never loaded into any agents context. It is an inbox for a human to review, not guidance.

This is the rung between dropping a retro proposal and asking a human to amend the shared catalog, and the shape was chosen to make the named risk structurally impossible rather than merely bounded. The risk in the plan is bypass by accretion - guidance that shapes a machines sessions while never being reviewed - which is a near neighbour of the recorded non-goal of an agent-writable catalog, where a bad implementation bounces off a gate but a bad fragment is absorbed and silently degrades every later lane. An expiring lane that did shape sessions was considered and rejected on that ground: expiry bounds the exposure without removing it.

So the value kept is that a finding is not lost between sessions. The value deliberately not taken is that it never influences behaviour until a human has promoted it through the normal catalog path and its gates.

## Notes

The file must be git-ignored, and it must not live anywhere a projection or a hook would pick it up as guidance - the whole guarantee is that no agent reads it. Assert that rather than assuming it: a test that the path is absent from every projected output and from every always-on file is what makes the claim checkable.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/`
- `.gitignore`

payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-25: two pushes in a row failed the pages deployment. The second reported "Deployment request failed due to in progress deployment. Please cancel <sha> first or wait for it to complete", after the first had already aborted on its own timeout with the status stuck at updating_pages. No docs changed in either push, so the live site was never wrong - the deployments were simply queued behind each other by the push cadence a factory produces.

The reason it cannot be fixed today is the interesting part: pages here is GitHub's built-in dynamic workflow from a branch, so there is no workflow file in the repo to give a concurrency group. The only lever is a repository setting, which is exactly the kind of fix that must not be how correctness is established - it lives outside the repo, nobody else can see it, and it does not travel.

Taking ownership means adding a real workflow that builds and deploys the site with a concurrency group that cancels superseded runs, and switching the pages source from branch to actions. That is a deployment change, so it needs explicit approval before implementation rather than being folded into a prose pass.

Consider also whether the docs site needs to deploy on every push at all: it changes far less often than the tracker does, and a paths filter would remove most of the contention outright.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given two pushes in quick succession that do not change the site when the pages workflow runs then the superseded deployment is cancelled or skipped rather than failing, and the workflow lives in the repository so the behaviour is reviewable and travels with a clone

## Scope

- `.github/workflows/`
payload.title: Own the pages deployment so consecutive pushes cannot wedge it

payload.text: Blocked on an owner decision, not on code. repos/niksavis/basicly/pages reports build_type=legacy with source branch main path /docs, so Pages deploys straight from the branch and there is no workflow file in the repo to give a concurrency group. Implementing this means two halves that must land together: add .github/workflows/pages.yml, and flip the Pages source to GitHub Actions - a repository setting, so half the change cannot be reviewed in a diff and if either half lands alone the site stops updating. Not urgent: the wedged deployment cleared itself and pages is green again at 77bad78.

WONTFIX evidence, owner decision 2026-07-25.

Measured, not assumed: 2 failures in 100 pages-build-deployment runs, both on 2026-07-25 and 22 minutes apart, nothing since across 8 further deployments.
  https://github.com/niksavis/basicly/actions/runs/30162284901  14:46:09 -> 14:56:28 (10m19s)
  https://github.com/niksavis/basicly/actions/runs/30163026489  15:08:31 -> 15:08:51 (20s)

Mechanism, corrected from the original report: this is not slow build time. The build finishes in about 25 seconds every run. GitHub Pages permits one active deployment per environment, and the deploy step queues for that exclusive slot - the first failure waited 10 minutes for it and aborted with 'Timeout reached, aborting!', cancelling deployment d6d0e32; the second was rejected outright in 20 seconds. A faster or simpler site would not help, because the contention is on the deployment slot rather than on the build. The earlier characterisation as a rapid-consecutive-push problem is also unsupported: these two were 22 minutes apart.

Impact is nil. Pages publishes the current state of the branch rather than a per-commit artifact, so a skipped deployment is not lost work - the next successful run carries the missed commit's content too. The site is never left permanently stale. The cost is a red run in the Actions list plus a window, worst observed about 10 minutes, where the site serves the previous commit.

Why not fixed: the only real fix is a concurrency group, which can only be declared inside a workflow, and this repo is build_type=legacy deploying straight from main:/docs with no workflow file to put one in. It would take adding .github/workflows/pages.yml AND flipping the Pages source to GitHub Actions - a repository setting. Either half alone stops the site updating: the workflow without the flip is ignored because the branch deploy still wins, and the flip without the workflow deploys nothing at all. Trading a real silent-outage risk for a cleaner Actions tab is not worth it at a 2 percent transient failure rate with no user-visible effect.

Reopen if the Actions status needs to be unambiguous for automated scanning (an autonomous run reading gh run list cannot tell this apart from a real red), which is the one argument that would justify owning the deployment.

payload.description:
## Context

Retro finding from 2026-07-27. Owner asked for it to be tackled first thing next session.

`basicly loop run` imports `merge`/`verify`/`loop` from the base checkout at process start, then merges the harness branch into base during that same process. Modules are never reloaded, so a landing is scored by the code as it was **before** the merge it just performed.

On basicly-kjc5.56 this made a correct fix look broken: attempt 2 ran the previous attempt's matcher against a message only the new one recognised, did not match, and escalated at rework 2/2. The bead spent its entire rework budget proving nothing. Commit timestamps on main show the process starting at 23:34:20 and the fix merging at 23:34:26.

## Notes

Placement decided deliberately. The retro rule in the `session-finish` skill says an environment or timing trap becomes a quirks-fragment bullet, but this catalog has no quirks fragment - and the `harness-loop` **skill** already carries the sibling traps as blockquote warnings: never record the verify gate by hand, and commit the build's work on the branch before you advance. This belongs beside them.

Putting it in an on-demand skill rather than an always-on fragment is the point: the always-on baseline is at its cap with roughly 1700-2000 chars of headroom, and only someone driving a landing needs this. Zero always-on cost.

Content to add: a change to the landing-scoring modules is scored by the pre-merge code, so the first landing will not exercise it. Do not read that verdict as evidence the change is broken and do not spend rework retrying. Verify the new behaviour by calling it from base after the merge, then recover with `basicly verify --mode full --issue <id>` from base followed by `loop advance`.

Engine-side counterpart is basicly-kjc5.57, which makes the loop say this itself. This bead is the guidance half and does not wait on it.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/skills/harness-loop/skill.yaml`

payload.description:
## Context

Retro finding from 2026-07-27. Owner asked for it to be tackled first thing next session.

Building basicly-kjc5.56 I presented a build plan stating the fix needed no re-run, because the signature would be matched on the first failure. The premise was false: `verify._run` called `subprocess.run` with no capture, so no check result carried any output to match against. The owner approved provisioning a worktree on the strength of a mechanism I had not checked.

The same session produced a second instance. The first signature register held only br's singular message shape; the plural shape existed and was not checked for, and that bead's own landing then reproduced only the plural one.

## Problem with the current wording

`core-rules` says back claims with evidence - files read, commands run, tests. `quality-gate` covers verifying work after it is done and stating the scope actually exercised. Neither covers the artefact in between: **the plan an owner is asked to approve**. A plan is not a claim about finished work, so the existing rules do not bite, yet it is the thing a confirm-code checkpoint is spent on.

## Notes

One clause, not a section. The always-on baseline is at its cap with roughly 1700-2000 chars of headroom, so the edit must be a sentence in an existing fragment rather than a new one - and `quality-gate` is already the fragment about not overstating what you know.

Suggested substance, to be worded during the work: when a plan names a mechanism, the parts resting on unread code are stated as assumptions rather than as design, because an approval spent on a false premise costs the checkpoint and the rework budget behind it.

Verify the change against what the agent is actually told, not the file edited - the discipline recorded in `catalog-efficacy-design` after basicly-m4zv.8.

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/fragments/project/quality-gate.fragment.yaml`

payload.text:
[harness-info] SCOPE EXTENDED 2026-07-30 by an approved retro finding. This bead already proposes extending the quality-gate evidence rule from claims to the plan an owner approves. Extend it once more, to the same rule's weakest point: a claim published to a CONSUMER-FACING SURFACE.

The incident. I wrote 'gates enforced at commit time' into README.md, site/index.html and the GitHub repository About description as the differentiator against a competitor whose drift check is CI-only - and it was false on the axis that mattered. protect-generated-commit compares a STAGED generated blob against the manifest, so it catches a hand-edited output but is blind to a stale one: editing a fragment does not stage the generated file at all, so its bytes still match. The four projection gates ran in one CI job and appeared in no verify mode, and test_docs_drift covers docs-to-code rather than projection, so pytest at pre-push did not cover it either. Edit a fragment, skip the rebuild, commit, push - nothing local objected. Fixed afterwards in basicly-m4zv.11 by wiring the gates into fast, which made the claim true rather than requiring it to be walked back.

The rule to add: a competitive or capability claim published to a surface a consumer reads - README, the site, the repository description, release notes - must be exercised before it is published, not merely believed. The existing quality-gate wording already says to state only the verification scope actually exercised and never to upgrade 'expected to work' to 'works'; what it does not say is that a marketing surface is covered by that rule too. Three surfaces carried the false claim for about an hour because nothing connected the two ideas.

Note the asymmetry worth capturing: a wrong claim in code is caught by a gate, a wrong claim in a README is caught by a reader who may be a prospective consumer.

payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-29 while sequencing the spend-forecast fix for the release. basicly-jr0l.21
requires a spend forecast calibrated from run-record history. That history cannot exist
today, and no amount of running more work will produce it, because the forecast and the
actual are written to disjoint classes of record.

Measured over `.basicly/usage/run-records.json` - 122 records across 115 beads:

- 61 records carry `forecast_tokens`; every one is agent `manual` and none carries an
  actual token count
- 12 records carry a real token count; every one is agent `claude` and none carries a
  forecast
- 0 records carry both, so the forecast error has never once been computable
- `model` is a declared field on all 122 records and is null on all 122

So what basicly-jr0l.21 describes as a forecast that under-shot actual spend by 160 to
420 times is really a missing join. Nothing pairs the estimate with the outcome on one
carrier, so there is no error signal to calibrate a forecast against and no way to
detect that a forecast has drifted.

Write the forecast onto the same record the dispatch outcome lands on, so every
completed dispatch yields a forecast, an actual, a resolved model and a task class
together. This is a hard prerequisite for basicly-jr0l.21 rather than a sibling of it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a dispatch that carried a working-set forecast when the dispatch completes then
  a single run record holds the forecast alongside the actual tokens the resolved model
  and the task class, and a report over the log computes the forecast error per record
  and refuses to report an error for a record missing either half, with tests
payload.title: Pair the forecast with the actual on one run record so an error signal exists

payload.text:
[harness-info] Measurement re-taken 2026-07-31 over 149 records in .basicly/usage/run-records.json,
before starting the work. The bead's central claim holds and is in fact stronger than stated; two of
its figures do not.

    field              key present   non-null
    forecast_tokens           88          0
    scope_tokens              88         27
    tokens (actual)          149         12
    model                    149          0
    records with both halves                0

So "61 records carry forecast_tokens" is not reproducible: the field is non-null on **zero** records
and always has been, because **no writer passes it**. `runner.record_dispatch` accepts
`forecast_tokens` (runner.py:1089) and no call site supplies it — `loop._run_agent` passes
`scope_tokens` only, `supervise._dispatch_lane` passes neither, and the rubric and decider dispatches
pass neither. The 88 is key presence, which `asdict` writes for every declared field whether it was
populated or not.

That changes the shape of the work, not the verdict. This is not a join between two existing writers;
the forecast has no writer at all, so the fix is to start computing it at dispatch and to land it on
the same record the outcome lands on.

Scope boundary held deliberately: `model` is non-null on zero records too, and that is
basicly-kjc5.59's job (refuse to dispatch an unresolved model), not this bead's. The field is already
on the same record, so it populates when kjc5.59 lands; nothing here needs to resolve a model.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given an active spend ceiling and a dispatch whose adapter reports no measurable usage when the grant meter is computed then the estimated sample is not counted at face value and the run is either refused or recorded as unsafely metered with the reason surfaced to the operator, and given every dispatch in a session reports measured usage then the meter is unchanged, with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-29 while assessing basicly-2rn9. `policy.session_spend_tokens` is the autonomy
grant's meter and its docstring states the invariant plainly: "Estimated (chars/4) samples
count too - a spend ceiling must err toward halting, never toward uncounted spend."

The implementation cannot satisfy that. `runner.py:778` computes the estimate as
`(len(result.stdout) + len(result.stderr)) // 4` - over the *captured output only*. It cannot
see the prompt, the system prompt, the tool definitions, or cache writes, which is where
nearly all of an agentic dispatch's tokens are. So the estimate is structurally a floor far
below reality, not a conservative over-count.

Measured on a live copilot probe: 5514 bytes of stdout gives 1378 estimated tokens against
24210 real input tokens read from the session store - 17.6 times under. With default text
output the captured answer was two characters, so the estimate is about 1 token against
24210, roughly 24000 times under.

basicly-2rn9 fixes the copilot case by reading real usage. This bead fixes the class: any
adapter with no usage format, now or later, inherits the same silent under-count, and the
grant ceiling it meters cannot fire. A declared safety property that the code does not
enforce is worse than an absent one, because the docstring stops the next reader from
checking.

Two candidate stances, to be decided in the work: refuse to dispatch under an active spend
ceiling when usage cannot be measured, or treat an estimate as a floor with a stated
inflation multiplier and mark the grant as unsafely metered so the operator sees it. Either
way the estimate must stop being counted at face value.

Scope: `src/basicly/policy.py`, `src/basicly/runner.py`.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Run `copilot -p "reply with exactly: ok" --output-format json` and note the stdout byte
  count; the harness estimate is that count divided by four.
- Read `~/.copilot/session-state/<result.sessionId>/events.jsonl` and take
