payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-29 by probing a freshly installed codex CLI (codex-cli 0.146.0) in WSL.

`codex exec --json "<prompt>"` blocks on stdin. It prints "Reading additional input from
stdin..." and waits, producing zero bytes of output. Redirecting stdin from /dev/null makes
the identical command complete in seconds.

The harness inherits the parent's stdin for every arg-prompt runner. `runner.py:678` sets
`stdin = prompt if spec.prompt_via == "stdin" else None`, and `runner.py:695` passes
`stdin=subprocess.PIPE if stdin is not None else None` - so an arg-prompt dispatch gets
`stdin=None`, which in Popen means **inherit**, not close.

The codex adapter is `prompt_via="arg"`, so a headless codex dispatch inherits the
supervisor's stdin, blocks, and is eventually hard-killed at the dispatch timeout. It reads
as a stalled lane to the StallWatchdog rather than as the misconfiguration it is. This means
the codex adapter has never worked headless, which went unnoticed because this repo runs the
manual runner.

The repo's own non-interactive rule already covers this class: use non-interactive flags for
operations that can hang on a prompt. Closing stdin is the same measure applied to the
dispatch seam. It is a one-line fix and it hardens every current and future arg-prompt
adapter, not only codex.

## Steps to Reproduce

- `timeout 100 codex exec --json -s read-only "reply with exactly: ok"` - hangs until the
  timeout, stdout empty, stderr shows "Reading additional input from stdin..."
- The same command with `< /dev/null` appended - exits 0 in seconds with four JSONL events.
- Expected: a dispatch that supplies its prompt as an argument never waits on stdin.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an arg-prompt runner when a dispatch executes then the child process gets a closed
  stdin rather than inheriting the parent's, and given a stdin-prompt runner then the prompt
  is still written to the pipe unchanged, with tests
payload.title: A dispatch inherits stdin so codex blocks until the timeout

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a completed codex dispatch when its usage is read then the run record carries the uncached input the cached input the cache-write and the output token counts separately rather than a single summed total, and the reasoning token count is recorded with its relationship to output tokens verified rather than assumed, with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-29 while verifying the codex adapter against codex-cli 0.146.0. The `--json`
event stream's terminating event carries more than the harness reads:

    {"type":"turn.completed","usage":{"input_tokens":16383,"cached_input_tokens":10496,
     "cache_write_input_tokens":0,"output_tokens":5,"reasoning_output_tokens":0}}

`runner._CODEX_TOKEN_KEYS` is `("input_tokens", "output_tokens")`, so the token total is
about right but three fields are dropped: `cached_input_tokens`, `cache_write_input_tokens`
and `reasoning_output_tokens`.

That matters for cost rather than for volume. Cached input is priced roughly a tenth of
uncached, so a forecast that cannot see the cache split cannot price a codex dispatch - on
this probe 10496 of 16383 input tokens were cached, so a cost computed from the total alone
overstates it substantially. basicly-jr0l.21 needs the split to calibrate per model, and
basicly-kjc5.61 already puts per-tier cache_read and cache_write prices in the model map, so
the price side exists and only the measurement is missing.

Also confirm whether `reasoning_output_tokens` is additive to `output_tokens` or a subset of
it before summing, rather than assuming; the probe's zero value does not settle it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a completed codex dispatch when its usage is read then the run record carries the
  uncached input the cached input the cache-write and the output token counts separately
  rather than a single summed total, and the reasoning token count is recorded with its
  relationship to output tokens verified rather than assumed, with tests
payload.title: Codex usage drops the cache and reasoning token split

payload.text: Reasoning-token semantics VERIFIED 2026-07-31 by an authorised live probe of codex-cli 0.146.0 (the AC's verified-not-assumed requirement is now met; do not re-derive). Probe: codex exec --json -s read-only -c model_reasoning_effort=high on a prompt requiring multi-step arithmetic, so reasoning_output_tokens came back NON-ZERO for the first time - every prior sample on this machine was 0, which is why the question could not be settled from existing data. Observed turn.completed usage: input_tokens 12764, cached_input_tokens 9984, cache_write_input_tokens 0, output_tokens 155, reasoning_output_tokens 147. The session rollout records total_token_usage for the same turn as total_tokens 12919, and 12764 + 155 = 12919 exactly. So reasoning_output_tokens is a SUBSET of output_tokens and must NOT be added - summing them would double-count 147 of 155 output tokens. Corroborated by the payload itself: the visible answer was the 4-character string 2101, so 155 output minus 147 reasoning leaves the ~8 tokens the answer plus framing actually cost. This also reconfirms cached_input_tokens is a subset of input_tokens and excluded from codex's own total. Use the observed envelope above as the test fixture - the existing _CODEX_EVENTS fixture in tests/test_runner.py is hand-composed (documented-shape, never probed) and is missing cache_write_input_tokens, reasoning_output_tokens and total_tokens, which is precisely how the dropped-fields defect survived.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the built-in codex spec when a dispatch is executed against the installed CLI then the argv parses and the run completes rather than exiting on an invalid approval value, and given a spec whose approval or sandbox value the CLI does not accept then a check reports it by name before any dispatch is attempted, with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-29 immediately after basicly-jr0l.36 removed the stdin hang, by dispatching the
built-in codex spec through `runner.run` against codex-cli 0.146.0. The dispatch no longer
hangs but exits 2 in under a second with no output, because the argv is invalid:

    error: invalid value 'on-failure' for '--ask-for-approval <APPROVAL_POLICY>'
      [possible values: untrusted, on-request, never]

`RunnerSpec` for codex sets `approval="on-failure"`. That value is not in the CLI's enum, so
every codex dispatch fails at argument parsing. Together with basicly-jr0l.36 this means the
codex adapter has never completed a dispatch: it hung on stdin, and had it not hung it would
have failed to parse.

Flag placement is *not* the problem and should not be changed - `-a` is rejected when it
follows `exec` ("unexpected argument '-a' found"), so the existing pre-subcommand injection is
correct.

Choosing the replacement is a real decision, not a typo fix. The spec's comment states the
intent: fail safe in headless exec, where there is no approver, so an escalation must be
denied rather than auto-granted. Against the current enum, `never` paired with the existing
`--sandbox workspace-write` matches that intent best - the sandbox is the safety boundary and
`never` avoids waiting for an approver that cannot exist, with execution failures returned to
the model. `untrusted` and `on-request` both escalate to a human who is not there.

Because this changes an approval default in a distributed harness, the chosen value and the
reason belong in the commit and in the spec comment, and the enum should be validated rather
than trusted: a dry-run check that the configured approval and sandbox values are ones the
installed CLI accepts would have caught this at authoring time instead of at dispatch.

## Steps to Reproduce

- In a worktree: `uv run python -c "import basicly.runner as r; from pathlib import Path;
  s=next(x for x in r.BUILTIN_RUNNERS if x.name=='codex');
  print(r.run(s,'reply with exactly: ok',Path.cwd(),timeout=60).returncode)"`
- Observed: returncode 2, empty stdout, duration under a second.
- Directly: `codex --sandbox workspace-write -a on-failure exec "x" --json` prints the invalid
  value error and the three accepted values.
- Expected: a built-in adapter's default flags are accepted by the CLI it targets.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the built-in codex spec when a dispatch is executed against the installed CLI then the
  argv parses and the run completes rather than exiting on an invalid approval value, and given
  a spec whose approval or sandbox value the CLI does not accept then a check reports it by
  name before any dispatch is attempted, with tests
payload.title: The codex adapter pins an approval value the cli rejects

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given an operator at the final checkpoint when the prompt is displayed then it states that the merge has already happened and that approving publishes nothing and that there is no un-approve, with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Raised by the owner 2026-07-29, reading a live checkpoint prompt: "aha, ship is to bring it
back to main? we usually connect ship with release." The owner of the harness misread its own
phase name. That is the strongest possible signal - a consumer has strictly less context.

The name is wrong twice over. `ship` reads as *release* or *publish*, and it actually means
tear down the worktree and `br close` the bead. And it sits *after* the merge it sounds like
it performs: the merge happens one step earlier, at the build to verify advance, which the
engine already calls landing.

This has already cost us. The recorded incident: approving the ship checkpoint before the
landing advance printed `[merged]` short-circuits `derive_phase` to ship and wedges an
unmerged node, and there is no un-approve. That failure is downstream of the name - an
operator who believes ship means publish has no reason to wait for a merge line first.

Distinct from basicly-kjc5.45, which retires metaphor terms because they are poor retrieval
keys *for a model*. This one is an operator-facing safety defect: the word invites approving
the wrong thing at the wrong time.

Two options, and the owner picks:

- **Rename the phase**, most likely `ship` to `close`, since `br close` is exactly what it
  does and `land` is already taken by the merge step. v0.6.0 is already a breaking minor bump,
  so the rename is never cheaper than now.
- **Keep the name and fix the prompt**, stating plainly what the checkpoint does and does not
  do. Non-breaking, nearly free, and it alone would have prevented this misreading.

They are not exclusive; the prompt should be explicit either way.

Migration constraint if renaming, and it is the real work: the token is recorded state, not
just output. Existing beads carry `checkpoint ship: APPROVED` comments that `derive_phase`
reads, plus the `[policy] checkpoints` config, `loop status` and `advance` output, the
`--shipping <node>` flag on `basicly release`, and the harness-loop skill. A rename must keep
*reading* the old token while writing the new one, or every in-flight bead's history becomes
unreadable and phases derive wrongly.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Drive any leaf bead to its final checkpoint and read the prompt: it says "checkpoint ship:
  CONFIRMATION REQUIRED" and never states that approving publishes nothing.
- Observed: a reader concludes ship means release, or means the merge to main.
- Expected: the phase name and the prompt both make clear that the merge already happened and
  that nothing leaves the repo.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an operator at the final checkpoint when the prompt is displayed then it states that
  the merge has already happened and that approving publishes nothing, and given the phase is
  renamed then a bead whose recorded history uses the old token still derives its phase
  correctly, with tests
payload.title: The ship phase name reads as release and invites approving the wrong thing

payload.text: [decision] 2026-07-31, owner: OPTION 2 - fix the prompt, do NOT rename in v0.6.0. The bead argued 'v0.6.0 is already a breaking minor bump, so the rename is never cheaper than now'; that is overstated - v0.7.0/0.8.0/0.9.0 are all still pre-1.0.0 minors, so the real deadline is the 1.0.0 semver freeze (plan 1.1), not this release. Two further grounds: basicly-jr0l.49 (closed this session) removes the destructive consequence of the mis-approval, so what remains is a comprehension defect rather than a safety hole; and the owner narrowed this epic on 2026-07-30 to only what is most critical for the release. The rename to 'close' with its read-old/write-new migration is deferred to basicly-kjc5.45, the terminology pass, which must land before v1.0.0. Scope here is the prompt only, and the acceptance criteria are narrowed to match.

payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-25 while triaging whether any implemented bead had been left open. The first audit reported zero findings and was wrong: br list --json --limit 600 returns 50 issues and silently excludes closed ones, so the control set was empty and the comparison could only ever come back clean. The limit flag is accepted and ignored.

That is the exact failure mode the batch-query guidance already warns about - a whole-tracker audit that answers all clean because it never saw the tracker. The existing note says to prefer one batch query over a per-item loop, which is right but insufficient: the batch query itself was the lie here.

The reliable source for a whole-tracker question is the exported ledger, .beads/issues.jsonl, one JSON object per line, which carries every status including closed and tombstone. It is also far cheaper than shelling out per bead.

Say this in the tool-br skill, where br list is already documented, and pair it with the rule that any zero-finding audit must first be shown to detect a known-bad item - the control that caught this one was checking that closed beads appear in the commit set at all.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the projected tool-br guidance when an agent needs a whole-tracker answer then the prose states that br list json excludes closed beads and caps its page regardless of the limit flag, names .beads/issues.jsonl as the source that carries every status, and requires proving a zero-finding audit against a known-bad item before reporting it clean, with the projection gates green

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/skills/tool-br/skill.yaml`

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a grant issued on a root whose track is assembled from gating edges when a covered bead reaches a checkpoint the grant's level permits then the checkpoint is delegated without a confirm relay, and given any grant issuance then the output states how many beads the session covers so single-leaf coverage cannot be mistaken for track-wide coverage, with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-07-29 while testing an L3 grant on the release epic. The grant was issued on
basicly-m3od and the first `loop run --root basicly-m3od` still demanded a classify confirm
code, so the grant covered nothing.

Cause: `policy._session_issue_ids` walks **parent-child** dependents only. The release epic
gates its work with `blocks` edges - which is correct, since a bead's parent is its epic of
origin and nothing is re-parented - so none of the release's beads are in m3od's session tree.
A grant on m3od therefore covers a session containing only m3od itself, and its token ceiling
meters nothing.

This is a structural gap rather than a wiring mistake. A release, or any cross-cutting track,
gates work that lives under several different parents: this one spans m4zv, jr0l, kjc5, imnu
and u6jq, plus standalone beads such as sco6, z25w, l7zo, kvx5 and g7os that have no parent at
all. No single grant can cover it, because grant coverage is defined by descent while the
track is defined by dependency. The available workarounds are all poor: one grant per phase
epic still misses the parentless beads, and a grant per bead costs exactly the confirm relay it
was meant to remove.

Worth noting the ledger is also misleading in this state, not merely ineffective: it reports an
issued L3 with a 25000000 token ceiling, which reads as coverage over the release while
covering one bead. A grant whose session is a single leaf should say so.

Two candidate directions, for decision in the work: let a grant's session optionally follow
gating edges as well as parent-child, or let a grant name an explicit set of roots. Either way
issuance should report how many beads the grant actually covers, so a grant that covers one
cannot be mistaken for one that covers twenty.

## Steps to Reproduce

- `basicly policy grant basicly-m3od --level L3 --autonomy L3 --token-budget 25000000` then
  confirm; observe "grant: ISSUED L3".
- `basicly loop run basicly-m4zv.10 --work-type bug --root basicly-m3od`
- Observed: "checkpoint classify: CONFIRMATION REQUIRED" - the grant did not delegate, because
  basicly-m4zv.10 is a `blocks` dependency of m3od and a parent-child child of m4zv.
- Expected: a grant on the root a track is organised under covers that track's checkpoints, or
  issuance states plainly that it does not.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a grant issued on a root whose track is assembled from gating edges when a covered
  bead reaches a checkpoint the grant's level permits then the checkpoint is delegated without
  a confirm relay, and given any grant issuance then the output states how many beads the
  session covers so single-leaf coverage cannot be mistaken for track-wide coverage, with tests
payload.title: An autonomy grant cannot cover a track assembled from gating edges

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a br call that fails only on the updated_at-before-created_at validation error when the seam retries it within a stated bound then the call succeeds without the caller seeing the defect, and given a gate the engine has classified as unreliable when it recurs beyond that bound then the lane escalates to a human rather than blocking indefinitely, with tests
payload.description:
## Context

Hit twice consecutively 2026-07-29 while landing basicly-m4zv.10, blocking the lane both times
with a different victim test each run:

    br update fx-fv6 --external-ref worktree:... failed:
      Error: Validation failed: updated_at: cannot be before created_at
    br update fx-tmg -t task failed: same

This is the known upstream br clock defect. br rejects an update whose `updated_at` precedes
its `created_at`, and on this host the clock can move backwards by a hair between two
consecutive br calls, so a create-then-update pair in an integration fixture fails. Different
victim each run, which is why it reads as flakiness rather than as the resource limit it is -
the same misreading basicly-9s59 corrected for the machine-global br write lock.

Two distinct problems, and the second is ours:

1. The defect is upstream, so per the repo's own rule we do not fix br. We make our own call
   sites resilient, and the proof becomes a committed gate. This is also requirements input for
   basicly-vkh0.6, which already exists to carry the br defects we have paid for into the
   replacement.

2. **An unreliable gate blocks advancement indefinitely.** basicly-55yh correctly stopped a
   flaky gate from spending the lane's rework budget - observed `rework: verify=0` after two
   failures - but the lane still cannot advance, and the loop reports "verify full failed on
   pytest but passed unchanged on re-run" each time. A gate the engine has itself classified as
   unreliable is now a livelock rather than a bounded cost: while the flake recurs the lane
   never lands, and no rework counter ever escalates it to a human either. The bounded-rework
   design has no state for "untrustworthy result", only for "wrong work".

The fix for (1) is a bounded retry inside the br seam for exactly this validation error, named
and commented as a carried-forward dependency defect rather than a general retry. The fix for
(2) is a decision about what the loop should do with a gate it has classified as unreliable -
retry within a bound then escalate, rather than block forever.

## Steps to Reproduce

- With a lane committed on its harness branch, run `basicly loop run <issue>` twice.
- Observed both times: one integration test in tests/test_integration_loop.py fails on
  `Validation failed: updated_at: cannot be before created_at`, 1499 others pass, the loop
  reports the gate unreliable, `rework: verify=0`, and the phase stays at build.
- Expected: a gate classified as unreliable is retried within a bound and then escalated, and a
  known dependency clock defect does not fail our own call site.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a br call that fails only on the updated_at-before-created_at validation error when the
  seam retries it within a stated bound then the call succeeds without the caller seeing the
  defect, and given a gate the engine has classified as unreliable when it recurs beyond that
  bound then the lane escalates to a human rather than blocking indefinitely, with tests
payload.title: An unreliable gate livelocks a lane instead of escalating

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a br call rejected for clock skew when the retry runs then the ledger records the number of attempts and the observed timestamp gap, and given that evidence then the backoff bound is set from the measured distribution rather than a guessed constant, with tests
payload.description:
## Context

basicly-jr0l.41 added a bounded retry for br's updated_at-before-created_at rejection and the
defect recurred once afterwards, on basicly-m4zv.10's landing, with the verify gate's own
classification naming the same cause: "known dependency defect, pytest: br rejects its own write
when the host clock steps backwards between two writes".

The retry was present in that run - the worktree was rebased onto main and its 1508 collected
tests include jr0l.41's - so the coverage is incomplete rather than absent. The likely reason is
that the backoff is too short: `_CLOCK_SKEW_BACKOFF_S` is (0.05, 0.1, 0.2), so four attempts span
only 0.35 seconds of waiting, and a WSL clock step can exceed that comfortably. A skew larger
than the total backoff fails every attempt.

Not yet characterised, and that is the first task: the magnitude of the step is unmeasured, so
the right bound is unknown. Five subsequent full-suite runs passed (two on main, one in the
worktree, two integration-only), so the frequency is low, which is exactly why it needs
instrumentation rather than a guessed larger constant.

Worth noting what did work: the escalation half of basicly-jr0l.41 behaved correctly in the
field, blocking with "gate merge is unreliable: it failed and then passed unchanged 3 times" and
queueing a decision instead of deferring the lane forever.

The measurement belongs in the retry itself - it already routes every attempt through `_spawn`,
so the usage ledger can carry how far apart the two timestamps were and how many attempts were
needed. That turns the bound from a guess into a number, and it is the same evidence
basicly-vkh0.6 wants for the replacement.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Run a landing whose verify executes the full suite under `-n 4` repeatedly; roughly one run in
  several fails one arbitrary integration test with the clock-skew rejection.
- Observed: the retry does not always rescue it, and `basicly loop decisions <issue>` shows the
  unreliable-gate escalation naming the dependency defect.
- Expected: either the retry spans the real skew, or the skew's magnitude is recorded so the
  bound can be set from data.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a br call rejected for clock skew when the retry runs then the ledger records the number
  of attempts and the observed timestamp gap, and given that evidence then the backoff bound is
  set from the measured distribution rather than a guessed constant, with tests
payload.title: The clock-skew retry backoff is unmeasured and sometimes too short

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given the orchestration path when its integration coverage is assessed then either an end-to-end test drives loop dispatch through the real runner subprocess seam with a stand-in agent CLI and asserts the work lands through the merge queue, or the architecture reference states that agent-CLI integration is proved by dogfood run only and names which modules are unexercised
payload.description:
## Context

Raised by an external review of the repo on 2026-07-30, and confirmed by reading `tests/`.

The orchestration modules are heavily tested as logic: 8806 lines across `test_loop.py`,
`test_supervise.py`, `test_merge.py`, `test_runner.py`, `test_decisions.py` and
`test_rubrics.py`. `test_merge.py` and `test_worktree.py` exercise **real** git repositories -
real `git init`, real commits, real conflicts - so the merge and worktree logic is not mocked.

What is mocked everywhere is the **agent-CLI boundary**: 335 monkeypatch calls in
`test_supervise.py` and 335 in `test_loop.py`, and no test anywhere spawns a real `claude`,
`codex` or `copilot` process. `runner.py` is the seam and its subprocess invocation is always
replaced.

So the claim "the factory runs multiple agents concurrently and lands their work" rests on the
`basicly-kjc5.22` dogfood run recorded in the tracker - 3 concurrent lanes, landed through the
merge queue, no human editing code - and not on anything repeatable. That is real evidence but
it is a one-off, it cannot regress-detect, and it is exactly what an evaluator probes first.

This is not a request to run paid agents in CI on every push. The likely shape is a fake agent
CLI on PATH that behaves like a real one - reads the prompt, writes a commit, exits - so the
loop, the worktree provisioning, the merge queue and the gate recording are exercised end to
end through `runner.py`'s real subprocess path rather than around it. The unresolved question,
and the reason this is a task rather than a chore, is whether that proves enough to be worth
its maintenance, or whether the honest move is instead to state the dogfood-only boundary
explicitly in the architecture reference so nobody over-reads the coverage.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the orchestration path when its integration coverage is assessed then either an end-to-end test drives loop dispatch through the real runner subprocess seam with a stand-in agent CLI and asserts the work lands through the merge queue, or the architecture reference states that agent-CLI integration is proved by dogfood run only and names which modules are unexercised
payload.title: Close or declare the gap where no test drives a real agent CLI through the loop

payload.text: [harness-decision] Owner decision 2026-07-30: build the fake-agent-CLI e2e test - a stand-in binary on PATH driven through the real subprocess seam, asserting dispatch through landing via the merge queue. The declare-only alternative was rejected. Deciding evidence: basicly-jr0l.38 shows the codex adapter has never completed a dispatch, exactly the defect class this test catches deterministically in CI. Real-CLI behavior stays proved by dogfood.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a lane whose committed changes touch a file outside its declared scope when the build to verify landing runs then the out-of-scope paths are recorded against the bead as evidence and the configured policy for a collision with another live lane's scope is applied deterministically
payload.description:
## Context

From the 2026-07-30 analysis of `automazeio/ccpm` (`reference-repos/_analysis/ccpm.md`).

`decompose.py` treats a child's declared file-scope as a **planning input only**. `group_children`
(`src/basicly/decompose.py:160-188`) computes grouping from the scope globs and
`govern_working_set` sizes the plan from them, and after that nothing ever checks the declaration
again. A lane is free to edit any file it likes.

So a wrong or stale scope declaration is not detected when it is made - it surfaces later and
indirectly, as a conflict in the merge queue (`src/basicly/merge.py`), by which point two lanes
have already done work that fights. The plan was wrong at decompose time and we found out at
landing time.

The fix is cheap and needs nothing new: at the build-to-verify landing, compare the lane's actual
changed set against its declared scope. `git diff --name-only` against the merge base is already
available on that path, and the declared globs are on the bead. A file outside the declared scope
is a finding about the *plan*, and it is the same class of evidence the loop already records for
gates.

Design question this bead must answer rather than assume: whether an out-of-scope edit should
**block** the landing or be recorded as an advisory finding. Blocking is the deterministic choice
and matches the rule that deterministic checks are authoritative, but a plan authored by an agent
will sometimes be legitimately incomplete, and a hard block converts every such case into a
rework cycle. A defensible middle is to block only when the out-of-scope file is inside *another
live lane's* declared scope, which is the case that actually causes the collision.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane whose committed changes touch a file outside its declared scope when the build to verify landing runs then the out-of-scope paths are recorded against the bead as evidence and the configured policy for a collision with another live lane's scope is applied deterministically
payload.title: Verify the declared file scope at landing instead of trusting it at decompose

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a decomposition where several children declare one shared path in their scopes when the plan is grouped then the children are not all collapsed into a single serial group by that path alone and the decompose output names the path that would have caused a collapse
payload.description:
## Context

From the 2026-07-30 analysis of `automazeio/ccpm` (`reference-repos/_analysis/ccpm.md`), and
confirmed by reading our own code.

`group_children` (`src/basicly/decompose.py:160-188`) is union-find over the **transitive closure**
of pairwise scope overlap: any two children whose scopes can match a common path are merged into
one group, and one group is serialized into a single `blocks` chain.

The pathology that follows is not theoretical. If several children each legitimately declare a
shared file - `pyproject.toml`, a lockfile, a shared `__init__.py`, a config manifest - then every
one of those children overlaps every other through that single file, the transitive closure
collapses them all into **one group**, and the decomposition serializes work that was almost
entirely parallel. The more realistic the scope declarations, the worse it gets, because a careful
author is *more* likely to declare the manifest they will touch.

ccpm's answer is a designated owner for a shared file (`execute.md:212`): exactly one work item
owns it, and the others are not serialized against it.

What this bead must decide is how to express that here without letting an agent-authored plan use
it to hide a real collision. Options to weigh, not a chosen design:

- a per-child declaration splitting scope into owned paths and touched-but-not-owned paths, with
  only owned-versus-owned overlap serializing;
- a catalog-level list of paths that never serialize (manifests, lockfiles), which is simpler and
  needs no plan change but is a blunt instrument;
- keeping the current behaviour and instead reporting, at decompose time, *which single path*
  caused a group to collapse - the cheapest option, and it may be enough, because the current
  failure is silent rather than wrong.

Note the interaction with `basicly-jr0l.16` and the sizing governor: a collapsed group changes the
serial chain length, which changes the forecast, so this is not purely a throughput question.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a decomposition where several children declare one shared path in their scopes when the plan is grouped then the children are not all collapsed into a single serial group by that path alone, and the decompose output names the path that would have caused a collapse

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Author a decomposition where four children each declare a scope that includes `pyproject.toml` plus a distinct module of their own.
2. Run `basicly decompose <feature> --plan plan.toml --dry-run`.
3. Observed: all four children land in one group and are chained serially, so no two can run in parallel. Expected: the distinct modules keep them parallel, or the report names `pyproject.toml` as the collapsing path.
payload.title: Stop one shared path collapsing every child into a single serial group

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a lane landing through the merge queue when the merge function returns a merged status then it has asserted that the lane head is an ancestor of the target ref after the push and a lane whose branch moved after it was queued is refused rather than landed
payload.description:
## Context

From the gastown analysis (`reference-repos/_analysis/gastown.md`), and the one technique there
worth taking. Gastown never believes its own merge: after merging and pushing it re-resolves the ref
and *proves* the submitted commit is an ancestor of the target, and it refuses to land at all if the
lane branch moved since it was queued (`engineer.go:1478-1499`, `:1538-1560`,
`internal/git/git.go:2091-2144`).

We have the ancestry check, but only at the **ship** gate (`src/basicly/loop.py:299-304`) - a
backstop that fires after the fact. `merge.py` can return a merged result without ever proving the
commit landed.

This repo has recorded the resulting incident **twice**: a bead closed with its code stranded
unmerged. Both times the recovery was manual. Both times the proof that would have caught it is
about twenty lines of `rev-parse` plus `merge-base --is-ancestor`, with no dependency.

Two distinct assertions, and both matter:

1. **Post-merge proof** - after the merge and push, re-resolve the target ref and assert the lane's
   head commit is an ancestor of it. A `MergeResult(status="merged")` must be unreachable without
   that assertion passing.
2. **Pre-merge staleness refusal** - record the lane branch's head when it enters the queue, and
   refuse to land if it has moved since. A lane that grew a commit while queued was verified in a
   state that no longer exists.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Land a lane through the merge queue while something else advances the target ref.
2. Observed: the merge reports merged on the basis of its own return code; only the later ship gate
   can notice a discrepancy, and if ship is reached by another path the bead closes with code
   unmerged. Expected: the merge itself refuses to report success without proving the commit is an
   ancestor of the target.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane landing through the merge queue when the merge function returns a merged status then it has asserted that the lane head is an ancestor of the target ref after the push, and a lane whose branch moved after it was queued is refused rather than landed
payload.title: Prove the merge landed instead of trusting the merge return code

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a worktree teardown where a git invocation fails or returns an unparsable result when the teardown decides whether to remove then it refuses and reports the indeterminate state rather than deleting and the decision is made by a pure classifier with a test for each fail-closed branch
payload.description:
## Context

From the gastown analysis (`reference-repos/_analysis/gastown.md`). Its worktree-teardown guard
stack (`internal/polecat/manager.go:1138-1305`) layers six checks behind a fail-closed pure
classifier, and the rule worth stealing is one line of policy inside it: **a transient git error must
never authorize a deletion.**

Our `worktree.py` teardown decides from git state whether a worktree is safe to remove. If a git
invocation fails transiently - a lock held by a concurrent lane, a filesystem hiccup, an interrupted
index write - a reader that treats "could not determine" as "nothing to keep" deletes work. The
failure is silent and unrecoverable: the branch and its commits go with the worktree.

This is the same class as `basicly-vkh0.8`, where a worktree teardown discarded telemetry it had
recorded. That one cost measurements; this one would cost committed work.

What to check and fix: every branch in the teardown path where a git failure or an unparsable
result leads to a removal rather than a refusal, and whether the classifier that decides is pure and
separately testable. Fail closed - an undetermined state must hold the worktree and surface, because
holding costs disk and deleting costs work.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Make a git query in the teardown path fail transiently (for example hold the index lock from a
   concurrent process) while a worktree carries unmerged commits.
2. Observed: the teardown path treats the indeterminate result as safe and removes the worktree and
   its branch. Expected: it refuses, holds the worktree, and reports why.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a worktree teardown where a git invocation fails or returns an unparsable result when the teardown decides whether to remove then it refuses and reports the indeterminate state rather than deleting, and the decision is made by a pure classifier with a test for each fail-closed branch
payload.title: Never let a transient git failure authorize a worktree deletion

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given derive_phase when it is reviewed for accidental complexity then each rung predicate is either justified in a comment or removed the landed invariant is unchanged and still covered by a test and the existing phase-derivation tests pass without modification
payload.description:
## Context

From the Symphony analysis (`reference-repos/_analysis/symphony.md`), kept as a separate concern
after declarative phases were rejected on 2026-07-30.

Symphony's engine knows only **three** predicates about a work item - active, terminal, neither - and
drives a seven-stage lifecycle on that alone. Our `derive_phase`
(`src/basicly/loop_state.py:106-143`) uses a five-rung ladder over five inputs: status, approved
checkpoints, worktree binding, gate status, and has-children.

The point is not to copy their model - they pay for that simplicity by holding all real state in RAM,
which is why the same analysis rejects their state design outright. The point is that a much simpler
engine drove a longer lifecycle, which is grounds to check ours for accidental complexity rather than
essential complexity.

Specific questions to answer, with the answer "it is all essential" being an acceptable and useful
outcome:

- Is `has_children` doing work that the worktree binding or the gate status does not already imply?
- Do `classify` and `decompose` need separate rungs, given both are checkpoint-gated and the
  decompose rung already ORs in `has_children`?
- Could the ladder be expressed as one ordered table of `(phase, predicate)` pairs where every
  predicate is a named function, making each independently testable? That keeps everything typed -
  it is a refactor for reviewability, explicitly *not* the rejected move to data.

Hard constraint: the `verified`/landed term must survive intact. It encodes the invariant from
incident `basicly-k35r` and is the reason declarative phases were rejected; a simplification that
loses it is a regression, not a simplification. Any change here needs the existing derive_phase tests
green unchanged, plus a case per rung.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given derive_phase when it is reviewed for accidental complexity then each rung's predicate is either justified in a comment or removed, the landed invariant is unchanged and still covered by a test, and the existing phase-derivation tests pass without modification
payload.title: Review the phase ladder for accidental complexity without moving it to data

payload.text: [harness-info] Review evidence 2026-07-30 at 2a0ba60: the ladder is not over-long (seven outcomes including closed and intake). The accidental complexity is two things: (a) the verified composite's conjunct (worktree is not None or has_children) is redundant inside the ship rung - when worktree is None the rung's own disjunct already fires, and when it is not None the conjunct is trivially true, so has_children never influences ship, only verify; (b) the ship rung's worktree is None conflates torn-down-after-merge with never-provisioned, which is now filed as basicly-jr0l.49. Scope this review to naming and justifying those two predicates; no rung is unreachable.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a leaf with no worktree binding and no recorded landing when ship is approved out of order then derive_phase does not report ship and loop advance refuses to close it, and given a node whose worktree was torn down after a proven merge then ship still derives and closes as today, with a regression test per branch
payload.description:
## Context

From the 2026-07-30 architecture review, confirmed at 2a0ba60. The derive_phase ship rung
(loop_state.py:132-135) reads: ship in checkpoints and (worktree is None or verified).
`worktree is None` was meant to mean torn down after merge, but a leaf that never built also
has no binding. approve_checkpoint enforces no phase ordering (policy.py:468-473), so a ship
approval recorded out of order on an unstarted leaf derives phase ship, and _on_ship skips the
_worktree_landed guard when the binding is None (loop.py:317-326) and closes the bead with zero
work done. The basicly-k35r fix covered only the bound-worktree case.

Interacts with basicly-jr0l.39: that bead fixes the name that invites the mis-approval; this one
fixes the ladder hole that makes the mis-approval destructive.

Fix direction: the ship rung must distinguish never-built (require landed evidence) from
torn-down-after-merge. The green required gate is that evidence - it is recorded by the
build->verify landing and by nothing else a never-built node has run.

## Steps to Reproduce

- Call derive_phase directly with the two states that must differ:
  `uv run python -c "from basicly import loop_state, policy;
  no_gates = policy.GateStatus(can_advance=False, required_passed=(), required_failed=(),
  required_missing=('verify',), advisory=());
  green = policy.GateStatus(can_advance=True, required_passed=('verify',), required_failed=(),
  required_missing=(), advisory=());
  print(loop_state.derive_phase('open', ('ship',), None, no_gates, False));
  print(loop_state.derive_phase('open', ('ship',), None, green, False))"`
- Observed at 34ab45e: both print `ship`. The never-built leaf and the landed-and-torn-down leaf
  are indistinguishable, so `loop advance` runs _on_ship on the never-built one and closes it.
- Expected: the never-built leaf derives a phase below ship and cannot be closed; the
  torn-down-after-merge leaf still derives ship.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a leaf with no worktree binding and no recorded landing when ship is approved out of
  order then derive_phase does not report ship and loop advance refuses to close it, and given a
  node whose worktree was torn down after a proven merge then ship still derives and closes as
  today, with a regression test per branch
payload.title: An out-of-order ship approval closes a never-provisioned leaf with zero work

payload.description:
## Context

A backwards wall-clock step made the tracker reject its own writes (updated_at before created_at) during the basicly-kjc5.21 integration work. The engine itself was already correct - every duration and timeout uses perf_counter/monotonic - but that is a convention, not a gate, and nothing stops the next change measuring an interval with time.time().

The two remaining wall-clock reads are structurally forced: supervise compares against a filesystem mtime, policy persists a TTL across processes. Both must stay allowlisted with the reason recorded.

The tracker half is the durable lesson for our own work tracker: an event log must order by sequence, and timestamps must be evidence, never a constraint that can refuse a write.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the engine when an elapsed-time measurement is taken from a wall clock then a guard test fails naming the offending site, with the two cross-process sites allowlisted and each carrying its reason
- Given docs/work-tracker.md when the storage design is read then it records that our tracker orders by sequence and never rejects a write on timestamp ordering

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a lane whose branch is already an ancestor of base with no verify gate recorded when the landing advance runs then it records the gate and completes the landing instead of reporting not-ready and no rework is charged, covered by a test that interrupts the flow between merge and gate recording
payload.description:
## Context

From the 2026-07-30 architecture review, confirmed at 2a0ba60. `_verify_and_land` merges first
(`merge.py`) and records the verify gate after (`loop.py:633`). A crash, kill, or lost connection
between the two leaves the branch already an ancestor of base with no gate recorded.

The phase then re-derives to `build`, the next advance re-runs `merge_worktree`, and
`_worktree_land_readiness` sees `rev-list base..branch == 0` and reports `not-ready` with the
misleading message "no committed work to land" — when in truth the work landed and only the gate
record is missing. Under the supervisor that routes to `_route_failed` and burns the dispatch
rework cap (`supervise.py`), so a lane that succeeded is charged for it.

Related: basicly-jr0l.46 put the ancestry proof inside the merge. This bead is the forward
recovery of the half-landed state that proof can now recognise.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Drive a leaf bead to the build->verify landing so `merge_worktree` merges the branch into base.
2. Interrupt the process after the merge commit exists but before the verify gate is recorded
   (the window between `merge.merge_worktree` returning merged and `_record_verify` running).
3. Re-run `basicly loop advance <id>`.
4. Observed: the landing reports `not-ready` — "no committed work to land: <branch> has no commits
   ahead of main" — and a supervised pass charges the lane a rework attempt for it. Expected: the
   landing recognises the branch is already an ancestor of base, records the gate, and completes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane whose branch is already an ancestor of base with no verify gate recorded when the landing advance runs then it records the gate and completes the landing instead of reporting not-ready and no rework is charged, covered by a test that interrupts the flow between merge and gate recording
payload.title: A crash between merge and gate recording strands the lane as not-ready

payload.description: From the 2026-07-30 architecture review, confirmed at 2a0ba60. policy.gate_status (policy.py:243-259) trusts any recorded gate result regardless of provider or author, and a dispatched lane agent shares the real tracker via the worktree beads redirect (worktree.py:264-272) - so a single br gate report --gate verify --status pass issued from inside a dispatch satisfies a required gate. The hard constraint that no model holds authority over a required gate currently holds only by agent good behavior. The code already acknowledges the marker channels as mitigation-not-boundary (policy.py:476-483, 602-609); grant and checkpoint marker forgery is the same class and stays acknowledged there. The narrowest hardening available today is cheap: for the required set, count only gate results whose provider is the engine's own GATE_PROVIDER (verify.py:29). Advisory gates keep accepting any provider.

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a lane flagged as stalled whose dispatch then completes when the pass ends then the stall decision is consumed or auto-answered and the next pass dispatches the lane normally, with a test covering the held-landing case
payload.description:
## Context

From the 2026-07-30 architecture review, confirmed at 2a0ba60. `flag_stalled_lane` enqueues a
`stall` decision mid-run when the `StallWatchdog` sees no commits and no file changes for
`stall_after` seconds. The item deliberately does not stop the run — it asks a human whether to
intervene now or let the hard kill arrive.

Nothing ever consumes it. If the flagged dispatch subsequently finishes on its own, the pending
item survives the run, and its question is now moot: the hard kill it asks about will never
arrive. The next pass then drops the lane from `ready_lanes` (via `has_pending`) and from the
carry (`_carried_outcomes` filters by `ready_lanes` eligibility), so a lane that was merely slow
parks on an unanswerable question until a human clears it by hand.

The held- or bounced-landing case is the one that bites: a green dispatch whose landing is held
still ends the pass with the stall item pending.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a short `stall_after` so the watchdog flags a lane mid-run.
2. Let the flagged dispatch finish normally (no `runner_timeout`), with its landing held or
   bounced rather than merged.
3. Start the next supervised pass.
4. Observed: the lane is absent from `ready_lanes` because a `stall` decision is still pending,
   asking whether to intervene before a hard kill that already cannot happen; a human must answer
   it before the lane moves again. Expected: the stall flag is consumed or auto-answered when its
   dispatch completes, and the next pass dispatches the lane normally.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a lane flagged as stalled whose dispatch then completes when the pass ends then the stall decision is consumed or auto-answered and the next pass dispatches the lane normally, with a test covering the held-landing case
payload.title: A stall decision outliving a green run parks the lane on a moot question

discriminate and the behaviour is really present, rather than passing vacuously.

payload.text:
Measured evidence, 2026-08-03, from a live three-lane pass on basicly-tcmy. Every lane exceeded its declared scope, and the declarations were not careless - they were written from the bead's description and were still wrong.

| lane | files touched | outside declared scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| basicly-tcmy.5 | 15 | 7 (cli.py, config.py, decisions.py, rubrics.py, runner.py, test_cli_loop.py, test_config.py) |
| basicly-tcmy.6 | 8 | 2 (test_cli_policy.py, test_merge.py) |
| basicly-tcmy.22 | 7 | 1 (test_docs_claims.py) |

Two things this says, and they pull in opposite directions.

The overruns are **coherent with the work**. tcmy.5 unifies the phase name recorded for a write dispatch, and that name is passed at every record_dispatch call site - so decisions.py, rubrics.py and runner.py are where the change has to land. A landing check that simply refused an undeclared file would refuse correct work.

But the *sizing* rests on the declaration. tcmy.5 was admitted at 66780 working-set tokens against globs covering 8 files, then read 15. So the estimate that cleared the band described roughly half the work, which is the same failure basicly-qorx describes from the other end: the declaration is a self-report the engine both funds and gates on.

Worth noting who declared these: the driver widened tcmy.5 from 5 files to 8 in base before dispatch, precisely to avoid a mid-run scope rewrite, and still missed 7. So 'the decomposer should declare better' is not the fix. Either the check has to tolerate a bounded overrun and report it, or the estimate has to stop being a function of a human-written glob list - which is where basicly-agzx.2 (AST-derived localisation) actually pays off, since reachable surface is derivable and a glob list is a guess.

Also relevant to the merge queue: all three lanes are editing src/basicly/cli.py concurrently, which none of the three declared as shared. The serial queue rebases the second and third landings onto the first, with no agent present to resolve a conflict.

payload.description:
# Bead draft — seed_lanes reports seed-blocked after successfully provisioning lanes

Type: bug
Priority: P1 (it makes the documented one-command supervised run fail on a cold root)

## Summary

`seed_lanes` provisions the root's child worktrees, then routes the outcome on whether the
*root's own* advance progressed. For a package root that is parked awaiting children, no
advance can ever progress — so a pass that successfully provisioned N lanes reports
`seed-blocked` and stops, discarding the work it just did.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Cold root with open children and no live worktrees (`basicly loop preflight <root>` shows
   `worktrees: 0 live`, `lanes: 0 dispatchable now`).
2. Ensure a grant with a token budget covers the root, so the metered-runner check passes.
3. Run `basicly loop supervise <root> --autonomy L1`.

Observed, on basicly-jr0l at main 66500a1:

```
Created worktree 'basicly-jr0l-35'   (x5, each with uv sync + npm install)
dispatch: (no ready build-phase lanes)
routed:   basicly-jr0l -> seed-blocked - no lane could be provisioned from 28 open child(ren)
          - building: 28 child track(s) still open
```

The message is false in its own terms: five lanes *were* provisioned. Probing immediately
after the pass exited:

```
supervise.ready_lanes(repo, derive_session(repo, 'basicly-jr0l')) -> 5 lanes, all live=True
```

Running the identical command a second time dispatched all four fundable lanes.

## Root cause

`src/basicly/supervise.py:2422-2438`. `seed_lanes` calls `loop.run_until_blocked(repo_root,
session.root_issue)` and then:

- `if any(step.progressed for step in steps): -> "seeded"`
- otherwise `-> "seed-blocked"`

`progressed` describes the *root's* phase movement. The root here is an epic at phase
`decompose` with `advance BLOCKED, missing: verify` (`basicly loop status basicly-jr0l`), so
it cannot progress by construction — while `loop._ensure_child_worktrees`, reached on that
same advance, has already bound worktrees to the children. Provisioning success and root
progress are two different facts and only the second is consulted.

`should_continue` then reads the non-retriable `seed-blocked` outcome and ends the pass, so
the newly ready lanes are never dispatched in the pass that created them.

## Suggested fix

Route on whether any lane became ready, not on root progress: re-evaluate `ready_lanes`
(or count new bindings) after `run_until_blocked` and return `seeded` when the ready set is
non-empty, keeping `seed-blocked` for the genuinely-nothing-provisioned case. The
termination guarantee the docstring is protecting still holds, because the retry condition
becomes "lanes exist to dispatch" rather than "the root moved".

Regression test: a root that cannot advance (blocked gate) but whose children acquire
worktrees must route `seeded`, and the pass must proceed to dispatch.

## Scope

- src/basicly/supervise.py  (seed_lanes routing, ~15 lines)
- tests/test_supervise.py   (one regression test for the blocked-root-but-lanes-provisioned case)

## Notes

Cost of the bug: one wasted provisioning cycle (5x `uv sync` + `npm install`) and a false
"cannot start work" report. It masquerades as the basicly-t73d regression, which it is not —
t73d's seeding does run and does work; only the reporting and continuation are wrong.

payload.acceptance_criteria: The unsizeable-lane bound is derived from a printed distribution rather than judgment and its observed overrun rate against recorded actuals meets a stated target; an assumed-bound dispatch records a forecast so basicly usage forecast can pair it with the actual; a test pins the estimator against a recorded bimodal sample.
payload.description:
## Problem

The unsizeable-lane bound that `basicly-vz78` introduced underestimated every lane in the first
multi-lane proof run by 2.3x to 2.9x, so a pass forecast at 16,316,972 tokens actually spent
43,599,830 - a 108% overrun of the 21,000,000 grant ceiling that funded it.

`decompose.unsized_lane_tokens` returns the median of recent measured lane actuals, which was
4,079,243 at dispatch time. The four lanes dispatched on 2026-08-01 measured:

| Lane | Tokens | Cost | Duration | Ratio to bound |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| basicly-jr0l.35 | 9418977 | $7.36 | 1010.6s | 2.31x |
| basicly-jr0l.43 | 11867602 | $9.46 | 1102.6s | 2.91x |
| basicly-jr0l.44 | 10834801 | $8.24 | 1048.3s | 2.66x |
| basicly-jr0l.45 | 11478450 | $8.67 | 1084.5s | 2.81x |
| total | 43599830 | $33.73 | | 2.67x |

Every one is above the bound and none is close to it. The estimator is not noisy around the
truth, it is biased low, so the error does not cancel across a pass - it multiplies by lane count.

The median was chosen (correctly, on the evidence then available) because the recorded population
was bimodal: leaves at 856k-4.08M and packages driving sub-tasks at 7.67M-20.6M, with no run-record
field distinguishing them. These four were leaves by that definition - `ready_lanes` excludes
sub-task lanes - yet they all landed in the package band. So the bimodality the median was
protecting against is not leaf-versus-package; the leaf population itself spans an order of
magnitude and the median of the old sample does not describe the new one.

Corroborating signal from the same run: all four lanes crossed the 120,000 context ceiling
(`context_ceiling` 0.6), finishing at 159120, 209226, 172628 and 165331 tokens. A lane that
overruns its context budget by 33-74% is doing far more work than the token bound assumed, so the
two overruns are one phenomenon measured twice.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Ensure `.basicly/usage/run-records.json` holds the historical sample whose median is ~4.08M.
2. Grant a budget and run `basicly loop supervise basicly-jr0l --autonomy L1` with four
   unsizeable leaf lanes ready (no `## Scope` section, so `decompose.dispatch_sizing` returns None).
3. Read the printed `spend:` line - it forecasts 4 x 4079243 = 16316972 and admits the pass.
4. Let the pass complete and read the halt line and the run records.

Observed: `halted: L1 grant token_budget spent (43599830/21000000 tokens under this grant)`.
All four records carry `estimated=false`, so this is measured spend, not the meter defect that
`basicly-jr0l.35` fixed in the same run.

## Root Cause

`decompose.unsized_lane_tokens` picks a central-tendency statistic for what is used as a *bound*.
A median is the value half the population exceeds; using it as a ceiling guarantees roughly half
of all lanes overrun, and says nothing about by how much. The forecast it feeds is consumed by
`supervise.admit_pass_spend` as if it were an upper estimate.

The deeper issue is that the sample is not stationary. The bound is learned from past lanes, but
the work being dispatched changes with the tracker, so a bound calibrated on one epoch's leaves
silently misprices the next. Nothing in the pass compares the bound against what the lanes
actually did afterwards, so the error is invisible until a grant halts.

## Suggested Direction

Not "use the max" - that was already refuted, because a max drawn from the package band refuses
passes that genuinely fit. Options worth evaluating against the recorded sample, printing the
distribution first:

- An upper quantile of the *leaf-only* population once leaves are distinguishable in the record
  (which requires recording whether a lane drove sub-tasks - currently no field does).
- A bound with an explicit safety factor over the median, chosen so the observed overrun rate
  matches a stated target rather than by judgment.
- Treat the bound as advisory and rely on a real in-flight ceiling instead (see the sibling bead
  on pass admission never interrupting a running lane) - a correct estimate is not required if
  spend is actually enforced while it accrues.

Whichever is chosen, the pass must record forecast-vs-actual per lane so the bound can be
calibrated from outcomes. Note that today an assumed bound does not count as a forecast for
pairing: after this run `basicly usage forecast` still reports "No dispatch carries both a forecast
and a measured actual", now 17 actual with no forecast. So the telemetry that would detect this
bias is not being produced by the very mechanism that needs it.

## Scope

- src/basicly/decompose.py  (unsized_lane_tokens estimator)
- src/basicly/supervise.py  (record the assumed bound as a forecast so it pairs with the actual)
- tests/test_decompose.py   (estimator behaviour against a recorded bimodal sample)
- tests/test_supervise.py   (forecast/actual pairing for an assumed-bound lane)

payload.acceptance_criteria: A fan-out whose grant remainder is exhausted part way starts no further lanes and says so before spending; already-running lanes are allowed to finish; a test drives a pass whose budget runs out mid-fan-out and asserts the later lanes never start.
payload.description:
## Problem

No mechanism stops a supervised pass while it is spending. `dispatch_lanes` evaluates admission
once, before any runner starts, and never re-checks; the retrospective halt fires only after every
lane has already exited. On 2026-08-01 a pass admitted at a 16,316,972 forecast ran to completion
at 43,599,830 tokens ($33.73) against a 21,000,000 grant, and the halt line printed after the money
was spent:

```
halted: L1 grant token_budget spent (43599830/21000000 tokens under this grant; 124411514 lifetime)
```

This is the same failure shape `basicly-vz78` documented for one lane, now demonstrated at four.
`vz78` fixed the *forecast* half - unsizeable lanes are now counted rather than silently admitted -
but a forecast can only refuse a pass at its start. Once four runners are live nothing can stop
them, so the accuracy of the forecast is the only thing standing between a grant and an arbitrary
overrun. The sibling bead shows that forecast is biased low by 2.3-2.9x, which is what turned an
inaccuracy into a doubled bill.

The one hard ceiling, `runner_timeout` (1800s), did not bind: lanes ran 1010-1103s. At the observed
~10400 tokens/s a lane running to that timeout would spend ~18.7M tokens - so a *single* lane can
consume nearly an entire 21M grant without ever tripping the only enforced limit. The timeout
bounds wall clock, not spend, and the two are only loosely related.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Grant a token budget smaller than what a pass will actually spend.
2. Run `basicly loop supervise <root> --autonomy L1` with several ready lanes.
3. Watch the `spend:` line admit the pass, then watch `running:` heartbeats continue past the point
   where cumulative spend exceeds the grant.
4. Observe the `halted:` line appears only after the last lane finishes.

Observed 2026-08-01: four lanes, 43599830 tokens against a 21000000 ceiling, halt after the fact.
No lane was interrupted; all four completed and merged.

## Root Cause

Admission is a pass-entry predicate, not a running constraint. `supervise.admit_pass_spend` is
called once with the working-set admissions for the pass; `dispatch_lanes` acts on its verdict and
then hands control to the runners. `policy.spend_status` is consulted again only on the next pass.
There is no accounting of in-flight spend, and per `basicly-wctc` there cannot be yet: `runner.run`
uses `proc.communicate`, so no incremental usage is available from a live lane - totals arrive only
at exit. The reporting gap and the enforcement gap are the same gap.

Note this is deliberate in one respect and the design should be preserved: killing a working agent
mid-task destroys its context and its uncommitted work, and the standing decision is that cost is
bounded by sizing the work, never by killing a working agent. So the fix is probably not "kill the
lane at N tokens" but "stop admitting the next lane once the pass is over budget", which requires
in-flight totals that do not exist yet.

## Suggested Direction

Ordered by how much they depend on `basicly-wctc`:

1. Independent of wctc: stagger admission. Re-evaluate `spend_status` before each *additional*
   lane is started rather than once for the whole pass, so a pass that starts over-budget cannot
   also start lanes 2..N. This bounds the overrun to one lane's worth instead of N.
2. Needs wctc: consume the existing `--output-format stream-json --verbose` usage stream to
   maintain a running total per lane, so the supervisor knows its live spend.
3. With (2) available: refuse to start further lanes when live spend plus the bound for the next
   lane exceeds the remainder, and surface the projected overshoot rather than reporting it after.

A lane already running should still be allowed to finish, consistent with the standing decision.
The goal is that the grant bounds how much work is *started*, which today it does not.

## Scope

- src/basicly/supervise.py  (dispatch_lanes admission cadence; per-lane rather than per-pass)
- tests/test_supervise.py   (a pass whose budget is exhausted mid-fan-out starts no further lanes)

payload.acceptance_criteria: A bead with no declared scope is not silently admitted by the band gate; a genuine read failure remains indeterminate and is distinguished from an undeclared scope; the pass output distinguishes checked-and-fits from never-checked; a test covers a scopeless bead reaching admit_working_set.
payload.description:
## Problem

The working-set band gate admits any lane whose scope cannot be read, so the sizing rule that is
supposed to keep a dispatch inside the model's effective reasoning window never applies to the
majority of the tracker. `basicly-vz78` closed exactly this hole in the *spend* gate - an
unsizeable lane is now counted at an assumed bound instead of being dropped - but left the
identical hole open in the *band* gate beside it.

Measured on the 2026-08-01 multi-lane proof run. All four dispatched lanes were unsizeable and all
four were admitted with no size check at all:

```
WorkingSetAdmission(issue_id='basicly-jr0l.35', sizing=None, violation=None, refused=False)
WorkingSetAdmission(issue_id='basicly-jr0l.43', sizing=None, violation=None, refused=False)
WorkingSetAdmission(issue_id='basicly-jr0l.44', sizing=None, violation=None, refused=False)
WorkingSetAdmission(issue_id='basicly-jr0l.45', sizing=None, violation=None, refused=False)
```

All four then crossed the context ceiling (120000 tokens at `context_ceiling` 0.6), finishing at
159120, 209226, 172628 and 165331 tokens, and all four had to spin remainder beads
(basicly-jr0l.53 through .56) because they could not finish inside one dispatch. That is precisely
the outcome the band is meant to prevent, and the band never looked at them.

The only bead the band gate has ever refused, `basicly-jr0l.24` at 114559 tokens, never ran. So
`working_set_max` has to date refused exactly one lane that produced no evidence and admitted four
that produced evidence of being too large. The gate's own effectiveness is unmeasured.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take any bead with no `## Scope` section, so `decompose.dispatch_sizing` returns None.
2. Call `supervise.admit_working_set(repo_root, issue_id, sizing)`.

Observed: `WorkingSetAdmission(issue_id=..., sizing=None, violation=None, refused=False)` - the
lane is admitted regardless of how large it really is.

## Root Cause

`src/basicly/supervise.py:1038-1042`:

```python
resolved: decompose.DispatchSizing | None = None
with contextlib.suppress(RuntimeError, ValueError, OSError):
    resolved = decompose.dispatch_sizing(repo_root, issue_id)
if resolved is None:
    return WorkingSetAdmission(issue_id, None, None, refused=False)
```

The indeterminate case admits, on the documented reasoning that an unreadable tracker or tree
should not block a pass. That reasoning is sound for a *transient read failure* and wrong for the
*structural* case of a bead that simply has no declared scope - which is not an error condition at
all but the normal state of a hand-filed bead.

Consequence beyond sizing: because these lanes carry no estimate, they also produce no forecast to
pair with their actual, which is why `basicly usage forecast` still reports zero pairs after a
completed four-lane run.

## Suggested Direction

Distinguish "could not read" from "nothing declared", and treat only the first as indeterminate.
For the second, the same choice `basicly-vz78` already made for spend is available: assume a bound
rather than waive the check. Options to evaluate together with basicly-jr0l.58, since both are
asking what a lane with no declared scope should be assumed to cost:

- Reuse the assumed bound as the band input, so an unsizeable lane is checked against the band at
  its assumed size rather than skipped.
- Require a `## Scope` section as a DoR condition for dispatch, which fails closed but would block
  most of the tracker until beads are backfilled - the same objection that made fail-closed the
  wrong answer for basicly-vz78.
- Escalate rather than refuse: admit but queue the sizing question, so a human sees the lane was
  never checked instead of it passing silently.

Whichever is chosen, an admitted-without-checking lane must be visible in the pass output. Today
nothing distinguishes "checked and fits" from "never checked" in either the log or the admission.

## Scope

- src/basicly/supervise.py  (admit_working_set indeterminate vs undeclared)
- src/basicly/decompose.py  (surface which of the two cases dispatch_sizing hit)
- tests/test_supervise.py   (a scopeless bead is not silently admitted by the band gate)

payload.acceptance_criteria: A pass whose forecast exceeds the remainder starts the affordable dispatch-order prefix and reports plus queues the deferred lanes; a pass funding no lane still refuses entirely; a band-refused lane is retained so its sizing escalation still queues; the jr0l.22 all-or-nothing test is restated deliberately rather than deleted.
payload.description:
## Problem

A pass whose combined forecast exceeds the grant remainder dispatches **nothing**, even when the
remainder comfortably funds some of its lanes. With four ready lanes forecast at 4M each and 5M
remaining, the engine starts zero lanes and waits for a human to re-grant, although starting one
would fit the budget with room to spare.

This is a deliberate contract, not an oversight: `basicly-jr0l.22` shipped with the stated
acceptance criterion "nothing dispatches", and `tests/test_supervise.py`
`test_pass_is_refused_when_its_forecast_exceeds_the_remaining_budget` pins it with the docstring
"The acceptance criterion: nothing dispatches, and the message carries both numbers." This bead
proposes changing that criterion, so it must be an explicit decision rather than a side effect of
another change.

The cost of all-or-nothing is human latency, which `basicly-jr0l.20` identifies as the thing that
dominates a factory's wall clock. A near-miss forecast stops the entire fan-out and parks it on a
human who must notice, judge, and re-grant, when the engine already holds every number needed to
start the affordable prefix immediately.

## Proposed Change

Dispatch the **dispatch-order prefix** of lanes whose cumulative forecast fits the remainder,
instead of refusing the whole pass. Refuse the pass only when the remainder funds no lane at all.

A prefix rather than a subset, because lanes arrive in scheduler-rank order: taking a prefix starts
the highest-ranked work and never reorders the lanes ahead of a dropped one. A band-refused lane
must be retained regardless of funding - it spends nothing, and its sizing escalation is the only
thing that tells a human why it never ran (`basicly-jr0l.24`).

The deferred lanes must be both reported on the pass line and queued as a decision, on the same
reasoning as every other spend refusal: a client reading only the decision queue would otherwise
see a pass start fewer lanes than were ready with nothing to explain it.

Prototyped during `basicly-jr0l.59` and backed out rather than landed, because it changes a shipped
gate's semantics. Measured on the real numbers from the 2026-08-01 run: with the corrected per-lane
bound of ~10.9M against a 21M remainder, the prefix rule starts 1 lane of 4 - about $8.70 instead
of the $33.73 that pass actually cost.

## Why this is not a safety regression

The property the gate protects is "never start work the grant cannot cover". The prefix rule
preserves it exactly: cumulative forecast of the started lanes is by construction at or below the
remainder. It relaxes only the *policy* of refusing everything when the total does not fit. The
started lanes are bounded by precisely the same numbers that would have refused them collectively,
so the change is neutral in safety and strictly better in throughput.

It does depend on the per-lane figures being trustworthy, which today they are not
(`basicly-jr0l.58`: the unsizeable-lane bound runs 2.3x-2.9x low). That is an argument for
sequencing this after `basicly-jr0l.58`, not against the rule - the pass total it replaces is built
from the same per-lane numbers and is no more trustworthy.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Grant a token budget that funds one lane but not the pass.
2. Make two or more lanes ready.
3. Run `basicly loop supervise <root>`.

Observed: `refused:` on the pass, zero lanes dispatched, the whole fan-out parked on a human.
Expected after this change: the affordable prefix starts, the rest are reported and queued.

## Scope

- src/basicly/supervise.py  (PassSpendAdmission per-lane contributions and the fundable prefix; dispatch_lanes truncation and its queue item)
- tests/test_supervise.py   (restate the jr0l.22 criterion; cover prefix, none-affordable, and band-refused retention)
- CHANGELOG.md
payload.title: start the lanes a short remainder funds instead of refusing the whole pass

payload.acceptance_criteria: Given a root whose ready children come back from br in an order differing from ready_ranked when the build advance provisions worktrees then it provisions the highest-ranked ready children up to the concurrency cap and skips any child whose working set is over the ceiling while still provisioning an unsizeable one
payload.description:
## Steps to Reproduce

On main at `d0b8aab`, with `[worktree] concurrency = 5`, ask which children of
`basicly-jr0l` a supervised pass would provision:

```
uv run python -c "
import json, subprocess
from pathlib import Path
from basicly import loop_state, supervise
from basicly.config import load_sizing_config, load_worktree_config
r = Path('.'); s = load_sizing_config(r); w = load_worktree_config(r)
ready = {n.issue_id for n in loop_state.ready_ranked(r)}
rec = json.loads(subprocess.run(['br','show','basicly-jr0l','--json'],
                                capture_output=True, text=True, cwd=r).stdout)
rec = rec[0] if isinstance(rec, list) else rec
kids = [(d['id'], d.get('status','')) for d in rec.get('dependents') or []
        if d.get('dependency_type') == 'parent-child']
picked = []
for cid, st in kids:
    if len(picked) >= w.concurrency: break
    if st == 'closed' or cid not in ready: continue
    picked.append(cid)
for cid in picked:
    a = supervise.admit_working_set(r, cid, s)
    print(cid, a.sizing.estimate.total if a.sizing else 'unsized', a.refused)
"
```

Observed - the five slots go to `basicly-jr0l.61`, `.56`, `.54`, `.29` (all
unsized, each counted at the 16002352-token unsizeable-lane assumption) and
`.28` (3573, under the floor). Meanwhile five children of the same root are
both in band and DoR READY and none is provisioned: `basicly-kjc5.38` (54093),
`basicly-kjc5.33` (53190), `basicly-kjc5.47` (51768), `basicly-kjc5.52`
(14223), `basicly-jr0l.4` (12945).

Expected - the pass provisions the lanes it can actually dispatch, in the
ranked order the function already computes.

Two distinct causes, both in `_ensure_child_worktrees`:

1. The ranking is computed and thrown away. `ready = {node.issue_id for node
   in loop_state.ready_ranked(...)}` reduces an ordered result - documented as
   "ranked by `br scheduler` (highest priority first)" - to a membership set,
   and the provisioning loop then iterates `children` in br's dependents
   order. Because provisioning is capped at `concurrency`, that arbitrary
   order decides the *set* of lanes in the pass. `supervise.ready_lanes` does
   rank-order dispatch, but it can only order the set provisioning chose.

2. A slot is spent on a lane dispatch will refuse. Provisioning consults no
   sizing at all, so an over-ceiling child (`admit_working_set(...).refused`)
   gets a worktree, and `escalate_working_set` then leaves a pending decision
   that makes `ready_lanes` drop it. The slot is consumed and nothing runs in
   it. Four children of `basicly-jr0l` are currently over the ceiling.

Neither behaviour is pinned by a test: the sole `_ensure_child_worktrees` test
(`test_ensure_child_worktrees_publishes_claims_first`) stubs `ready_ranked` to
`()`, so no case exercises ordering or sizing.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a root whose ready children are returned by br in an order that differs
  from `ready_ranked` when the build advance provisions worktrees then the
  lanes chosen are the highest-ranked ready children up to the concurrency cap
  rather than the first ones in br's dependents order
- Given a ready child whose working set is over the ceiling when the build
  advance provisions worktrees then no worktree is created for it and its slot
  goes to the next admissible ranked child
- Given a ready child whose scope cannot be sized when the build advance
  provisions worktrees then it is still provisioned, because an unreadable
  scope is not a refusal and must not silently drop work

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_loop.py`
payload.title: Lane provisioning discards its own ranking and spends slots on lanes that dispatch refuses
