Found 2026-08-15 while verifying the `basicly-u2hl.56` fix by hand.

`_on_verify` now resolves the ship checkpoint through `policy.approve_checkpoint_guarded`
with `ctx.grant_root`. The supervisor passes `session.root_issue`, so the supervised path
reaches the grant. `basicly loop advance` accepts no `--root`, so `ctx.grant_root` is None
and the guarded call defaults to the issue itself - which carries no grant when the grant is
on the epic.

Observed - `basicly loop advance basicly-b2n2` returns
`[blocked] verify -> verify: ship checkpoint awaiting human approval` while
`basicly loop preflight basicly-u2hl` reports `ship pending - the live L3 grant delegates
it`, because the grant is on `basicly-u2hl` and nothing tells `advance` so.

This is not the same defect as `u2hl.56`, which was the parked path not asking at all. This
is the hand path having no way to say which session it belongs to. `loop run` already takes
`--root` for exactly this.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Read the two surfaces side by side - this alone establishes the defect:

       uv run basicly loop advance --help
       uv run basicly loop run --help

   Observed 2026-08-19: `loop run` carries
   `--root ROOT   Session root issue whose autonomy grant may cover the checkpoints
   (default: the issue itself)`, and `loop advance` carries no `--root` at all - its options
   are `--work-type`, `--children`, `--mode`, `--runner`, `--autonomy` and nothing else.
2. Put an L3 grant on an epic and take one of its children to the ship checkpoint.
3. Ask the hand path to advance the child:

       uv run basicly loop advance <child-id>

4. Ask the preflight, on the epic, whether the grant covers that same ship:

       uv run basicly loop preflight <epic-id>

5. Read the code path that explains the disagreement:

       rg -n 'approve_checkpoint_guarded' src/basicly/loop.py
       rg -n 'grant_root' src/basicly/cli.py

Observed - this record's measurement 2026-08-15, verifying the `basicly-u2hl.56` fix by hand:
step 3 returned

    [blocked] verify -> verify: ship checkpoint awaiting human approval

while step 4 reported `ship pending - the live L3 grant delegates it`. `_on_verify` resolves
the ship checkpoint through `policy.approve_checkpoint_guarded` with `ctx.grant_root`; the
supervisor passes `session.root_issue` and so reaches the grant, but `loop advance` accepts no
`--root`, so `ctx.grant_root` is None and the guarded call defaults to the issue itself -
which carries no grant, because the grant is on the epic.

Expected: `loop advance` takes `--root` with the same meaning and default `loop run` already
gives it, so the hand path can name the session it belongs to and reaches the same grant the
supervised path does. This is not `basicly-u2hl.56`, which was the parked path not asking at
all; this is the hand path having no way to say which session it is in.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a grant on an epic and a child at the ship checkpoint when `basicly loop advance
  <child> --root <epic>` runs then the checkpoint is approved under that grant and the
  advance proceeds, rather than blocking on human approval.
- Given `basicly loop advance <child>` with no `--root` then the behaviour is unchanged, so
  the default stays the issue itself and nothing silently widens.
- Given `basicly loop advance --help` then `--root` is described in the same terms
  `loop run --help` uses, because two spellings of one concept is what this record is about.
- Given a `--root` naming a record that carries no grant then the advance blocks and says the
  named root carries no grant, rather than reporting the child's own absence of one.
- Demonstrated by: `uv run basicly loop advance <child> --root <epic>` advancing past the ship
  checkpoint, against a control run without `--root` on the same record that still blocks.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/cli.py`
- `tests/test_cli_loop.py`

## Steps to Reproduce

```
uv run basicly loop supervise basicly-u2hl --label u2hl-pass-2
rg "^(wip|routed):" <the pass log>
```

Observed, two passes on 2026-08-15:

```
pass 1  wip: 0/5 unlanded downstream of build; 2 lane(s) admitted
        routed: provisioned 2 of 3 lane(s) selected by label
pass 2  wip: 0/5 unlanded downstream of build; 1 lane(s) admitted
        routed: provisioned 1 of 2 lane(s) selected by label
```

Both passes had **zero** work in flight against a headroom of five, and both left a
selected lane unprovisioned with no line saying why. Pass 2 then provisioned the
remaining lane on a later tick, after the first had shipped - so the two lanes ran
serially despite disjoint declared scopes and a wholly empty WIP bound.

Expected - when a selected lane is not provisioned, the pass says which lane and on
what rule.

## Why this is worth a bead rather than a shrug

The visible cost is throughput: pass 2 was two lanes with no scope overlap and it ran
them one after the other, so the pass took the sum rather than the maximum.

The invisible cost is worse and it is what happened here. A reader who sees
"provisioned 1 of 2" cannot tell a deliberate refusal from a defect, so the first
reading of pass 1 attributed it to `basicly-0p8n` being a `feature` and therefore not
a leaf track - which was true of that bead and does not explain pass 2, where both
`ho3t` and `u2hl.30` are leaf types with a readable `## Scope`. One plausible cause
was tested and refuted: `br blocked` does **not** propagate a blocked parent to its
children - measured, 45 entries against 32 with a real open blocks-edge, and every one
of the 13 extra is an epic with open children, with zero false negatives. So the cause
is still unknown, and that is the point.

`wip.py:169` admits `ready[:headroom]`, so the remainder is upstream of the WIP bound
in whatever produces `ready`. The line already prints on the admitted path
deliberately (`wip.py:105`); it needs to print on the withheld one too.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a pass that selected N lanes by label and provisioned fewer when the `routed:` line
  prints then it names each lane it did not provision and the rule that withheld it, so a
  deliberate refusal is distinguishable from a defect.
- Given the WIP bound withheld a lane when the pass reports then `wip.WipAdmission.coverage`
  prints the withheld ids on the *withheld* path, as it already does on the admitted one.
- Given two selected lanes with disjoint declared scopes and zero work in flight against a
  headroom of five when the pass ticks then both are provisioned in the same pass, or the
  output names the rule that stopped the second - the pass must not silently take the sum of
  two lanes where it could take the maximum.
- Given a pass in which every selected lane was provisioned then no reason line prints, so the
  new output is news rather than noise.
- Given the cause of the shortfall is not yet known then the change reports the rule the code
  actually applied rather than asserting a diagnosis - a wrong reason is worse than the
  current silence.
- Demonstrated by: `uv run basicly loop supervise <root> --label <label>` followed by
  `rg "^(wip|routed):" <pass log>`, with a named reason present for every lane in the gap
  between selected and provisioned, against the two 2026-08-15 passes above as the control
  that print no reason at all.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/supervise.py`
- `src/basicly/wip.py`
- `tests/test_supervise.py`

## Context

Re-probed 2026-08-09 against copilot CLI 1.0.78. The tier kit's copilot installer installs
nothing and explains that copilot "exposes no hook surface that fires for a spawn, so its
working path is static frontmatter plus copilot --model". Both halves of that explanation are
now false:

- copilot ships hooks, including one that intercepts a subagent finishing **before its results
  return to the parent** (`.github/hooks/*.json`, plus inline definitions in config)
- copilot carries per-subagent selection in **config**, at
  `subagents.agents.<name>.{model, effortLevel, contextTier}`, configurable with `/subagents`

The second is the load-bearing one. It means a copilot spawn is pinnable **without a
frontmatter `model`**, which is exactly what D30 requires and what the installer currently
reports as impossible.

## Scope

- Resolve the declared tier through the D31 vendor walk and write the result into copilot's
  per-subagent config at install time, not into the agent file.
- The installer stops reporting a no-op for copilot and reports what it wrote.
- `effortLevel` and `contextTier` have no equivalent in our tier vocabulary. Decide whether
  they are derived from the tier, declared separately, or deliberately left unset - and record
  which, because an unset field on a multi-vendor surface is a silent default.

## Constraint

No provider model id in any agent file, generated or not (D30). The projected `.agent.md` must
stay model-free; the resolved id lives in config, which is generated and rewritten on install.

## Correction already landed

The stale explanation is corrected in the `tier-injection` skill in place rather than left
beside the new claim, and it names this bead as the fix.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an agent declaring `tier: low` when `basicly install` runs against a repo whose
  selection includes copilot then the generated copilot config carries the tier resolved
  through the D31 vendor walk at `subagents.agents.<name>.model`, and
  `.github/agents/<name>.agent.md` carries no `model` line - which is D30 held on the surface
  it constrains.
- Given the tier kit's copilot installer runs then it reports what it wrote to config, and no
  longer reports that a spawn cannot be pinned - the stale reason it prints today
  (`.basicly/core/kit/tier/install_hook.py`, the `"copilot"` entry, "no copilot hook is known
  to fire for a spawn ... frontmatter plus `copilot --model` instead") is gone rather than
  left beside the new claim.
- Given `effortLevel` and `contextTier`, which have no equivalent in this repo's tier
  vocabulary, then the decision to derive them from the tier, declare them separately or
  leave them unset is recorded with its reason - an unset field on a multi-vendor surface is a
  silent default, so it must be a stated one.
- Given `basicly install` runs twice with the same selection then the second run leaves the
  copilot config byte-identical, matching the convergence the kit already claims for the
  hook path.
- Given a repo whose selection excludes copilot then no copilot config is written and no
  copilot line is reported.
- Given the vendor facts this rests on were probed against copilot CLI 1.0.78 on 2026-08-09
  then the implementation re-probes the live surface before writing the config path, and
  records the version it probed - the claim being replaced was stale precisely because it
  pinned no version.
- Demonstrated by: install into a scratch repo, then show the generated copilot config
  carrying the resolved model for a `tier: low` agent while `.github/agents/<name>.agent.md`
  carries no model line.

## Demonstration

Install into a scratch repo, then show the generated copilot config carrying the resolved model
for a `tier: low` agent while `.github/agents/<name>.agent.md` carries no model line.

payload.description:
## The defect

`repair_brief.clip_output` keeps the **tail** of its input:

```
return "…(earlier output cut)…\\n" + text[-MAX_REPAIR_OUTPUT_CHARS:]
```

with `MAX_REPAIR_OUTPUT_CHARS = 2000`. Keeping the tail is right for **command output**, where a stack trace ends with the useful line. It is wrong for a **reviewer finding**, which is structured prose that opens with the defect and ends with what was checked and found clean.

The two populations have opposite shapes and one function serves both.

## Observed, 2026-08-19, on a real repair

The correctness lens produced 2023 characters on `basicly-gvlpxm`. Clipped to 2000 from the tail, the brief handed the repairing agent this:

- **dropped**: the heading and the opening of the finding, so the defect being reported is gone.
- **kept**: the closing sentence of the remedy, the whole *Checked and clean on this axis* section, and the coverage boundary.

So the brief that exists to tell a repairing agent what to fix delivered four paragraphs of what is **not** wrong and cut the one paragraph that said what is. 23 characters over the bound cost the entire defect statement.

A repairing agent reading that brief either guesses, or re-derives the review from scratch, which is the cost the brief exists to avoid.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Find or compose a review finding longer than 2000 characters that opens with a heading and a defect statement and ends with a checked-and-clean section.
2. Pass it through `repair_brief.clip_output`.
3. Observe the return value begins with the earlier-output-cut marker and the defect statement is absent.
4. Observe the checked-and-clean section survives whole.
5. Positive control: pass a 1999 character finding and observe it returns unchanged, so the clip is what removes the statement rather than the composition.

Observed: the clip keeps the least actionable end of a structured review.
Expected: a structured review keeps its opening, or is summarised rather than sliced, and the marker says which end was cut.

## Why not simply raise the bound

Because the shape problem returns at any bound. A review is not output, and this is the same lesson as the per-event cap that this repository has already paid for twice: a bound applied by where text sits rather than by what the text is will cut the load-bearing part. The fix is a second function for a structured review, or a clip that keeps the head and the tail and names the elision in the middle.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a review finding over the bound when the brief is composed then the opening defect statement is present.
- Given command output over the bound when the brief is composed then the tail is kept, as it is today.
- Given either kind when it is clipped then the marker names which end was removed.
- Given a finding under the bound when it is clipped then it is returned unchanged.
- Given a repairing agent handed a clipped review then the gate name and the defect statement are both reachable from the brief alone.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/repair_brief.py`
- `tests/test_repair_brief.py`

body.post_ship_action: PRE-DECLARED BEFORE THE TAG MOVES. (1) Ordering constraint that decides everything else: `basicly release` reads the changelog from the tagged commit, so a fragment edited after the tag never publishes. The `client_name` correction must land in changelog.d/basicly-e2mz.48.1.added.md AND in .basicly/core/skills/interface-facts/skill.yaml (re-projected via `basicly skills-build`, re-gated via `basicly skills-check --all-default-roots` + `basicly catalog lint`) BEFORE `basicly release` runs — my recommendation is to hold the tag for that one sentence, since it is a bold factual assertion about a third party that a consumer can refute in one curl. (2) If the owner ships as-is: the shipped CHANGELOG entry cannot be amended, so file a follow-up record under the existing dependent basicly-e2mz.48.2 ("refuse a document that asserts a third party interface behaviour with no source and version and date") to (a) restate the `client_name` line as a dated, network-conditional observation in skill.yaml, (b) fix "twelve rows"→eleven and "three of the twelve"→two, (c) name pyproject-fmt and pytest-xdist in the catch-all row, and ship the correction as a `fixed` fragment in the next release. ## The defect

A `git push` that runs while a landing is in flight rolls back, and the reported cause names a stash rather than contention.

`pre-commit` 4.6.0 stashes unstaged changes before it runs a hook stage and restores them after. Our `pre-push` stage runs `.basicly/core/hooks/pre-push.py`. A landing that writes the ledger inside that window changes the tree under the stash, so the restore conflicts and the push aborts with `Stashed changes conflicted with hook auto-fixes`.

The commits themselves are intact. The operator loses the push and, worse, reads a stash message as a local mistake rather than as two engine operations racing.

This is the third surface of one contention class. `basicly-kjc5.63` is the same race on the base checkout commit during dispatch. `basicly-kjc5.62` is adjacent. On each surface the failure text names a git mechanism, never contention, so an operator diagnoses it wrongly every time.

## Why it has no record until now

It was carried as prose in `HANDOVER.md` and as a comment on another record, never as a record of its own. Measured 2026-08-20 over the 980 record ledger: a search of every record's fields for `Stashed changes conflicted` and for `pre.push.*stash` returns **zero**, against a mid frequency control of `rework` at **95** and a negative control at **0**. Seven sibling traps in the same handover each have a record; this one is the only one that does not.

That is the finding `basicly-askx4j` needs: the handover is almost entirely derivable, and this record is the positive instance of the one class it carried that the ledger did not.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Start a landing that writes the ledger, for example `basicly loop run <id>` reaching its tracker commit, or any `basicly tracker write`.
2. While that write is in flight, run `git push` in the same checkout.
3. Observe `pre-commit` stash the unstaged tree for the `pre-push` stage.
4. Observe the landing write the ledger inside that window.
5. Observe the restore conflict and the push roll back with `Stashed changes conflicted with hook auto-fixes`.
6. Observe `git log` shows the commits are unharmed, so the message describes the stash and not the actual fault.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a ledger write in flight when a push reaches the pre-push stage then the push refuses with a message naming the contention and the operation that holds the tree, rather than reporting a stash conflict - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_hooks_pre_push.py -k contention -q`
- Given no ledger write in flight when a push reaches the pre-push stage then the push runs unchanged - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_hooks_pre_push.py -k quiet -q`

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/hooks/pre-push.py`
- `tests/test_hooks_pre_push.py`

## Working Set

- `.basicly/core/hooks/pre-push.py`
- `tests/test_hooks_pre_push.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_hooks_pre_push.py -q`

[analysis 2026-08-20, answering the open question this record says must be settled before any code]

The question was which parts of a handover are derivable and which are irreducibly human. Answered by classifying the whole of the 2026-08-19 HANDOVER.md against surfaces that exist today, then probing the one class that looked human.

DERIVABLE, and every one of these already has a reader. Branch, head, push state and tree cleanliness from git. Record and event counts from the ledger. Test count from pytest. Release content completeness from the release check. Worktrees and their staleness from worktree list. The ready set with its ranks and scores, and the blocked set with its blockers, from tracker ready and tracker blocked. A parked lane's phase, which gate failed, its rework count and its checkpoints from loop status, which is how this session found basicly-gvlpxm at validate with validate-as-consumer failed and rework 1 of 2 without reading the file. The live grant and its remaining budget from policy. Owner decisions, because a decision is a tracker comment: four were recorded that way this session and needed no prose home.

FILED BUT NOT SURFACED AS A CLASS. The traps. This is the section that reads most like human knowledge and is not. Measured over the 980 record ledger, searching each record's own fields with a mid frequency control of rework at 95 and a negative control at 0: the scope section backtick trap is basicly-tuy6 closed, with basicly-dauf open on the adjacent literal versus glob defect; supervise seeds nothing is basicly-kjc5.62; the concurrent dispatch race is basicly-kjc5.63; the drop in and fragment scope refusal is basicly-kjc5.64; a lane emitting no output is basicly-jr0l.72; clip_output keeping the tail is basicly-jr0l.74. Seven of eight traps in the handover are records. What is missing is not knowledge, it is a QUERY: nothing asks for open defects that sit on the operator's own path, so a reader who wants them has only prose.

IRREDUCIBLY NOT IN THE LEDGER, and it is exactly one class and it is small. A trap observed and never filed. The positive instance is the push during a landing trap, which the handover states plainly and which returned ZERO against the same probe and controls above. It is now basicly-u3b65o. So the class is real, it is one item wide, and the honest remedy is a rule rather than a document section: a trap worth telling the next session is a trap worth filing. A trap that cannot be filed cannot be trusted either, because nothing dates it and nothing retires it.

THE OUTCOME THIS IMPLIES, stated so the acceptance criterion can be checked against it. The handover retires. It does not shrink to a gated remnant, because the analysis found no irreducible remnant, only one unfiled record and one absent query. The orientation command therefore owes three things beyond the derived state this record already lists: the ready and blocked sets with reasons, which exist; the live grant and budget, which exists; and a NEW section, open defects on the operator's own path, which is the query that replaces the traps section. Reading order for documents is not part of it: that is standing guidance and belongs in a fragment or a skill, per the owner rule that if you need memory to run basicly then the repo is wrong.

WHAT THIS ANALYSIS DID NOT ESTABLISH. Whether the operator path query can be expressed without a new field on a record. The eight traps were classified by hand; they carry no marker that distinguishes an operator path defect from any other bug, and a previous gate in this repo failed for exactly that reason, absence being ambiguous between a defect and a record that predates the rule. So the query probably needs a discriminator its own producer writes, and that is the first thing the build must settle. Also not established: whether any trap was in the handover that I failed to classify, since the eight were taken from the file's own trap section and its parked work section, not from a sweep of the whole file.

[measured 2026-08-20, and it narrows this record rather than widening it]

Research section 11.3 adopts P5 as two halves. One half is a declared token cost on a catalog source, which is this record. The other half is the sharper import, stated as: every exemption list in basicly is machine validated against the population it exempts from, taken from the harness verify-package-readme-limitations.ts which fails an entry naming a package that no longer exists.

THE SECOND HALF IS ALREADY DISCHARGED. Measured across every exemption list in the tree, by reading each gate's comparison rather than its docstring:

- wired_or_deleted.BASELINE validates. Line 657 computes stale as BASELINE minus the reproducing findings and line 674 fails with `is in BASELINE but no longer reproduces`.
- check_module_size frozen entries validate, at lines 245 and 248, through ratchet.stale, with two distinct reasons: a waiver replaces the frozen entry, and no readable tracked module is at this path.
- check_comment_density frozen entries validate, at lines 225 and 228, the same way.
- recall_eval.FAMILY_BASELINE validates, at lines 141 to 145, failing when a baseline rule has no anchors and would score zero for free.
- check_noqa_debt validates, by a DIFFERENT mechanism, and this is the one that needs recording because the obvious probe reports it as missing. It does not import ratchet.stale, so a search for stale callers returns four hits and misses it. It iterates the UNION at line 285, `for code in sorted(set(counts) | set(ratchet.frozen))`, so a frozen code with zero occurrences is still visited and fires _fell at line 231 with `the record still licenses N`. Same effect, no stale call.

Probe discipline for whoever re-checks this: searching for ratchet.stale callers is the wrong probe and it under reports by one of five. The right probe is whether the gate's comparison visits the frozen set independently of the observed set. My own first reading of check_noqa_debt was wrong for exactly this reason, and the union at line 285 is what corrected it.

Note dropin.compose_ratchet line 133, `kept = {key: value for key, value in composed.items() if value != 0}`, drops a composed zero from the baseline rather than reporting it. That is not a hole here, because each gate visits its own frozen set, but it means a fragment can retire an entry silently and no gate names the retirement.

SO THIS RECORD SHOULD NOT CLAIM THE EXEMPTION VALIDATION RULE AS NEW. Its scope is the declared token cost only, in YAML because section 10.2 requires every catalog source to be YAML, enforced by basicly catalog lint, as section 36.7's fifth gate kind, a catalog source assertion on declared token cost. A release note claiming basicly gained machine validated exemption lists would be false: it had five of five before this record starts.

RELATED, and possibly the real remaining defect in this area: basicly-oa9f says the suppression lists cite the wrong file and carry a stale count. That is a stale citation and a stale number inside lists that DO self validate, which is a different failure from an unvalidated list. Check whether oa9f is the actual residue of P5's second half before filing anything new.

The record says five kinds have no handoff.record caller and no entry_verdict reader. Confirmed, with a correction that changes what the build is for one of them. Positive control repo_root at 67 files, negative control at 0.

WIRED, three, each with a producer and a reader:
- implementation-plan: produced decompose.py:2031, read loop.py:361
- change-summary: produced loop.py:1579, read loop.py:2064
- release-record: produced curate.py:58, gated loop.py:670 on handoff.adopted

UNWIRED, and they split three ways by WHY, which is the thing the record asks to decide per kind:

1. PRODUCED BY THE MARKER PATH, SCHEMA UNEXERCISED. classification. It has a producer today, classify.py:74 calling _record_classification, persisting `[harness-classification]` as declared at integrity.py:52. So the data exists and the typed contract does not see it. This is a MIGRATION onto the typed-event path pp7q4i built, not a build from scratch, and it is the cheapest of the five by a wide margin.

2. SCHEDULED, PRODUCER ALREADY A RECORD. solution-design. It is the one kind with no schema at all. basicly-u2hl.19, emit a solution design at intake with six checked sections, is its producer and is in the ready set. So declaring it unwired today is correct and temporary, and the inventory should not treat it the same as a kind nobody has planned.

3. NO PRODUCER OF ANY KIND. change-shape, verification-evidence, validation-transcript. Each has a schema and zero references outside handoff.py and tests. Note validation-transcript is the odd one: loop._dispatch_validation already runs a validator whose output is a transcript in substance, so the artifact is unwired while the work it describes runs every validate. That is the strongest candidate of the three, and the weakest argument for deleting a schema.

A PROBE FAILURE WORTH RECORDING, because it is this repo's recurring trap. My first probe grepped the literal string `classification` and returned six files, which reads as a wired kind. Five of the six are the ENGLISH WORD or the marker constant, not the artifact kind. The discriminator is that a wired kind appears as a handoff.<CONST> symbol at its producer, per the control taken on curate.py:52 and :58; only three such constants exist in handoff.py. So the probe for wiredness is the constant, never the kind's name. A reader who greps the name will over count by one and conclude classification is wired.

THE DESIGN POINT THE BUILD MUST SETTLE FIRST, and it is the same trap this repo has paid for before. How does the inventory KNOW a kind is unwired. Deriving it from absence, no constant or no caller found, makes the check ambiguous between unwired and probed wrongly, which is exactly how my own six-file miss happened. Bind it on what the producer declares instead: let the kind list carry its producer symbol per kind, and let the inventory verify that symbol exists and is called. Then a kind with no declared producer is unwired BY DECLARATION and the gate cannot fail open. That also makes the three-way split above expressible, because a declared-but-scheduled kind and a declared-nothing kind stop looking identical.

WHAT THIS DID NOT ESTABLISH. Whether any of the four schema'd unwired kinds is read by a test in a way that would break if the schema changed, so a schema that refuses nothing in production may still be pinned by a fixture. Check `rg -l '<kind>' tests/` before proposing a deletion; a regenerated artifact in this repo usually has a captured fixture behind it.

## The defect

The landing path has TWO merge call sites and only one records a `change-summary`. So a repair that re-lands leaves the artifact describing the superseded landing, which is the same defect `basicly-gvlpxm` fixed, reached by the other route.

- `loop._verify_and_land` merges and then calls `_record_change_summary`, which after `basicly-gvlpxm` correctly records `result.landed_head`.
- `loop._repair_from_validate` calls `merge.merge_worktree` directly and then `_dispatch_validation`. It never calls `_record_change_summary`. Nothing re-records the artifact for the merge it just performed.

The consequence is precise, because the artifact's own docstring states its contract: it is written "at the one point where the build is finished and the branch facts still exist". After a repair re-land, the recorded head, path count and digest describe the FIRST landing, and `basicly-gvlpxm`'s defect statement applies again word for word: its count and digest describe a tree that is not what landed.

## Observed, on gvlpxm's own repair landing

The repair for `basicly-gvlpxm` was committed as `c536d56f`, rebased to `be36146b`, gained a regeneration commit `6799e757`, and merged as `7381a145`. main advanced. The artifact on the record still reads:

- `commit`: `d3422f8175ddf0f60fda96b60d01abe2d0b48b5f`, the pre-rebase head of the ORIGINAL landing
- `self_check.detail`: `merged harness/basicly-gvlpxm into main @ 9534ca05`, the original merge base

Neither value describes the landing that actually put the fix in main. The fix's own re-land demonstrated the sibling gap.

## Why this is not a duplicate of gvlpxm

`basicly-gvlpxm` fixed WHICH head is read at the site that records. This record is about a merge site that does not record at all. Fixing the first cannot fix the second, and the repo rule is root cause not symptom: check other call sites before calling a single-site patch complete. The other call site was not checked, and this is it.

## The design question this must answer, not assume

Whether a repair re-land SHOULD re-record BUILD's artifact. Two readings and this record does not choose:

- It should. The artifact's contract is that it describes what landed, and after a re-land it does not. `handoff.record` is content addressed rather than write once, so a corrected payload records as a second artifact event and nothing is overwritten.
- It should not, and instead the phase model is wrong to let a merge happen outside the state that owns the artifact. `_repair_from_validate`'s docstring says the phase deliberately does not fall back to build, because that would hand the unit a phase whose work base already holds. If the artifact belongs to build, a merge outside build is the anomaly.

Whichever is chosen, an artifact that silently describes a superseded tree is the outcome to refuse.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take a record at phase `validate` whose `validate-as-consumer` gate failed and whose worktree branch carries a repair commit base does not hold.
2. Read its `change-summary` artifact and note the recorded `commit`.
3. Run `basicly loop advance <id>`.
4. Observe `_repair_from_validate` merge the branch, and observe main advance to a new head.
5. Read the `change-summary` artifact again.
6. Observe the recorded `commit` is unchanged and still names the pre-repair head, so it describes a tree that is not what landed.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a repair that re-lands from validate when the merge succeeds then the change summary records the head that merge took rather than the earlier landing's head - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_handoff_states.py -k repair_reland -q`
- Given a repair re-land that fails to merge then no change summary is recorded for it and the existing artifact is left as it was - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_handoff_states.py -k repair_reland_failed -q`

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_handoff_states.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_handoff_states.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_handoff_states.py -k repair_reland -q`

payload.description:
## The defect

A dispatched validator can execute successfully, be charged for, and leave the loop in **exactly** the state it was in. No gate event, no queued decision, no rework charged. The advance exits and the operator cannot tell the run happened from any loop surface.

So a lane at `validate` cannot leave `validate` by advancing, and the only signal that anything ran is the spend.

## Measured on basicly-gvlpxm, 2026-08-20

`basicly loop advance basicly-gvlpxm` merged the repair (main advanced to `7381a145`) and then dispatched, per the `[harness-run]` records on the record, all with `outcome: executed` and `returncode: 0`:

- one `claude --agent validator`
- two `claude --agent reviewer`, lenses `correctness` and `security`

One of those runs alone records `cost: 1.1256025` and `tokens: 506272`.

**The ledger holds two gate events for this record and both predate today:**

```
2026-08-19T20:18:36 | {"gate": "verify", "passed": true}
2026-08-19T20:27:10 | {"gate": "validate-as-consumer", "passed": false}
```

Event kinds for the record: `created 5, status 1, edge 2, field 2, comment 20, artifact 1, gate 2`. After the advance, `loop status` still reports `failed: validate-as-consumer` and `rework: validate-as-consumer=1`, both unchanged, and `basicly loop decisions basicly-gvlpxm --json` returns `[]`.

Positive control, required because this is a claim about an absence: gate events ARE written by this engine and have the right shape - the two above are them. So the mechanism works and today's validator run did not reach it.

## Why the wrong probe is the trap here

Gate results are **ledger events**, not comments, and `basicly tracker show` does not surface them. I first probed the record's comments, found no validator verdict among 16, and nearly filed a different bug. The reviewers DO leave `[harness-review]` comments, which makes the absence of a validator comment look like the defect. It is not. **Probe `.basicly/ledger/events-*.jsonl` for `kind: gate`; a comment scan cannot see a gate either way.**

## Why this matters more than one stuck lane

The lane is wedged in a way that costs money to discover and burns the rework budget to escape. Because the gate stays `failed`, the next advance re-enters `_on_validate`'s `required_failed` branch. The branch now has no commit base does not hold, so `_repair_from_validate` takes `_worktree_landed` to `_repair_in_place`, whose brief was consumed on read - so it returns None, `_repair_from_validate` returns None, and `_on_validate` falls through to `_rework`. That charges the second and last rework slot for a round in which nothing was wrong with the code.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take a record at phase `validate` whose `validate-as-consumer` gate is recorded failed and whose worktree branch carries a repair commit base does not hold.
2. Run `basicly loop advance <id>`.
3. Observe the merge succeed and base advance.
4. Observe `[harness-run]` records appear on the record for a validator and one reviewer per lens, each `outcome: executed`.
5. Run `grep -h '<id>' .basicly/ledger/events-*.jsonl` and count events of `kind: gate`.
6. Observe the count is unchanged from before step 2, and `loop status` reports the same gate verdict and the same rework count.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a validator that executes at validate when the advance completes then a gate event is recorded for validate-as-consumer carrying its verdict - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_loop_validate.py -k records_a_gate -q`
- Given a validator that executes and returns no usable verdict when the advance completes then the advance blocks with a queued decision naming the validator rather than exiting with no state change - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_loop_validate.py -k no_verdict_blocks -q`
- Given an advance in which no validator was dispatched then no gate event is recorded so the fix does not manufacture a verdict - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_loop_validate.py -k undispatched -q`

## Scope

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/validate_gate.py`
- `tests/test_loop_validate.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `src/basicly/validate_gate.py`
- `tests/test_loop_validate.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_loop_validate.py -q`
payload.title: a validator executes and records no gate event so the advance changes nothing and the next one burns rework

payload.description:
## The defect

The owned tracker can add a dependency edge and can never remove one. So a design decision that **inverts** an edge cannot be enacted, and the only ways round it are a cycle or destroying a record.

`mirror._MIRRORED_WRITES` (`src/basicly/mirror.py:269-276`) holds exactly six verbs:

```
close, comments add, create, dep add, gate report, update
```

`drafts()` raises `TrackerDivergenceError` for anything else, and its own docstring says why the list is closed: the surface "was frozen by measurement (`basicly.tracker_usage`), so a write outside it is a new dependency on br that nobody decided to take". Removal was therefore never mirrored because the retired external tracker's removal verb was never used - so the gap is inherited from a usage measurement, not chosen.

## Observed, and it is blocking real work

`basicly-rn0o.10` landed 2026-08-20 carrying an owner decision that promotes unit G to first class. The consequence in the graph is that `basicly-rn0o.4` must precede `basicly-rn0o.3`. The graph today holds the opposite:

- `basicly-rn0o.3` dependencies include `('basicly-rn0o.4', 'blocks')` as a dependent
- `basicly-rn0o.4` dependencies include `('basicly-rn0o.3', 'blocks')`

Adding the reverse edge without removing the original creates a cycle, and this tracker's cycle detection is already recorded as order dependent and as missing mixed type paths. So the safe route does not exist, and unit G's promotion is inert in the tracker while being decided in the design.

## Why the workarounds are all worse

- **Add the reverse edge and accept the cycle.** The ready set is derived from the edges, so a cycle either wedges both records or is silently tolerated. Neither is acceptable and the detection cannot be relied on to refuse it.
- **Close the record and re create it.** Changes the id. `basicly-rn0o.3` is cited by name in `docs/requirements/harness-board.md`, and citations are a gated surface here, so this trades a graph defect for a stale citation and loses the record's history.
- **Edit the ledger by hand.** The ledger is append only and the engine seam exists precisely so nothing writes it directly.

## What the fix is

A `dep remove` translator in `mirror._MIRRORED_WRITES` with its ledger event, so an edge can be retracted the same way it was added. The event must be a **retraction that folds**, not a deletion: the ledger is append only, so the fold must yield an edge set with the edge absent while the history still shows it was added and withdrawn. That is the same shape the store already uses for a tombstoned record.

Two things the build must decide rather than assume, and neither is guessable from the code:

1. Whether retracting an edge that does not exist is an error or a no op. An error is the safer default because it catches a typo in a record id, and a typo here silently does nothing.
2. Whether a retraction may remove a `parent-child` edge. Removing one re parents a record, which changes what a fan out covers, so it may deserve a separate verb or a refusal.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Pick two records with an edge between them, for example `basicly-rn0o.3` and `basicly-rn0o.4`.
2. Run `uv run basicly tracker write -- dep remove basicly-rn0o.4 basicly-rn0o.3`.
3. Observe `Error: 'dep remove' is not a write this tracker knows how to record; the verbs that are: close, comments add, create, dep add, gate report, update`.
4. Observe there is no other engine seam that retracts an edge, so the edge cannot be changed at all.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an existing dependency edge when a retraction is recorded then the folded record no longer carries that edge and the ledger still shows it added and withdrawn - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_mirror.py -k dep_remove -q`
- Given a retraction naming an edge that does not exist then the write is refused naming both records rather than recording a no op - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_mirror.py -k dep_remove_absent -q`
- Given two records whose edge is retracted and re added in the opposite direction then the ready set derives from the new direction and no cycle is reported - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_owned_store.py -k edge_inversion -q`

## Scope

- `src/basicly/mirror.py`
- `src/basicly/owned_store.py`
- `src/basicly/owned_write.py`
- `tests/test_mirror.py`
- `tests/test_owned_store.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/mirror.py`
- `src/basicly/owned_store.py`
- `src/basicly/owned_write.py`
- `tests/test_mirror.py`
- `tests/test_owned_store.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly tracker write -- dep remove basicly-rn0o.4 basicly-rn0o.3` then `uv run basicly tracker show basicly-rn0o.4`

## Context

Unit B of `basicly-rn0o`. The full reasoning is `01-solution-design.md` on that epic's harness branch; this bead is the plan gate's view of it.

The producer reads only files - `.beads/issues.jsonl`, `.basicly/usage/run-records.json`, `.basicly/usage/verify-run.json`, `.basicly/usage/supervisor.lock` - and spawns zero subprocesses. That is the answer to the 11-second problem: the existing JSON surfaces each cost a process, and the whole point is a producer cheap enough to run on a tick. Building on this repo's committed corpus completes under 500 ms, against 15 ms measured, so the cap fails on a regression rather than on noise.

## Why this integrity level

L2, engine code with no consumer surface of its own.

## Scope

- `src/basicly/board_snapshot.py`
- `tests/test_board_snapshot.py`
- `.basicly/core/schemas/board-snapshot.schema.json`

Added 2026-08-20 after basicly-rn0o.10 landed. The schema file is in scope because the
revised design records a defect inside it: its own `description` still carries the deleted
store's field-selection figures. Unit B must open that file anyway, so it repairs the string
rather than leaving a second record for one line. Note the first line of that file warns its
prose is indexed by `wired-or-deleted` as field references, so changing it is gated.

## Plan

- integrity: `L2`
- budget: `140000`
- depends on: `basicly-rn0o.1`
- demonstration: `uv run basicly board --out - | uv run basicly board validate -` exits 0 and the snapshot validates against unit A's schema.

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly board --out - | uv run basicly board validate -` exits 0 and the snapshot validates against unit A's schema.

## Context

Found while building `basicly-he6200`. The edge payload has **two dialects**. `migrate.py` and
`differential.py` write `from`/`to`/`type`; `provenance.py` declares `target`/`edge_type` as "the one
spelling". `fsck.py:122-128` already documents the split.

The consequence is a fail open, not a cosmetic inconsistency: `provenance.fold_edges` cannot read a
single engine written edge, so `gating_edges` returns nothing for the whole population and any check
resting on it passes by seeing no edges. It is currently reached by nothing in `src/` or `.scripts/`
(grepped, with the kit's own internal users as the positive control), which is the only reason no
claim depends on it today.

A reader who wires it later inherits a silent zero. Pick one spelling, or make the reader accept both
and say which it saw.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `rg -n "edge_type|target" .basicly/core/kit/tracker/provenance.py` and note the declared spelling.
2. Run `rg -n '"from"|"to"|"type"' .basicly/core/kit/tracker/migrate.py` and note the written spelling.
3. Call `provenance.fold_edges` over the committed ledger's `edge` events.
4. Observe it returns no edges, while `differential.views_from_events` returns 1083 of them.
5. Observe nothing fails, because no caller compares the two counts.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given the committed ledger when the provenance fold reads its edge events then it returns the same edge count the differential fold returns - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_kit_tracker_provenance.py -k dialect -q`
- Given an edge payload in either spelling when the fold reads it then it is counted rather than skipped, or the fold refuses the unknown spelling naming it

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/provenance.py`
- `tests/test_kit_tracker_provenance.py`

## Working Set

- `.basicly/core/kit/tracker/provenance.py`
- `tests/test_kit_tracker_provenance.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_kit_tracker_provenance.py -k dialect -q`

## Context

Found while fixing `basicly-xd79u3`. `validate_gate.verdict_from_reply` strips only whitespace and
backticks, so a reply reading `**VALIDATION: PASS**` parses to `None`. Agents emphasise headings in
markdown as a matter of course.

This is the most likely reason the `basicly-gvlpxm` validator's verdict vanished on 2026-08-20: a run
costing 506272 tokens executed, returned zero, and moved no gate. `xd79u3` made that outcome a queued
decision instead of silence, so the failure is now visible - but the parse is still the thing that
fails, and every unreadable verdict costs a dispatch.

**Widen the parse against observed forms, never invented ones.** A previous fixture in this repo was
composed rather than observed and made a retry path dead code through two fixes.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Call `validate_gate.verdict_from_reply('**VALIDATION: PASS**')`.
2. Observe it returns `None`.
3. Call it with `VALIDATION: PASS` and observe a verdict, which is the positive control.
4. Observe that the None path now queues a decision (basicly-xd79u3) rather than passing the gate, so the cost is a wasted dispatch rather than a wrong verdict.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a verdict line wrapped in markdown emphasis when the reply is parsed then the verdict is read - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_validate_gate.py -k emphasis -q`
- Given a reply carrying no verdict in any observed form when it is parsed then None is still returned so the queued decision path is not bypassed

- `src/basicly/validate_gate.py`
- `tests/test_validate_gate.py`

- `src/basicly/validate_gate.py`

## Context

Found landing `basicly-e2mz.49`. Its new gate calls `ratchet.compose_ratchet(repo, "code_citations", ...)`,
which reads a `[ratchet.code_citations]` table from a `basicly.d` drop in. The config validator refuses

```
unknown section 'code_citations' in [ratchet]; [ratchet] accepts comment_density, module_size, noqa_debt
```

So the gate ships green and **can never be rebaselined by a lane**, which is the one route the gate's
own remedy text tells a lane to take. It failed 166 tests the moment a drop in used it. The gate was
green at merge because nobody exercised its rebaseline path - the recurring shape here is that a closed
record proves code exists, not that a route works.

The general control is the point of this record: **every gate name passed to `compose_ratchet` must be
registered in the config schema's accepted `[ratchet]` set**, bound by a test rather than by review.

3. Observe a ValueError from `config.py` naming the section, and a broad test failure rather than a single one.
4. Observe that `[ratchet.module_size]` in the same file is accepted, which is the positive control.

- Given every gate that calls compose_ratchet when the config schema is read then each gate name is in the accepted ratchet section set - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_config.py -k ratchet_sections -q`

## Context

`basicly worktree merge` rebases a branch before merging it, so the original branch ref never becomes
an ancestor of base. `basicly worktree cleanup` tests ancestry, therefore reports **every** correctly
merged worktree as unmerged and tells the operator to re run with `--force`.

Measured 2026-08-20: after `basicly-rn0o.10` merged cleanly at `208616cb`, cleanup reported
`kept branch harness/basicly-rn0o.10 and its record (unmerged - re-run with force to reclaim)`, while
`git diff harness/basicly-rn0o.10 main` showed the content identical.

**A check that is wrong every time trains the operator to pass `--force` without reading it**, and
`--force` is what deletes an unmerged branch. In this session that habit came within one command of
discarding a commit that genuinely was not in base: `git diff branch main` showed main *removing* 92
lines, and only that diff caught it. The content check is the one that carries the information; the
ancestry check carries none.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a worktree with `basicly worktree create <name>` and commit on it.
2. Land it with `basicly worktree merge <name> --bead <id>` and observe MERGED.
3. Run `basicly worktree cleanup <name>`.
4. Observe it reports the branch as unmerged and offers `--force`.
5. Run `git diff <branch> main` and observe the tracked content is identical, so the report is false.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a worktree whose content is in base when cleanup runs then it reclaims the session without --force - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_worktree.py -k rebase_merged -q`
- Given a worktree carrying content base does not hold when cleanup runs then it refuses and names the differing paths rather than offering a blanket force

## Scope

- `src/basicly/worktree.py`
- `tests/test_worktree.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/worktree.py`
- `tests/test_worktree.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest tests/test_worktree.py -k rebase_merged -q`

## Context

The worktree concurrency cap counts recorded **sessions**, not directories. Two ways a session outlives
its directory were both hit on 2026-08-20:

- `basicly worktree cleanup` without `--force` removes the directory and keeps the session, so the slot
  stays held while `worktree list` marks it `(stale: dir missing)`.
- `git worktree remove` leaves the session entirely, because nothing tells the engine.

The result was `worktree concurrency cap reached (5/5)` with only three linked worktrees on disk, and
the error names the cap rather than the stale rows. An operator raises the cap instead of reclaiming a
slot, which is what happened.

1. Run `basicly worktree create a` and `git worktree remove` its directory.
2. Run `basicly worktree list` and observe `(stale: dir missing)`.
3. Create worktrees until the cap is reached.
4. Observe `worktree concurrency cap reached (N/N)` while fewer than N directories exist.
5. Observe the message names the cap and not the stale sessions holding the slots.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a session whose directory is gone when the cap is evaluated then it does not count toward the cap - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_worktree.py -k stale_slot -q`
- Given the cap is reached and stale sessions exist then the refusal names them and the command that reclaims them

- `tests/test_worktree.py`

## Context

Measured 2026-08-20. `basicly-gvlpxm` and `basicly-kjc5.63` branched from the same commit. Both measured
`src/basicly/merge.py` and both found **exactly 2 tokens** of module size headroom. gvlpxm declared a
+79 rebaseline and spent that 2; kjc5.63 declared +190 against the same 15401 baseline and spent it
again. Composed on the rebase the module reads 15672 against a frozen 15401 + 79 + 190 = 15670, so the
gate refused by 2 and `test_check_module_size` failed with it.

Both lanes were green on their own branches. The failure exists only in the merge, and the operator sees
a two token overrun with no hint that two independently correct measurements caused it.

**A headroom figure is only valid against the tree it was taken on.** A drop in that recorded the base
commit its measurement was taken at could be refused when that commit is no longer an ancestor of the
head it is being applied to - which is a mechanical check, not a judgment.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take two records whose scopes both include one module frozen near its baseline.
2. Dispatch both from the same base commit.
3. Have each measure the module's headroom and declare a rebaseline that fits.
4. Land the first; observe green.
5. Rebase and land the second; observe the module size gate refuse by the headroom both lanes spent, and the gate's own test fail with it.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a ratchet drop in that records the base commit of its measurement when it is applied to a head that commit is not an ancestor of then the gate refuses naming the stale measurement - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_dropin.py -k stale_measurement -q`

- `tests/test_dropin.py`

## Context

Found independently by two lanes on 2026-08-20 and confirmed by a third. `architecture.md` section 34
states the tier and band counts of the layering contract, and **nothing reads them**: no script, no
test, and `docs-claims` asserts CLI coverage only.

Measured against `.importlinter` the same day: the document said 36 tiers where the contract had 37,
and its mermaid band labels summed to 98 modules where the contract had 102. One lane corrected only
the three numbers its own change moved and deliberately left two band figures alone, because band

## Context

`uv run basicly tracker write -- update basicly-nonexistent` prints `recorded: update basicly-nonexistent`
and exits zero. No event reaches the ledger and no record is created - verified, so nothing is corrupted

Measured 2026-08-20: `tracker show basicly-nonexistent` answers `"found": false`, and
`grep -c basicly-nonexistent .basicly/ledger/events-*.jsonl` returns 0, against a record count unchanged

exactly this reason.

4. Run `grep -c basicly-nonexistent .basicly/ledger/events-*.jsonl` and observe 0.
5. Run the same update against a record that exists and observe the same message, which is the positive control that the message does not discriminate.

## Context

`basicly worktree merge` takes a worktree name and merges whatever its branch points at **now**. There
is no way to say which commits were expected, and the report names the merge commit rather than the
branch tip it took.

This cost real work on 2026-08-20. An agent finished and reported its commit; a follow up message was
sent to it, which **resumed it**; it did another 92 lines and committed again; the merge then took the
tip that had been read earlier. Nothing in the landing said the tip had moved. It was caught only by a
routine `git diff <branch> main` run before cleanup, which showed main *removing* 92 lines, and the
commit was recovered by cherry pick.

The general defect: a landing is the one irreversible step, and it is the step with no statement of
intent to check against. An `--expect <sha>` that refuses a mismatch, or a report that names the tip and
the commit count it is about to take, closes it. The second is cheaper and helps even when no sha is
known in advance.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create a worktree, commit on it, and note the branch tip.
2. Commit again on the branch without re-reading the tip.
3. Run `basicly worktree merge <name> --bead <id>`.
4. Observe the report names the resulting merge commit and never the branch tip it took or how many commits it took.
5. Observe there is no flag by which the operator could have declared the tip they expected.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a landing when it merges then its report names the branch tip it took and the number of commits it carried - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_merge.py -k names_the_tip -q`
- Given an expected tip is declared and the branch has moved then the landing refuses naming both shas rather than merging

## Scope

- `src/basicly/merge.py`
- `src/basicly/worktree.py`
- `tests/test_merge.py`

- `src/basicly/merge.py`

payload.description:
## Context

`$?` after `cmd | tail` is `tail`'s status, so a failing gate reports success. The repo already carries
this as prose guidance and it keeps happening: **twice in one session on 2026-08-20**, once reading a
validate exit code and once reading `basicly board validate`, and previously as a background run that
notified "exit code 0" while the gate had failed.

Why it recurs is measurable rather than a matter of care. Per `basicly usage report` on 2026-08-20,
`head` is the **most used** terminal tool in this repository at 16394 invocations and `tail` is **third**
at 13960. The trap sits on the single most travelled path an agent takes, and the guidance against it is
a sentence in a fragment competing with everything else in the always on budget.

Prose has been tried. What has not been tried is a mechanical check. The proposal, for owner decision
because it changes a hook surface: a `PreToolUse` or `PostToolUse` hook that flags a shell command
whose pipeline ends in `head`, `tail` or `grep` **and** whose output the caller then treats as a
pass or fail signal - or, far simpler and cheaper, guidance that a gate is run with its output
redirected to a file and the summary line read from it, which removes the pipe rather than policing it.

**Do not weaken this to a note that says be careful.** The failure mode of the current control is
precisely that it is a note.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run any failing command piped into tail, for example `uv run pytest -q tests/some_failing.py | tail -3`.
2. Read `$?`.
3. Observe it is 0 while the command failed.
4. Run the same command without the pipe and observe a non zero status, which is the positive control.
5. Search the always on guidance and observe the rule is present as prose, so the recurrence is not caused by its absence.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a shell pipeline whose exit status is read when the guidance or a hook is applied then the operator is directed to PIPESTATUS or to a redirected file rather than the pipe's own status - check: `uv run basicly hooks-check`
- Given the control is a hook then it does not fire on a pipeline whose status is never read, so it refuses the defect and not the idiom

## Scope

- `.basicly/core/`
- `tests/test_hooks.py`

## Working Set

- `.basicly/core/`
- `tests/test_hooks.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run basicly hooks-check`
payload.title: reading an exit code after a pipe is the most travelled trap in this repo and nothing catches it

## Context

Measured by `basicly usage report` on 2026-08-20. The never used list includes **`root-cause`,
`falsify-first`, `repair-in-place`, `validate-as-consumer`, `worktree-isolation` and `decompose-plan`** -
six skills whose triggers describe, almost exactly, the work a full session had just done: a repair
briefed into a lane's own worktree, a consumer validation, five sibling worktrees, a root cause chased
to a control, and a design cut into dispatchable children.

All six were hand rolled instead. The session's briefs re-derived, in prose, guidance the catalog
already ships - and re-derived it **less completely**, because a hand written brief carries what the
author recalled rather than what the skill records.

So the defect is not that the skills are wrong. It is that **nothing makes a skill reachable at the
moment its trigger fires**, and a skill nothing reaches is indistinguishable from a skill that does not
exist. 11 skills have ever been invoked against 32 never invoked; the never used side is where every
process skill sits, while the used side is the four or five a session touches by habit.

Two candidate controls, and this record does not choose. **(a)** The dispatch brief names the skill
whose trigger the unit matches, so an agent is pointed at it by the engine rather than by an author's
memory. **(b)** A retro check that reports, per closed record, whether any skill covering its work type
was invoked - making the gap visible per unit instead of as one aggregate list. Neither is a culling
argument: the earlier reading of that list as culling candidates is what left these six unexercised.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `uv run basicly usage report`.
2. Read the Skills table and the never used list beneath it.
3. Observe root-cause, falsify-first, repair-in-place, validate-as-consumer, worktree-isolation and decompose-plan are all in the never used list.
4. Read those six skills' trigger sections and compare against the work of any recent multi lane session.
5. Observe the triggers match work that was done without them, so the skills were reachable in principle and unreached in fact.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a dispatched unit whose work matches a skill trigger when its brief is composed then the brief names that skill - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_dispatch_brief.py -k names_a_skill -q`
- Given a skill has never been invoked when the usage report runs then it is reported as unexercised rather than as a culling candidate, since the two are different claims

- `tests/test_dispatch_brief.py`

- `tests/test_dispatch_brief.py`

## Context

Observed 2026-08-20 by a lane during a nine lane pass. The session scratchpad is keyed by session, not
by lane, so **every concurrent subagent writes to one directory**.

The failure is silent substitution, which is worse than loss. A lane wrote a measurement script, a
sibling overwrote it between the write and the run, and the run **printed the sibling's files and
numbers under the first lane's command**. A shared backup directory held six other lanes' copies of
files, so a restore from backup would have written another lane's content into the wrong worktree.

The close out guidance already says anything worth keeping belongs in the repo rather than a temp
directory, and gives the reason as the scratchpad being cleaned without warning. Cross lane overwrite is
a second and worse reason: cleaning loses a file loudly, this substitutes one quietly, and no positive
control on the corpus catches it because the corpus was never wrong - the script was.

The blast radius is every number a lane measures through a scratchpad script, which in this repo means
every ratchet figure, every population count and every timing that reaches a commit message, a frozen
table or a design document.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Dispatch two or more concurrent lanes in one session.
2. Have each write a script of the same name into the scratchpad root and then run it.
3. Observe one lane's run execute the other lane's script, reporting the other lane's files and numbers with no error.
4. List the shared backup directory and observe files belonging to lanes other than the one reading it.
5. Observe a positive control on the measured corpus still passes, because the corpus is not what was swapped.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given two concurrent lanes when each writes a working file then neither can read or overwrite the other's - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_dispatch_brief.py -k scratch_isolation -q`
- Given a lane is briefed then it is told a working directory unique to it rather than a session wide path
- Given the close out guidance then it names cross lane substitution beside the cleaning hazard, because the two fail differently

## Scope

- `src/basicly/dispatch_brief.py`
- `tests/test_dispatch_brief.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/dispatch_brief.py`
- `tests/test_dispatch_brief.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest -q`

payload.description:
## Context

Found 2026-08-20 by the lane extracting a helper out of a module at its size cap. Its first measurement
of the extracted unit was an instrument fault, not a result.

`check_comment_density.prose_tokens` returns 0 for a source fragment that does not `ast.parse`. A loose
slice of a module - a docstring section, a function lifted out of its class, anything not a valid module
on its own - therefore measures as 0 percent prose, which reads as pure code.

That is the most dangerous possible wrong answer here, because the two ratchets pull opposite ways: an
extraction is only safe when the extracted unit is prose heavier than the module it leaves, and an
instrument reporting every fragment as 0 percent prose says the opposite of the truth every time. A lane
trusting it extracts the wrong cut, and the comment density gate then refuses the module it was trying
to relieve.

The lane caught it by deriving the number a second way, on a path sharing no step, and getting 66 percent
against 0. The rule it drew is the one to encode: do not measure an extracted unit as a raw slice - parse
it as the module it will become, or refuse to answer.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take any valid Python module and slice out a fragment that is not itself parseable, for example a docstring section or an indented method body.
2. Call `check_comment_density.prose_tokens` on the fragment.
3. Observe it returns 0, so the fragment reads as 0 percent prose.
4. Call the same function on the whole module and observe a non zero share, which is the positive control that the function works on valid input.
5. Observe there is no error and no way for the caller to tell that 0 from a genuine absence of prose.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a source fragment that does not parse when its prose share is requested then the instrument refuses rather than answering zero - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_check_comment_density.py -k unparseable -q`
- Given a valid module then the share is unchanged so existing measurements keep their meaning

## Scope

- `.scripts/check_comment_density.py`
- `tests/test_check_comment_density.py`

## Working Set

- `.scripts/check_comment_density.py`
- `tests/test_check_comment_density.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest -q`
payload.title: the prose share instrument reports zero on a fragment it cannot parse so an extracted unit measures as pure code

same surface.

`uv run basicly tracker write -- update <id>` with no field flags prints `recorded:` and appends nothing,
whether or not the record exists, verified both ways. The cause is in `mirror._update_drafts`, which
returns an empty draft list when no field flag is present, while the caller prints its confirmation
regardless.

This also corrects the premise of `basicly-6oypkd`. That record claimed nothing reaches the ledger for an
absent record, verified by a grep returning zero. The verification used a flagless probe, so the zero was
caused by this defect rather than by the one being reported. With a field flag, `update <absent> -t bug`
did append a field event and the fold produced a record. The absent record guard has since landed; this
one has not.

The general shape is worth keeping: a confirmation printed by the caller rather than derived from the
write is a claim about nothing.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run `uv run basicly tracker write -- update <an id that exists>` with no field flags.
2. Observe `recorded:` and exit zero, and observe no new event in the ledger.
3. Run the same against an id no record holds and observe identical output, so the message does not discriminate.
4. Run an update with a field flag against a record that exists and observe an event appended, which is the positive control.
5. Observe the caller prints its confirmation without consulting whether any draft was produced.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given an update carrying no field flag when the write runs then it is refused naming what it would have changed rather than reported as recorded - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_mirror.py -k flagless_update -q`
- Given an update carrying a field flag then it is recorded unchanged

## Scope

- `src/basicly/mirror.py`
- `tests/test_mirror.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/mirror.py`
- `tests/test_mirror.py`

`uv run pytest -q`

## Context

The guard landed by `basicly-xkqxp9` refused two of my own commands within minutes, and the second
refusal was a **false positive on the pattern the guard itself recommends**.

Its advice is to redirect a gate's output to a file and read the summary from it. A careful operator
therefore writes one block that does both: `cmd > out 2>&1; echo $?` for the gate, then
`grep ... out | tail -3` for the summary. The second pipeline reads no status at all - but the guard
sees a `$?` somewhere in the invocation and a pipeline ending in `tail` somewhere in the same
invocation, and fires.

So the pairing is **per invocation rather than per pipeline**. A compound command separated by `;` is
one invocation to the guard, and any block that both reads an exit code and pipes to a filter trips it,
regardless of whether the two are related.

This is the class the guard exists to fix, arriving in the guard: a check that refuses a correct case
trains its operator to route around it. The lane's own report claimed it fires only where the status is
read in the same command, which is true and is not the same as the status being read **of that
pipeline**.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Run a single shell invocation containing `cmd > out.txt 2>&1; echo $?` followed by `grep pattern out.txt | tail -3`.
2. Observe the guard refuse the invocation.
3. Observe the piped command's own status is never read, so there is nothing to mis-read.
4. Run the same two commands as two separate invocations and observe both are allowed, which is the positive control.
5. Observe the guard's own advice text recommends the redirect half of the refused block.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a pipeline whose own exit status is never read then the guard is silent even when the same invocation reads a status elsewhere - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_pipe_status_guard.py -k unrelated_status -q`
- Given a pipeline whose own status is read then the guard still refuses, so the five fire conditions are unchanged

## Context

This is the residue of `basicly-t10ipy`, and it is the larger finding behind it.

Record `basicly-vkh0.30` holds sequences 1 to 8 and 10 to 34. **No commit in this repository's history
ever contained a line at sequence 9**, probed with sequences 8 and 10 as the positive control - both are
found together in one commit. The writer assigns max plus one, so the line was written and lost **before
it was committed**. `t10ipy` fixed the classification of the symptom and deliberately did not touch this.

The question is durability, and it is open: does the append path fsync, and is a partial batch possible?
An append only log with no undelete cannot repair a lost event, so the only useful outcome is preventing
the next one. Which process dropped the line is not recoverable and no claim about it should be invented.

3. Search all history for a line at that sequence and observe none, using sequences 8 and 10 as the positive control.
4. Read the append path and establish whether it flushes and fsyncs before returning.
5. Establish whether a multi event append can partially complete.

- Given the append path then it either fsyncs before reporting success or its failure mode is documented and bounded - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_kit_tracker_events.py -k durable -q`

## Context

Observed on `basicly-gvlpxm` on 2026-08-20, and it is why that lane could not be closed by
advancing it.

The lane sat at phase `validate` with `validate-as-consumer` failed and rework 1 of 2. Its worktree
still held `.basicly/usage/repair-brief.json`, and that brief names the defect *recording the post
regeneration branch head*. **That defect was fixed and landed hours earlier** by a hand repair in the
same worktree, which became `merge.MergeResult.landed_head`. The brief has `findings: []` and
`evidence: []`; it carries only the two clipped reviews.

So `_repair_in_place` would have found the brief and **dispatched a full metered repair for work that is
done**. Nothing invalidates a brief when its defect is closed by another route - not the landing that
carried the fix, not the gate, and not the brief's own reader.

**The second half is the wedge, and it is why this is not merely wasteful.** A repair that finds nothing
to do commits nothing, so the branch carries nothing base does not hold, so the next advance takes the
same branch again. If the brief is consumed on read the following advance falls through to `_rework` and
charges the last slot for a round with nothing wrong in it. Either way the record cannot leave `validate`,
and its work is already in main and independently green.

I predicted the fall-through and was wrong: I assumed the brief had been consumed by the hand repair. It
had not. **Probe for the brief file rather than reasoning about whether it was taken.**

Related and visible in the same artifact: the reviews in this brief are clipped with a leading
`(earlier output cut)`, so the defect statement is what the clip dropped. That is `basicly-jr0l.74`,
still live.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Take a record at phase validate whose gate failed and whose worktree holds a repair brief.
2. Fix the named defect by any route other than a briefed repair - a hand fix, or a sibling lane - and land it.
3. Observe the brief file is still present and still names the fixed defect.
4. Run `basicly loop advance <id>` and observe it dispatch a repair rather than refuse the stale brief.
5. Observe the repair has nothing to commit, so the branch carries nothing unlanded and the next advance reaches the same state.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Given a repair brief whose named defect is already landed when the lane advances then the brief is refused as stale rather than dispatched - check: `uv run pytest tests/test_repair_brief.py -k stale -q`
- Given a repair that commits nothing when the advance completes then the lane is blocked naming that fact rather than charging rework or re-dispatching the same brief
- Given a brief whose defect is still open then it is dispatched unchanged

## Scope

- `src/basicly/repair_brief.py`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_repair_brief.py`

## Working Set

- `src/basicly/repair_brief.py`
- `src/basicly/loop.py`
- `tests/test_repair_brief.py`

## Demonstration

`uv run pytest -q`
payload.title: a repair brief outlives the defect it names so a lane is driven to repair work already landed

payload.text:
[closed 2026-08-20 with its true state, because no path through the loop could close it]

This record's work is IN MAIN and independently verified. The repair that closed its named defect is
`merge.MergeResult.landed_head`, landed through this worktree and then carried forward by the
rebases of later lanes. Main at c76f3692 reports `basicly verify --mode full` PASS across 31 checks
and 4466 tests.

Its loop state is stale, not failing. `loop status` reports phase validate, `validate-as-consumer`
failed, rework 1 of 2. That gate record dates from 2026-08-19 and was never re-recorded, because the
validator that ran on 2026-08-20 executed, cost 506272 tokens, and wrote no gate event at all - which
is `basicly-xd79u3`, now fixed. The fix does not retro-record this record's gate.

Why I did not advance it, having checked rather than assumed. The branch is an ancestor of main and
carries nothing unlanded, so `_repair_from_validate` takes `_worktree_landed` to `_repair_in_place`.
The worktree still holds `.basicly/usage/repair-brief.json`, and that brief names the defect
*recording the post regeneration branch head* - the one already fixed. So advancing would dispatch a
full metered repair for finished work, which commits nothing, which leaves the branch with nothing
unlanded, which returns the lane to this same state. Filed as `basicly-59fkfu`.

I predicted the brief had been consumed and would fall through to `_rework`. That was wrong: the file
is present. Probing for it is what corrected me.

So this is closed on the evidence rather than through the gate, and the gate's inability to close it
is recorded as a defect instead of being worked around silently. The worktree is removed.

[frequency measured 2026-08-20, and it raises this from a nuisance to a blocker]

Three false positives in one session, all the same shape, all on a compound invocation where the
`$?` and the pipeline belong to different commands:

1. `uv run ... docs_claims.py --fix ... && ... check_docs_citations.py ...`
2. `<gate> > out 2>&1; echo $?` followed by `grep FAIL out | tail -3`
3. `sed -n '...' FILE | head -20` followed by an unrelated `npx markdownlint ...; echo $?`

Only the first was a true positive. Cases 2 and 3 pipe into a filter whose status is never read, and
case 2 is verbatim the pattern the guard's own advice text recommends: redirect the gate, then read
the summary.

So the operator-facing cost is not one refusal, it is a refusal on most multi-step blocks - which is
the shape a careful operator writes, because the alternative is more round trips. Three refusals in
one session against one true positive is the ratio that trains a bypass, and this repository has
already paid for that once with `worktree cleanup` offering `--force` on every correct landing.

The narrow fix is to pair a status read with the pipeline it reads, not with the invocation. A
`;`-separated block is several commands and the guard currently treats it as one.
